Hanni and Hyein were in the living room when Solar returned from Thursday practice, the day after the girls tried on their costumes. The only thing she'd really had to worry about that day was her practice, since Thursdays were her easy day of the week. Still, there was something evident laying on her shoulders as she entered the living room to see her friends lounging there, beneath the same blanket with a bowl of popcorn between them. Hyein looked up the moment the front door had opened, eyes moving over Solar's practice bag and flushed cheeks, presumably from her walk home with Minji, a quiet tradition that had begun and no one else questioned.

\"How was practice?\"

\"Painful,\" the girl dramatically returns.

\"Sounds like character building,\" Hanni offers.

Solar leaned against the doorframe with her arms crossed, informing, \"Minji's coming at seven thirty tomorrow.\"

\"Perfect,\" Hyein clapped her hands together, \"I'm doing makeup!\"

\"That's fine with me,\" Solar shrugs, \"but Minji might be a different story.\"

\"Well, good thing I'm not asking.\"

Solar chuckled, pushing away from the doorframe before turning towards the stairs, too tired to have much more of a conversation, calling behind her, \"goodnight, guys.\"

\"Goodnight, Sol!\" the two called back in unison.

They waited until the sound of her bedroom door closing upstairs echoed faintly. Before them, the television continued to play, its light moving silently over the living room walls. Hyein reached beneath the blanket for her phone, opening the note she'd began that morning.

Beneath the list of Mark gestures, she typed a final line.

FRIDAY - ASK HAECHAN

Hanni was leaning over her shoulder, watching her thumbs fly across the screen, the popcorn forgotten in her lap.

\"That's all,\" she reminds her friend.

Though, neither of them sounded convinced.

But they knew it had to happen, because something was off with Mark Lee.

And they were going to get to the bottom of it.

51: the decision

As promised, Minji arrived at Alpha Phi at exactly 7:30, carrying her camera bag, a smaller duffel, and the expression of someone who’d spent the entire walk preparing herself for the wrath of Hyein. The front door had barely opened before Hyein appeared in the entryway, wearing a bright blue top, half of her makeup finished and one sock missing.

“On time!” She cheers, reaching out to take Minji’s bag from her with a beaming smile.

“I’m never late,” Minji affirms, stepping inside the house and following Hyein towards the stairs.

The two had only made it halfway up the steps when Hanni appeared from the hallway, a makeup brush in one hand and jewelry in the other. “Oh,” she cries at the sight, “welcome, Minji!”

Minji returned the warm greeting, following the two girls towards the second floor bathroom, which had been claimed in the name of Halloween. Makeup covered the counter, curling irons occupied both outlets, and four costume bags hung from the shower curtain rod because Hyein had decided the steam would release any wrinkles. A speaker played softly from the windowsill, mostly drowned out by Hyein talking over it.

And there sat Solar Lee on the closed toilet lid, where Hanni casually went back to working a small brush across her eyelid. Her orange satin top was already on, hanging loosely against her shoulders, but tight in the places that mattered, paired with the short green skirt she’d spent the previous night arguing about. The small translucent wings waited besides her on the floor, their gold straps carefully repaired.

Even with only portions of her makeup done, she was, in all honesty, entirely astonishing.

“Don’t move,” Hanni was lecturing Solar, who had attempted to turn to Minji to greet her before Hanni had gripped the side of her chin to turn her head back towards her.

“Gee, this seems serious,” Minji observes, leaning against the doorway.

“Don’t look so ecstatic,” Solar remarked.

“Come sit,” Hyein was motioning to the counter, where she had been focusing on clearing space for Minji to come sit, “your turn!”

Immediately, Minji wrinkled her nose, “I can do my own.”

“I’m sure you can,” the sassy girl nodded in agreeance, “but I’m doing it tonight.”

“And if I say no?”

Hyein sent her an unimpressed glare, holding up the makeup brush and pointing it to the counter.

Solar who had watched the interaction, trying not to seem like she was staring, called out dully, “might as well accept it, Ji.”

Knowing she was right, Minji exhaled, placing her bags beside the bathtub and reluctantly climbing to sit on the edge of the counter. A squeal of success left Hyein’s lips as she turned to inspect her face from several angles, leaning forward, brows furrowing in concentration.

“Nothing crazy,“ Minji warns, cautiously watching the brush hover in front of her face.

“I know, I know,” Hyein muttered, “I get it, chillax.”

“I mean it,” Minji continued anyway, sternly, “no glitter.”

“I heard you.”

“Right, like you ever hear anyone.”

“I hear criticism and choose to ignore her,” she brightly retorts, beginning to paint the girl’s face before she could say another word.

Meanwhile, Hanni smiled to herself while she returned to Solar’s eyeliner. Her hand was steady, but Solar could feel the girl looking at her through the mirror every few seconds, checking something beyond the symmetry of her makeup. It wasn’t only Hanni, though, she also could feel Hyein doing it, too.

The two had been overattentive since Wednesday, their happiness always arriving half a second before anything happened, like they’d rehearsed it. Solar had considered asking what they were hiding again, but she’d already spent the week trying to force answers out of people who had no intention of giving them.

After all, she thought, if they had something to tell her, they would, and she trusted that.

“Okay, ta-da!” Hanni exclaims proudly, standing up to assess her work.

Solar nervously turned towards the mirror, daring to meet her own eyes in the mirror. Gold shimmer sat at the corners of her eyes, catching beneath the bathroom light whenever she moved. Hanni had kept everything else warm, soft around the edges, except for the eyeliner that made her eyes look ten times sharper than she felt.

For once, looking at herself didn’t make her think about which photograph would appear online later.

She got lost, for a moment, staring at herself, so lost that she didn’t fully process Minji sitting right there on the counter next to her. The thing was, she was already watching Solar, a small smile on her lips that she didn’t try to hide when their eyes met.

“Wow,” she hums, “almost respectable, Sol.”

Solar narrowed her eyes at her, shaking her head, “almost, huh?”

“The wings are really hurting your credibility.”

“They aren’t even on yet!”

“Exactly, still time to make the right decision.”

Hyein gasped as she finished one side of Minji’s eyeliner, “don’t corrupt her.”

“Too late,” Minji deadpanned.

Solar chuckled despite herself, lifting a hand to touch the gold beneath her eye before Hanni slapped it away gently, “don’t smudge!”

“My bad,” Solar pouted, dropping her hand back down to her side.

Her friend then turned, reaching for the wings that were on the floor and walking to stand behind Solar, guiding the thin straps over her shoulders. Solar geld her hair out of the way while she fastened the clasp, the transparent material settling just below her shoulder blades.

Eager to see the results, Hyein had stepped back from doing Minji’s eye makeup to review Solar. Her eyes lit up in excitement, “Oh my God… you’re literally Stella!”

“Please don’t start calling me that.”

“I won’t, Stella.”

“I’ll change right now.”

In fits of giggles, Hyein lunged forward to wrap both of her arms around Solar’s waist before she could do such a thing, pressing the side of her face against the satin top. The wings bent underneath one of her arms, causing Hanni to cry out in horror, “Hyein, careful!”

Hyein stepped away with a sigh, “she just looks… so good… I’m so proud,” she wiped a fake tear off of her face.

“Thanks,” Solar monotones, “don’t do that again, though.”

Minji watched from the counter, one eye covered in blue eyeshadow, the other still bare, looking far too entertained by the struggle of friendship.

And by 8:15, the four were dressed.

Hyein had committed entirely to Bloom, red hair extensions clipped beneath her own brown locks, blue glitter dusted across her collarbones. Hanni’s Flora costume was soft pink and green, the translucent wings resting behind her shoulders like petals. And Minji, Minji had gotten her cargo pants indeed, paired with the blue top, silver cuffs, and smaller wings Hyein had eventually accepted as a compromise.

The four squished together in the bathroom, in front of the not quite loud enough mirror. Minji had set her camera at an angle, everyone stepping back far enough to get a proper photo, setting the timer. They all scurried to get into a proper position, Minji sliding into the space beside Solar. Hyein threw one arm around Hanni, the other around Minji, pulling everyone together so aggressively that the first photograph caught Solar mid-laugh and Hanni desperately trying to rescue her wings.

Of course, they took several. The first was because one of them kept blinking, someone kept making a weird face, and then Hyein disagreed with the basic concept of enough.

By the time Minji checked the results, Solar’s cheeks hurt from smiling. She leaned over the camera with Hanni pressed against one side and Hyein practically climbing onto her back from the other.

In the best picture, the four were crowded together, bright and ridiculous. It looked… happy, perhaps the happiest she had been in the last week.

-

The walk to Sigma Chi required coats over costumes, which Hyein viewed as a personal attack. She’d complained for the first block about how nobody could appreciate the full concept, even though there were students in costumes moving in every direction, all of them making the same sacrifice to the Syracuse cold.

Solar kept her hands in the pockets of her coat, the folded wings knocking lightly against her back with each step. Hanni walked beside her, close enough that their sleeves brushed, while Hyein and Minji debated whether Musa would actually ever wear cargo pants if the show had been made by people with taste.

As always, the boom of the music reached them before the mansion did.

It sat low beneath the night, bass traveling through the sidewalk, growing louder as they turned the final corner. Sigma Chi appeared at the top of the street, every front window lit orange and purple, fake cobwebs stretched across the porch railings. A line curled down the walkway, full of students in costumes already shivering or drunk enough not to care.

Hyein gripped Solar’s arm in excitement, “this is gonna be so fun!”

They continued up the sidewalk, the front sidewalk, as Solar decided that she no longer cared to have the escort from the side gate, and Hyein and Hanni had accepted this decision with bright joy that surprised her.

Until finally, they reached the end of the line. Students turned, noticing the group of girls, noticing Solar, and naturally, they began to step back.

“No way,” Hanni muttered, “we’re like… celebrities.”

“VIP coming through!” Hyein had yelled out, throwing her arms in the air as the four pushed their way through the open line.

Sigma Chi was as chaotic as anyone would expect it to be on Halloween, which was, the party of the year that everyone longed to be invited to. Jeno had seen them at the gate, in a costume that was more like a single pair of pants and nothing, and had bowed dramatically as he remarked, “hello, beautiful ladies,” before his eyes landed on Solar, “and Solar Lee, as fine as ever, I see, a pleasure.”

Though, Solar didn’t really find him as annoying as she once did, she just pushed past him into the yard, sending him a single wave, “uhuh, thanks Jeno.”

It took more effort than she’d hoped to reach the front porch. Her friends were close behind her, and they all stopped to take in the scene once they were standing there at the front door, only to see Renjun standing there. Hyein saw him first, nearly jumping for joy as she offered out, “Renjun… what are you?”

The boy was smoking a cigarette, blowing the smoke into the air as he boredly looked to the four of them, “tired.”

“No, like, for real.”

“A vampire,” he sasses, like she should’ve noticed.

Hyein was still perplexed, “you look like you always do, but with a cape.”

“That’s why I chose it.”

His eyes moved toward Hanni, something knowing passing through them before he glanced to Solar, “shocked to see you here.”

“In the flesh,” Solar deadpanned, “I need a drink.”

“There’s plenty of those here,” he returns blankly, “Chenle’s in the kitchen… something about how he refuses to stand near the living room until the fog machine is confiscated.”

“See?” Hyein nods, proud, “honorary civilian.”

Renjun blew another cloud of smoke into the air, leaning against one of the wooden poles and grumbling, “no clue what that means.”

The four went inside them, the house swallowing them immediately. Bodies filled the living room beneath the orange lights, fake cobwebs hanging from the ceiling, catching in people’s hair as they moved. Someone had covered the framed chapter photographs with cheap bloody handprints. The dog machine Renjun mentioned sat near the speakers, sending a low white cloud across people’s ankles while a boy in a skeleton costume repeatedly tripped over it.

The air smelled like alcohol, sweat, artificial smoke, and something sweet enough to make Solar’s teeth hurt.

Hanni reached back for her hand before the crowd could separate them, and Solar caught Hyein’s wrist with her free one, while Minji followed closely behind, camera held against her chest to protect it from the bodies pressing around them.

They made it to the kitchen as a unit, pushing past the fewer people there, most of them making small talk or mixing drinks.

And then there was Chenle, who stood beside one of the islands wearing a long dark coat and a pair of round glasses, his hair combed neatly away from his face. He looked up from the soda he was pouring, noticing the sudden presence of his friends-but-not-friends, eyes looking across the four a few times as he seemed to process.

Hyein was waiting for him to say something, “well?”

But the boy was oblivious, or so he pretended, “well what?”

“Uh, our costumes,” she deadpans, half annoyed, “obviously.”

“I see them.”

“Okay, thoughts?!”

Chenle pursed his lips, looking at each girl individually, as though accuracy required a full inspection. “Solar’s wing to body ratio’s wrong,” he finally announces.

Solar had grinned, “thanks, Le.”

“Not a compliment!” Hyein snaps grumpily.

“I’m guessing the original design had a bigger wingspan, judging from the rest of you,” he observes, sipping his soda as he continues to assess the costumes, “those are maybe, what, point eight?”

“Yes, because she threatened not to come!”

“Hm, understandable engineering compromise,” he nods then, “accurate colors, though.”

Hyein accepted such as victory, clapping once before she spun on her heel to survey the rest of the party, or at least, what she could see of it. She stepped forward to walk to the doorway, eyes scanning across the living room, moving too deliberately.

Hanni followed her to do the same, looking carefully over her shoulder.

Solar watched her two friends, the same suspicion from Wednesday scratching faintly at the back of her mind. They were clearly looking for something they had yet to find.

Though, before she could properly question whatever they’d been up to, someone touched her elbow. She jumped at first, turning to see Mark Lee standing there. Only then, did she notice his costume, which took a second to register.

Mark was wearing dark framed glasses, a white button down left open enough to reveal the blue Superman symbol beneath it, a loosened tie hanging around his neck. His hair was combed, gently gelled to perfection, a look that suited him well, though the crowd had already begun undoing the effort.

For once, he didn’t greet her immediately. His mouth opened, then closed, eyes moving over the orange satin, gold at her waist, the glitter beneath her eyes, before he seemed to remember himself once his eyes reached the wings.

“Wow,” he clears his throat.

Solar rose a brow, “message received, Mark.”

“No, sorry I just…” he pushed the glasses higher on his nose, cheeks turning a light shade of pink, “you just… you look really good, Sol.”

“Thanks,” she tugged lightly on the front of his shirt in a playful manner, “Clark Kent?”

“Yeah,” Mark glanced down at himself, shy, like he’d forgotten about his own costume,”Jaemin said it was easy.”

“The costume or the comparison?”

“Hey, I could be Superman,” he defends in fake offense.

“Whatever you say, Mark.”

He laughed, the sound warm and unguarded beneath the music. For a split moment, the week fell away from his face, he looked like the boy she’d met on the first day, awkward, easy, visibly pleased that she’d chosen to stand in the same room as him.

“Oh, I got you something,” he recalls, turning to look for something on the counter.

Hyein and Hanni were standing very still at the doorway, watching the exchange. Minji was busy in the corner next to the breakfast table, chatting with Chenle, though even her eyes lingered over every few seconds, mind still fresh with the recent words Solar had told her.

Mark either didn’t notice or pretended not to, reaching around the edge of the island and lifted a clear cup filled with something bright pink. Her eyes cautiously glance down at it.

“Pink Punch,” he explains, holding it closer to her, “mostly… Jeno mixed it, so I remade it because his version probably counted as attempted murder.”

A chuckle left her lips, and she shrugged off the thoughts, taking the cup from his hands, “so thoughtful of you.”

Though the worst felt stranger than she wanted them to on her tongue.

Mark’s smile faltered by the smallest degree, “I just remembered, favorite flavor, right?”

“Mhm,” she hummed, lifting the drink to her lips, letting the familiar artificial sweetness settle over the alcohol, “thanks.”

With that, the smile returned to his lips as if it never left, individually explainable.

Across the island, Hanni reached for Hyein’s hand, quietly grabbing her attention to exchange a look of discomfort with her, like she wanted to check if the same thing was going through her head. Minji caught it too, pursing her lips in her own contemplation as she nodded her head along to whatever Chenle was talking about.

But Solar looked rather content standing there with Mark. For then, they decided to let it be.

So, for the next half hour, the party managed to be exactly what Hanni and Hyein had promised. Hyein dragged them into a loose circle, near the edge of the living room, where there was enough space to dance without getting trampled. Minji took photographs between songs, lowering the camera whenever Solar shook her head. Hanni laughed every time the wings bumped together, repeatedly stopping to untangle herself from the fake cobwebs hanging behind them.

Renjun remained near the kitchen doorway, cape folded around himself, watching the party with the disappointment of a vampire who’d lived long enough to know better. Chenle appeared beside him occasionally, offering precise updates on which decoration was most likely to cause an injury.

Solar finished the Pink Punch flavored alcohol without thinking twice about it. Mark brought her another, but asked first, of course. By the time the second cup was half empty, the warmth had reached her limbs. The music stopped striking her as noise and began moving through her properly, bass settling beneath her ribs, making the entire room feel several degrees softer around the edges.

It felt easy, simple. She stopped caring so much about all of the things that once crowded her, about Danielle, about the reality of her being behind the account, about her motives, the way she kept getting under her skin and how worried she really was about how true it might all be.

Right then, she felt like a college girl dancing with her friends, laughing when Hyein attempted to reenact something from Winx Club and nearly took out a girl dressed as an angel with one wing. Minji caught the aftermath on camera, Hanni bent forward laughing, and Solar let herself be pulled into the center of it.

Everything was fine, until her body noticed him.

It happened the way it always did, an awareness beginning somewhere beneath conscious thought, something along her spine turning before her eyes understood why. She looked past Hanni’s shoulder, through the moving bodies and fog, toward the far side of the room.

Haechan stood beside the hallway leading towards the stairs, wearing black, which wasn’t unusual enough to count as a costume, a button down with the sleeves pushed to his forearms, collar open at the throat. Someone had placed two small red horns in his hair, the ridiculousness should’ve made him look less like himself.

It didn’t.

His skin was still too pale beneath the orange lights, dark hair messy around the horns, one hand holding a cup low against his thigh while the other remained in his pocket. A girl dressed as a nurse was speaking beside him, leaning close enough that her shoulder touched his arm.

Though, he couldn’t seem to care any less about the random girl’s presence, because his eyes were on Solar.

The room seemed to fold inward on itself. There was no easy mockery in his face, no half lidded performance or private joke waiting at the corner of his mouth. He was entirely still, eyes moving once over her costume before returning to her face, and something hot and painful turned beneath Solar’s ribs.

Next to him, the girl said something else, touching his wrist and running her fingers up his forearm, slowly, before he’d pulled it away without looking at her. It was a slight motion, one he didn’t put much into, but the girl seemed hurt as she gawked in response. Still, she didn’t give up, they never did.

Clearing her throat, Solar forced herself to look away, turning forward again. Though, it wasn’t before Hanni saw where she was looking. Her smile faded, concern beginning to take it’s place, but before she could say anything, Mark appeared again from the shadows, having returned from a frat incident that he apparently had to go handle.

“Hey,” he offers, adjusting the glasses that’d began to slide down his nose, “Having fun?”

Shrugging, the brunette takes another drink, “something like that.”

He nodded, lips forming a straight line, rocking once on his heels, “chill…” he trailed off, glancing toward the center of the living room before looking back to the girl before him, “so… I do recall being promised a dance.”

“I said promise was a strong word,” she corrects.

“Then you agreed.”

“Under duress.”

Mark pressed a hand against his chest, “you wound me, Sol.”

The song changed, something slower in the rhythm but heavier underneath, causing the crowd to press closer toward the center of the room. Mark held out one hand, the gesture playful enough to give her room to refuse.

And somewhere far behind them all, past the crowds of sweaty bodies, was Haechan, remaining beside the hallway.

Solar’s eyes dared to look back down at Mark’s open palm. He’d shown up, she recalled to herself, he always showed up, with coffee, food, in the front row of her tournament, standing there every time her life turned for the worst. Whether there was any truth behind Danielle’s words, at least Mark was present enough to perform.

Solar was tired of missing someone who kept choosing absence.

With a deep sigh, she places her hand in Mark’s, “one dance.”

Mark led her toward the others, not pulling hard, his fingers loose around hers. Hyein made a loud sound, loud enough to carry over the music, though the drunken students around them didn’t seem to mind, while Hanni caught her arm, dragging her back before she could turn the moment into an announcement.

The dorky boy stopped once he’d found a spot with enough space, turning to face Solar with an uncertainty that didn’t match how confident he’d been asking, one hand hovering near her waist without landing, “okay?” he asked, raising one brow.

She didn’t really look at him, she just nodded, pondering to herself the way he waited, the patience of it, the carefulness of someone like Mark Lee, that almost felt too good to be true.

His palm settled against the side of her waist, warm through the thin orange fabric. Solar rested one hand on his shoulder, still holding her drink in the other, allowing the music to tell them what to do.

At first, Mark was exactly the dancer she expected him to be, careful to the point of awkwardness, moving as though there were instructions he had yet to be given. Solar burst into fits of laughter as he continuously nearly stepped on her shoe, “you’re such a liar!”

There was a smile playing on his lips as he kept trying, despite her insult, “I’m warming up, relax.”

“Sure,” she snorts, “believable.”

“I’m serious, just give me a second!”

The glasses slipped down his nose again, and instinctively, her finger reached up to push them back into place, causing him to laugh, the sound loosening something between them.

Easy, the word kept appearing in her thoughts before she could stop it, his hand shifting more securely around her waist.

Danielle was wrong, she thought then, entirely wrong, she had to be. There was no illness in those irises looking down at her, she couldn’t stand to face such a thing.

The alcohol made it easier to stop thinking about each individual choice she was making. So, she let herself move closer, let the beat find her hips, and Mark followed once she realized she was allowing him to, his other hand finding her side, still careful, still waiting for resistance.

The room blurred into orange light and moving bodies. Solar turned within his hands, her back briefly against his chest, causing his breath to catch near her ear from surprise. She could feel his smile, genuine and disbelieving, and for a few seconds, it was enough.

Though her eyes couldn’t help but trail back to that hallway.

Pushing it away again, she turned back to Mark, placing both of her arms around his neck, the empty cup still caught between two of her fingers. He was alarmed at the action, again, in his typical dorky manner, but didn’t make any effort to push her away. His eyes lingered down to her lips, biting down on his own gently, before they found their way back to her eyes.

He was contemplating, curious what she was doing, hopeful that she’d do what he wanted her to. He looked down at her like he was searching her face for something as she inched closer and closer to his face.

And whatever he found made his hands tighten at her waist.

Haechan, on the other hand, had heard the room change the moment Solar Lee entered it.

He hadn’t needed to look toward the front door, the party had shifted around her in small, measurable ways, just like the line. The way voices lifted, whispers floated, the sight of Renjun appearing looking slightly less bored, a high burst of Hyein arriving over everything else, somehow, even in a room as loud as this one. He hadn’t needed to, but he looked anyway.

Solar entered Sigma Chi dressed in orange and gold, wings tucked awkwardly beneath her coat, Minji beside her with a camera across her chest. Hanni and Hyein held onto her from either side as they moved through the crowd, as if the three of them had built a formation around something worth protecting.

He thought, then, that she looked happy, carefree, the way she was supposed to be. But registering such a thing seemed to be his first mistake.

The second was allowing himself to continue watching her when she’d entered the room to dance with her friends, until Mark Lee walked over to her with his hand in hers like it belonged there.

His hands were at her waist now, Solar’s arms around his neck, her face tipping towards him while the room continued to move like nothing was awry.

Vomit was coming up his throat before he could stop it, causing him to aggressively clear it, shaking his head so hard that his dark hair fell into his eyes. One of the girls next to him looked to him in concern, before she continued her conversation with one of the others that was also lingering around, hoping he was going to magically change his mind and want to talk to any of them.

All he did was take another drink, hoping to suppress it enough that he wouldn’t think about it anymore. But the alcohol had stopped changing anything an hour ago. Instead, his body simply felt slightly delayed, the music arriving a half second after the bass struck, the part of his mind he’d been trying to quiet remaining painfully exact. It counted every place Mark touched her, it noticed when Solar moved closer first, it understood that her eyes looked directly at him before doing it.

One of the girls touched his arm again, leaning forward over his ear, huskily whispering, “do you wanna go upstairs?”

He looked down at her for the first time, taking in the scandalous nurse costume, white dress, red crosses, fake blood at the corner of her mouth. He had no idea what her name was. She’d told him, presumably, but the information hadn’t found anywhere to stay.

“Mm,” he pretends to ponder, “I’m off duty today.” There had once been a time where he called girls princess, sweetheart, some ridiculous pet name that he didn’t reserve for the likes of anyone. Haechan was a sweet talker, he knew how to talk himself out of anything, how to get into anyone’s head before they realized he’d done so.

But doing things like that didn’t bring him the satisfaction they once had, not anymore.

She blinked in confusion, shocked, “Off duty?” she chuckled in disbelief, “On Halloween, Haechan? That’s the worst lie you’ve ever told.”

His eyes narrowed down at her, unimpressed and unbothered, “Nurse just isn’t doing it for me, better luck next year.” He pulled his arm from beneath her hand, finishing his drink with a single tilt of his head. The cup crumpled slightly in his grip before he noticed, the plastic cracking beneath his fingers.

The girl gawked in hurt from his words, her eyes staring up at his face that had already looked away from her, before they followed where his gaze was. Shaking her head, she turned to her friend, that was also confused from witnessing whatever just happened, muttering under her breathe, “it really is true, that’s fucking nuts.”

Across the room, Solar was laughing at something Mark said.

Haechan didn’t care to listen to the girls gossip about him and how disappointed they were that he didn’t want to sleep with them, nor did he want to continue to watch Mark pretend he was so infatuated with Solar Lee. So, he turned towards the stairs, the pills in his pocket suddenly calling his name like never before. He could feel them through the fabric when he put his hands in the pocket of his jeans, the feeling enough to take the room down several degrees, enough to make Mark’s hands simply hands and Solar’s laugh nothing more than a frequency buried in the mix.

He was only a couple of steps up when a pair of blue wings flew into his face, and a girl stood firmly in front of him with her arms crossed over her chest, having had literally jumped to beat him.

And as if that wasn’t enough, a pink one appeared next to her, a bit slower but present nonetheless, the wings catching underneath the dim orange lighting.

Naturally, he was entirely unfazed, face emotionless as he stared at the two of them, “if you’re looking for your friend, she’s quite occupied.”

“We’re looking for you, actually,” Hyein announces firmly.

His eyes returned to the living room before he could stop them, where Mark had turned Solar again, one hand remaining at her hip. She was grinding against him sensually, her head tilted back to lay on his shoulder. He was loving every second of it, in that calculated way of his, and it made him want to tear the entire house apart. He thought he’d won, and maybe he had, in his own sick and twisted way.

“Seems irrelevant,” he deadpanned finally, moving to step beside them to continue on his way, but Hyein had hurriedly stepped in front of him again, on the fifth step now.

Hanni followed, on the step next to him, her approach much gentler, “can we just have a moment, please?”

The boy didn’t care to consider, “No.”

Hyein had frowned, clearly offended by the quick efficiency of his answer, “you don’t even know what we want to talk about.”

“Pretty sure I know enough,” he exhaled, as if the conversation was ruining his day, “if you don’t mind, I’d prefer to be elsewhere.”

“That sucks,” Hyein retorts, matching his energy, “one conversation won’t kill you.”

“Wouldn’t be so sure,” he monotoned.

Hanni exchanged a glance with Hyein, who was looking at her as if she was asking for her to do something, like wave a magic wand that suddenly made him nicer. Pursing her lips, Hanni turns back to the boy with soft eyes, “It’ll be quick, Haechan, can we go somewhere quieter?”

“I’ve heard this one before,” he mutters, “No, I’m busy.”

“Doing what?” Hyein snapped, looking pointedly behind them up the stairs, “Running again?”

The words slapped him hard across the face. Something moved in his jaw that he didn’t acknowledge. But Hyein saw it, and she knew what that meant. “We can talk here,” she continues, “I’m very good at being loud.”

“Painfully aware,” Haechan breathes, glancing toward the living room again. A few people nearby had already began staring at the three of them standing there at the middle of the staircase, attention sharpening with the possibility of public drama.

So, with a short exhale through his nose, he turned back to the girls, before continuing up the steps and calling behind him before they could attempt to block his path again, “two minutes.”

Hyein desperately wanted to jump for victory, but they didn’t have the time. Instead, she grabbed Hanni’s hand, squeezing it for support as they hurriedly followed him up the steps of Sigma Chi.

Upstairs was pleasantly slightly quieter, the carpet soft under their heels as they walked down it, into the hallway that lead to the upstairs lounge room, doors lining the walls that lead into the various bedrooms the boys occupied. It was evident people had been up here, despite how upstairs was typically off limits, with a few bottles scattered here and there. The bass continued to boom through the floorboards, almost shaking them, though it wasn’t any louder than the beating of their hearts as Haechan stopped beside what they could only guess was his bedroom, leaning against the wall and chunking his plastic cup to the floor before shoving his hands in his pockets.

It was quiet for a second. Hanni stood several feet away, fingers twisting together at her waist. Hyein positioned herself between Haechan and the staircase, as if she was fearful he would make a run for it, back out into the chaos before they’d gotten any real answers.

“Okay,” Hanni cleared her throat, “so, can you tell us what happened with Solar?”

It was a poor attempt at a first question, maybe, because Haechan didn’t spare them a single look, “ask her.”

“We’re asking you,” Hyein affirms sternly.

“Ask a better question.”

Hyein looked to Hanni in awe, “fuck, he is annoying.”

“You’re the ones who approached me,” Haechan snorts, “in case you forgot.”

“Well, have you considered the fact you’re kind of a…”

Hanni reached for Hyein’s forearm, squeezing hard enough that she quieted her before she could finish. “Look, Solar thought that whatever you had going on was… real,” she explains gently, “then you… stopped speaking to her.”

His eyes wandered towards the ceiling, as if the words didn’t deserve a response for him, as if he didn’t have one to give.

“Mark told her that’s what you do,” Hanni continues anyway, “that none of it meant anything.”

“And?” he sighs.

“And she’s hurt, asshole!” Hyein exasperatedly exclaims.

“Hyein,” Hanni urged, slapping her arm in disappoval.

“What?” she counters, stubbornly, motioning at the careless acting boy, “he knows!”

Haechan’s thumb ran over the texture of the pills in his pockets, “I don’t see the issue, sounds like Mark explained it.”

“The issue is we already asked Mark,” Hanni puzzles, “now we’re asking you.”

She held his gaze that fell back to her then. For the first time, the hallway seemed quieter than the party surrounding it beneath them.

Haechan’s hand stilled inside his pocket.

Hyein stepped forward, feeling a surge of justice and confidence within her. “You keep letting him explain things for you even when you know you don’t agree,” she depicts, “we’ve seen you two, come on, does Mark really know what’s going on?”

“And is he telling the truth?” Hanni adds.

Haechan’s eyes went from one of them to the other, before a flat laugh left his chest, scraping on the way out. He shook his head, his hair falling back in his face for the second time, “never thought I’d see the day two Alpha Phi girls lecture me,” he grumbles bitterly, “what, spent a week watching relationship videos?”

“No,” Hyein retorts, “we’ve spent a week watching our friend pretend she doesn’t care about you.”

“Hyein!” Hanni warns again, though it was too late to retrieve the sentence.

Something tightened beneath Haechan’s sternum, though his face remained empty. He just stared blankly ahead at the wall, “sounds like a bad judgment call on her part.”

“See?!” Hyein cries, throwing both of her hands in the air in a total I told you so manner, her wings shuddering behind her, “That’s exactly it, you say the meanest thing you can think of so everyone decides you’re horrible and leaves you alone.”

“I’ve never been so lucky as to be left alone,” he monotones in response, alluding to the constant presence of girls at his side, no matter what type of mood he was in, no matter what state of mind he was in, they always wanted one thing.

The girls exchanged another perplexed look.

“We’re not leaving until you talk,” Hanni decides.

“Gonna be a long night.”

The angelic girl sighed in response, watching him carefully. She wasn’t loud like Hyein, which made the steadiness in her expression harder to dismiss. “We don’t know you,” she admits, “you were right about that before you said it, we don’t know what happened with Mark, or Jaehyun, or why you decided to ghost her…” She trails off, taking in the way his eyes sharpened at the sound of Jaehyun’s name. “But we know Solar,” she attests, “and we saw both of you before everything changed, the way she was always so much… brighter.”

“Brighter,” he repeats dryly, “people typically look that way at parties, yes.”

But the girls weren’t paying attention to his attempts at pivoting, not anymore. “We saw you cross an entire room because she walked into it,” Hyein goes on, “and you ignoring every girl around you the second she showed up. She texted us from your room, defending you when nobody asked her to.”

His jaw shifted then. He remembered the messages arriving against her bare stomach, the way she’d tried to hide her phone, Hyein’s name flashing over the screen while her cheeks turned the lightest shade of crimson.

Before he could say anything, Hyein crossed her arms over her chest, “we know the difference, you know,” she affirms, “between the way Mark looks at her and the way you look at her.”

Suddenly, his throat felt dry, like he hadn’t drank anything in ages. “You don’t know what you’re looking at, it seems.”

“Maybe we don’t,” Hanni nods, “but she doesn’t look at anyone else the way she does you.”

The pills in his pockets felt sharper than ever, but he let them go.

Downstairs, the song changed, the bass briefly dropping before another beat took it’s place. Screams could be heard across the bodies, the party continuing at full speed without their presence.

Haechan looked down at his crushed cup on the floor, “she needs to work on that,” he muttered.

Hyein made a strangled sound of frustration, taking another step forward, like she was going to knock some sense into his head, before Hanni caught her wrist.

“Tell us, Haechan,” Hanni calls, “was it a game?”

The directness of her words drew his eyes back to her. She stood very still now, no longer twisting her fingers, pink wings casting a faint shadow behind her.

“We’re not asking if you’re a good person,” she breathes, “we aren’t asking whether everyone else is wrong about you, we’re asking if Solar was a game.”

A part of him told him to give them the answer Mark already had, that’s what I do, that’s who I am, this is my lifestyle.

It would’ve ended the conversation. Hyein would hate him loudly, Hanni would hate him quietly, and they’d return to Solar with the uncomplicated certainty people preferred. He could go back to his room, take what was in his pocket, and let Mark continue to tell his story first. The option was sitting there in front of him, as familiar as ever.

“No,” he monotones, though his voice was barely above a whisper.

Hyein’s entire posture changed, her eyes widening slightly, head snapping to look at Hanni. She wanted to squeal, scream, to make any kind of noise that would leave her, but she was evidently holding it back with all of her might. Hanni had exhaled, in return, like she had finally gotten the answer she knew all along, “okay, okay, we can work with that.”

“So why’d you let her think it was?” Hyein asked, unable to stop herself, “What, you just let Mark feed her this story and did nothing about it?”

Haechan’s eyes drifted again toward the far end of the hallway, “it was better that way.”

“For who?”

He didn’t answer, causing Hyein to scoff, “God, you and Jaehyun must get along great,” she complains, “you both decide what’s best for her without asking.”

The accuracy of the sentence irritated him more than the comparison. Still, he didn’t respond, he just pushed himself off of the wall finally, “finished?”

“No!” Hanni demands, and it was the firmest even Hyein had ever heard her sound. The boy had stopped before he’d started, about to have walked right into his room and closed the door to all of the noise he desperately wanted to tune out, feeling like he’d already lost a chunk of his pride that night.

“Talk to her,” Hanni pleads, “not through Mark, we know he’s not the genuine one here… you owe her an answer from you.”

Haechan looked towards his bedroom door. The possibility lingered, for a split second, before he shook his head, “she seems happy, no?”

Hyein rose a brow, “you’re jealous, aren’t you?!”

“Listen, if she doesn’t want to hear you first, let her speak. If she tells you to leave her alone, drop it,” Hanni advises, “just… don’t decide for her.”

He stared down at the short girl for a few seconds, “I’m not sure what you’re expecting out of this.”

“The truth,” Hyein hums, “if Syracuse has taught us anything, it’s that everything you hear about someone isn’t always reality.”

The boy before them, for once, almost laughed, the first time in a while.

“I think Solar would say something about a mask,” Hanni added, “she does like to talk about that Media class.”

He bit down on his bottom lip, feeling the need to ponder, “why are you two doing this?”

“Easy,” Hanni responded, “we’re helping our friend.”

“And you’re clearly too dumb to help yourself,” Hyein piped.

“Hyein!”

A flat sound left Haechan, a slight chuckle that he immediately deflated. He shook his head once, looking towards the staircase. Downstairs, Solar was no longer dancing with Mark, she was on the sidelines with Minji, though the dorky boy was still present right next to her, the way he had been all night. She was smiling, with Mark’s fingers drawing circles on her upper arms, though it didn’t quite reach her eyes.

“Alright,” he exhales.

Hyein’s mouth opened in triumph, though his eyes noticed immediately, “don’t.”

“My bad.”

Hanni, however, remained entirely serious, “if we help make space for this, you can’t disappear the second it becomes difficult, okay?”

“It was already difficult,” he deadpans.

“Then you can’t disappear when it becomes real,” she corrects, “better?”

“Not quite.”

Hanni must have seen something in his face, because her voice softened again, “don’t make her regret believing you.”

“That’s why you’re fixing it!” Hyein chimes, “Now go!”

The last thing he ever imagined for himself was this, being bossed around by two cheery Alpha Phi girls who had never planned to step foot into the likes of Sigma Chi, who never planned to be on the side of someone like the campus heart throb that was only ever known for doing bad things.

But, as they learned, the things you saw online weren’t always the truth. The truth, in fact, was often hidden underneath the captions, just like Solar would say.

And for the first time in weeks, Haechan made the decision to stay.

52: remember that

So, the blue and pink winged girls would deviously make their way back down the stairs of the fraternity house. It was half till midnight, meaning the party was heating up more than it had been thus far that night. Someone had brought a keg to the middle of the ‘dance floor,’ where there was a crowd of girls and rowdy boys cheering on Jeno, who was doing one with one hand holding himself up on it. Now that he’d finished his shift guarding the entrance, he was entirely in party mode, high off the molly he’d taken an hour before. Jaemin, who had been making his rounds around the house, was wearing perhaps the most sexualized cowboy Ken outfit the eye would ever see. He had nearly ten girls trailing behind him in a line as he stopped by each crowd of friends, tipping his white cowboy hat and fully taking his costume seriously, being the social chair everyone knew him as.

Hyein and Hanni were standing next to the dance floor when he had stopped at them, seeming to decide they were friendly now that he had spoken to them a couple of times. “Ladies,” he offers, almost in what seemed to be a painful attempt at a country accent, “I see you’ve taken your costumes quite seriously, is that custom?”

Though they had been on a mission, Hyein had beamed from his question. “Why, yes!” she exclaims,”By yours truly, actually, I am a fashion designer, after all.”

He rose a brow at that, as this was new information to him, “Really? I might have to commission you soon,” he tipped his hat again, eyes catching someone else across the room he aspired to speak to, “enjoy, madams.”

And the girls trailed behind him as he went.

The two girls exchanged glances, Hanni shaking her head in dismay as she tried to hold in any comment that may sound mean. “Wow,” she exhales, “he is… truly a character.”

“Least he’s not half naked doing a handstand on a keg,” Hyein shrugs, and they momentarily glance back over to Jeno, “plus, I might’ve just gotten my first real client,” she pipes in excitement, clapping her hands together, having to shout over the bass, “if you think about it, this is kind of like free advertising for me…”

She trails off in thought about this, before Hanni had snapped her fingers in her face, grabbing her forearm, “That’s lovely, but we’re on a mission right now, Hyein.”

“Right!” she cries, squealing again as she recounts what just happened, “Oh my God, he totally is in love with her,” she was yelling, as if anyone other than Hanni could hear, “isn’t it the most beautiful plot twist? It’s really giving me Chuck and Blair vibes.”

“Hyein,” Hanni turns, stopping her walking to look at the girl in disappointment, “do not compare those two things… that feels… that feels wrong.”

“Well, I think it’s cute,” Hyein snaps, “God forbid a little toxicity, makes for way better…”

Hanni had turned again to pinch her, causing the girl to cut herself off by screeching. “Shush, we don’t have time to make weird comments!” she urges, “We need to find Minji.”

“Okay, operation find Minji!” Hyein agrees, knowing that they probably were indeed on a timer. After all, the two had left a boy upstairs in Sigma Chi with red horns in his messy hair and something rather raw sitting behind his face. The entire fragile architecture of what they’d just accomplished depended heavily on what happened in the next hour, meaning the plan had to keep moving before any of them, especially Haechan, had time to think more about it.

Pushing through the crowds, the two girls stop in a small open space to turn in search for their beloved friend. The music continues to boom in their eardrums, drunk screaming happening every way they looked. Still, they couldn’t seem to find their friend, even though they’d hoped the bright glitter of the giant wings would stick out.

“You think she’ll be okay?” Hanni leans in to ask Hyein as they spin around, both looking different ways around the living area turned party floor. Hanni didn’t have to clarify what she meant to Hyein, they both knew it well.

The girl purses her lips for a moment, considering her question with genuinity. “Um…” she pauses, “she’s… Minji,” Hyein discerns, which was actually more of an answer than one would think, “Solar talked to her, I think… she’s strong, though. She just wants her to be happy.”

Hanni let out a sad exhale, feeling a bit bad for her. Minji was simple, there was no doubt about that, she was innocent, harmless, much different to what Mark was. For Mark, it was a facade, which was what the two girls now fully believed. But Minji, she was just a girl that loved with intent, that was confident in herself, she was one of the most genuine people they had come to know on campus. And it was evident that what Solar felt with her wasn’t nothing, it wasn’t a straight friendship gone wrong. But they weren’t in the place, nor would they ever, try to tell their friend who she should be with. All they could do was support her in figuring it all out, what her heart truly wanted.

But it was hard to watch another one of their friends quietly ache in the process.

“She deserves someone who loves her fully,” Hanni assesses firmly after a moment of silence between them, “and I don’t think that’s Solar, as much as I love her… it’s… it’s clear who she loves.”

“Oh my God…” Hyein gushes, “you think she loves him? I mean, that’s a bit much, no?”

Hanni giggles, shrugging, “guess we’ll find out!”

They dropped it then, off to search deeper for Minji, after deciding that they would console her if she seemed sad over the subject. If she didn’t want to help, they weren’t going to push her. They would simply figure something else out, because Minji’s feelings mattered, too.

After running around the entire rather large living room, they finally found her at the edge, against the wall, near where they’d left the rest of their group. Solar was a few feet into the crowd, her now empty cup dangling from two fingers, laughing at something Mark was saying. The dorky boy in front of her, with his arms still loosely around her waist as they continued to sway to the beat of the music, was doing the thing he did, existing with his polite demeanor, never touching her anywhere too sensual, keeping his touch as gentle as possible.

Minji, on the other hand, was standing comfortably at the sideline, her camera resting against her chest. She wasn’t filming, for once, she was simply watching the room with the patient stillness she usually saved for kill feeds.

Her eyes looked curiously to the two girls appearing before her, and she didn’t waste the time to pend, “Alright, spill, what have you two been plotting?”

Hyein gasped, holding a hand to her heart, “plotting?! Why, excuse me, Minji… that is beneath us,” she firmly lectures, before clearing her throat and returning to her totally-innocent-not-plotting tone, “actually, we need your help with a costume emergency.”

Minji clearly did not believe a word of that. Her eyes raked across the girls, from Hyein, to Hanni, then to Solar, who looked like she was entirely too tipsy to care about a costume. “Costumes seem fine,” she deciphers.

“Well, either way, we need to talk to you!” Hyein exclaims, tired of playing around, and grabs Minji’s arm, steering her away towards the doorway of the kitchen.

Knowing there was no escape, Minji let herself be dragged, a bright Hanni following behind. It was obvious, due to their facial expressions, that they had rather breaking news. A part of her could only assume what, or who, it was about.

The kitchen at that time had surprisingly thinned out, as most of the party had migrated to the dance floor in the living room. The three girls fold into the corner, next to the fridge, where the noise gave them more cover. Hyein pokes her head around, checking the doorway a couple of times, leaning with the subtlety of a person with no clue how to be subtle.

“Okay,” Hanni breathes, a bit nervous to say the words, “so, we decided to speak with Haechan.”

Minji went very still. Although she already had an idea, it still felt weird to hear them say such a thing. It was a small stillness, the kind most people would’ve missed, but the kitchen light caught it anyway, the way her hand flattened slowly against the body of her camera like she was steadying it against her chest, or perhaps herself, “you did what?” she bluntly asks, because she was rather confused as to why they would do such a thing,”Isn’t he… bad news, now?”

“Well,” Hyein cleared her throat, “we thought so, until we heard Mark talking to Danielle.”

The girl before them’s eyes widened at this new information. She took a moment to process, before she almost looked angry. “Are you serious?” she deadpanned, turning toward the doorway, “We need to get him away from her then, clearly he’s feeding her information.”

“Wait!” Hyein cried, grabbing her wrist before she could go back into the living room,”Not yet, Ji, that’ll mess up the plan, okay? Hear us out.”

From the pleading look in her eyes, Minji exhaled, nodding her head a single time.

“We cornered his upstairs,” Hanni continues, “to ask him what really happened, since we don’t trust the story Mark’s been feeding to us after that… since he’s kinda stubborn, we asked him very simply if Solar was a game to him, like Mark keeps saying…” Her eyes carefully glance back towards the doorway, lowering her voice an octave, “and, he said no.”

“No, huh…” Minji repeats slowly.

“Yeah, listen, I was ready to beat him up,” Hyein chimes, “Seriously, my fists were fired up, but he… you should’ve seen his face… people don’t fake that face, I’ve never seen that man even make a face before.”

“Isn’t he still a jack ass?” Minji hums.

“Yep,” Hyein agrees without thinking, “oh, one hundred percent, total, absolute dick… but you know, Solar Lee is Solar Lee.”

Minji chuckled, shaking her head as her eyes looked towards the ground, “total understatement.”

“He agreed to talk to her,” Hanni offered, “so, that’s why we need you.”

The girl didn’t say anything right away, she just stared past them, towards the other doorway, to where the crowd opened up in flashes, orange light, with a pair of translucent wings connected to possibly the most daring girl on campus. Solar Lee, with her head tipped back, giggling away at whatever Mark was saying to her now, his hand still on the respectful place on her waist, not moving a smidge lower. She watched her, the way she watched footage she already knew she would keep, before she reached up to run a hand through her hair, exhaling deeply.

“Okay,” she sighs, “anything to get him away from her, then.”

“Exactly, so we were thinking the upstairs bathroom,” Hyein immediately goes into explaining the plan, eager.

Minji watched Hyein, in all of her excitement, and pursed her lips, “Because nobody suspects a bathroom?” she mutters, sarcastically, causing Hyein to stop her excited bouncing from foot to foot to glare at her. “Alright, fine, that’ll work, probably.”

“You’re in?” Hanni asks softly, for confirmation, reaching a hand out and placing it comfortingly on her forearm, “You don’t have to if you don’t want to, Ji, don’t feel pressured.”

“It’s cool,” she shrugs, casually, “do you want me to argue?”

“No!” Hyein cries instantly, “But if you did, I was prepared… with materials!”

Something crossed Minji’s face then, brief, unreadable, and gone before it even finished arriving. Instead, she was entirely collected, adjusting the camera strap across her chest with both hands, “she’s been checking the stairs all night,” she states plainly, “you guys found a door, you’re trying to help,” she hums, “I’m just… going to walk her to it.”

“Minji,” Hanni murmurs softly, because she could still hear what was hiding underneath those words.

“It’s fine,” Minji shakes her head, offering a small smile, voice perfectly level, which from anyone else would’ve been proof, but from her, it was craft, “think of it as me peeling for her.”

Hyein blinked at her, “I have no idea what that means.”

But they didn’t have the time to ask, because the invisible timer was ticking.

The three head back out into the doorway, once the plan was set in motion and they all understood what to do. Solar was three sips into a drink Jaemin had brought her, since her last one was empty, when Minji materialized at her elbow, camera pushed around to her back, wearing the expression she used for objectives.

“Sol,” she leans over her shoulder so she could hear her, and at her presence, Solar had turned away from Mark, who was still holding her waist, “I need the bathroom, line down here is too long, can you come with?”

The brunette had glanced back to Mark, before back to Minji, thinking for a moment. “Oh, uh… I guess, do you really need me to?” she puzzled, “It’s just to the left, end of hall, there’s really not much to see up there.”

Seeming to notice the two were having a conversation, Mark leaned over Solar’s shoulder, looking comfortably close to her, “everything okay?” He asked, eyes meeting Minji’s, “Is someone being weird? I can totally kick them out.”

Minji met his gaze for a moment, distaste burning in her brown irises now that she knew what he was really doing. Though she hadn’t seen it herself, Hanni and Hyein had no reason to ever lie about such a thing.

“Everything’s chill,” she assures him, blankly, before looking back to Solar, “come on, I don’t want to get followed by a creep, they never listen when I say I don’t swing that way.”

Solar exhaled, her irises softening, before she nodded. She turns back around in Mark’s grasp, pushing his glasses back up his nose with a finger before she pats his shoulder, “Be right back, Super-dork.”

Mark chuckled as he released her, faking a pout, “not nice, that’s maybe your meanest one yet.”

“You can take it,” Solar shrugs playfully, before Minji had dragged her away from the scene without another word.

The two girls headed back through the crowds of people, the scent of sweat poisoning their nostrils. Solar tried not to think too much about going upstairs, the last place she wanted to be that night, but she trusted that Minji was sincere, since she’d never been anything other than sincere. They were just going to the bathroom, she told herself.

Though, the staircase was cordoned off by nothing but reputation. A few people watched them go up, and Solar felt the eyes the way she always did, cataloguing, drafting captions, but she kept her chin level out of pure muscle memory, one hand skimming the banister, the wings knocking gently against her back with each step like a reminder that she’d agreed to this voluntarily.

Everything is fine, her head assured her, this is a girl’s Halloween… well, and Mark.

Minji stopped at the top of the stairs, turning to wait for Solar. The orange girl stopped next to her, her heels sinking into the plush carpet, eyes nervously scanning over the area, before realizing Minji had no idea where to go up here and that it was her entire purpose.

“Oh,” she pipes, “it’s to the left,” she points, “all the way down, it has some weird little green sign on it… don’t question it.”

She hated that she knew that, but she’d been up here a few times by now.

“Hold the stairs?” Minji turns to ask, “Or, maybe the corner, just in case.”

Solar chuckles, nodding in agreement, “Alright, but don’t take too long.” She tried not to listen to what her gut was trying to tell her, because none of that would make sense. Nothing was going to happen, her brain yells, you’re just waiting for your friend to use the bathroom.

But something in the delivery felt a little too smooth, the way a rehearsed line always sat slightly flatter than a real one, but the couple of drinks she’d had rounded the corners off her suspicion, and the booming music through the floor was rather loud, and she couldn’t be mad that Minji had to use the bathroom.

“Thanks, Sol,” Minji offers after a moment, before she walked off completely, a few steps away. Solar’s eyes meet hers, noticing the glowing smile on her lips, “you look good in gold, you know.”

Then she was gone, turning the corner before she could think about the way that landed, past a scatter of bottles someone abandoned along the wall. Solar bit down on her lip as she stepped further into the large opening room of the second floor, next to the wall where she could see anyone coming upstairs, in case, like they agreed. The bass continued to drop away beneath her until it was more pressure rather than sound.

Everyone’s weird this week, she thought to herself then. Hyein and Hanni had possibly been the weirdest of them all, even though she knew they were just worried about her, which was what she chalked it down to. But really, she was fine, in fact, Mark was even growing on her, even if she had her suspicions about him. At the end of the day, he was the one who was there.

She wouldn’t let herself look towards the right, as much as she was tempted to, because the right side of the hall was where a certain room was, and she did not want to think about that certain room. After all, he was probably busy with that nurse from earlier.

Something in her chest ached, before she could push it away. The feeling caused her to look, because she wanted to see if there were any full alcohol bottles up here somewhere, and the direction his room was in was also the direction the lounge sofas were at, where people had left the lingering bottles.

But she regretted looking the second her eyes landed on him.

Haechan stood in the hallway outside his bedroom door, shoulder against the wall, phone in one hand, thumb hovering over the screen like it’d been there a while. The little red horns were still in his hair, one of them knocked slightly crooked, and the sight of him this close, after two weeks of only seeing him across rooms and through rumors, in four second glimpses from sidewalks, hit her like a truck, all at once, physical, somewhere underneath where the alcohol lived.

She tried to tear her eyes away, to desperately find something to drink, but he’d looked up, and there was no ounce of surprise on his face.

Much later, she would realize there was never a line for any bathroom, that Minji’s delivery had been flat because Minji hated lying, that Hanni and Hyein’s cheeriness all week had been arriving half a second early because they were indeed carrying something, and most of all, that she had been walked, gently and lovingly, by committee, directly into a hallway with a boy she claimed she despised.

But then, in that moment, all she had was herself and Haechan Lee in a corridor.

Immediately, she spins on her heel, deciding that she was going to escape this situation, that she would come up in a few minutes when Minji was likely leaving. She could guard from downstairs, too, right?

Though the second she stepped, Haechan had pushed himself off the wall, padding across the carpet to reach out and grab her wrist, gently, just the lightest tug.

Flames were burning inside of her that she was trying to keep calm. She turned, her eyes looking up at him, stepping back, back towards the left wall where she’d been. “Is this a joke?” she deadpans, her voice sharp, armor sliding into place before she’d even chosen it, “You really think I’m gonna talk to you now?”

“Good to see you, sweetheart,” he returns, careful, not moving from where he stood next to the stairs now.

“Don’t,” she hisses, sharper than she intended for it to be. His jaw shifted in response, and a part of her, an ugly, hurt part, was almost glad to see it, thinking she had finally done damage to him, the kind that he’d done to her. It would still be easy, if she really wanted to, to push past him and go downstairs, but yet, she stayed there, because the flames were building, even though he hadn’t said more than a word, “It’s wild, you know, you feeding me all that shit on the rooftop, just for Mark to be right anyway,” she shook her head, grimacing almost, “that’s the worst part, everyone warned me, and I fell for it anyway, just like my brother said I would. I’m disappointed, you could’ve at least been original.”

His eyes scanned her face for a second. “You think I made it up?” he hums, “You think Mark told you the truth?”

“What else do I have to go off of?” She retorts, “He says a lot of things, Hyuck, cause he’s around to say them, that’s the difference, isn’t it? He shows up.”

Something was burning in his eyes, too, especially at the sound of that nickname. Haechan directed his eyes to the ceiling, “yeah,” he breathes slowly, but it wasn’t as flat as he tended to be. It was a crack in his typical monotone, a thin, dark thing moving underneath, “Yeah, I’ve seen him showing up, princess, front row… whole performance, he learn your drink order off a flashcard, or someone sell it to him?”

His words felt truer than she wanted them to, which only irritated her more. She hated how the things he said always made sense, how they always alluded to things she would only realize later. Never would she admit she was already suspicious of Mark, just based off Danielle’s weird comment when she confronted her. And then, she was too mad at him to let him have any sense of victory.

“You don’t get to do that,” she snaps instead.

“Do what, be correct?” he raises a brow, “Tell you what you don’t want to hear?”

“That,” she hisses, gesturing at him, the tone, the jaw, the too-precise way he was standing, “you’re not telling me what I don’t want to hear, Haechan, you’re fucking jealous, and you don’t get to be jealous,” she scoffs, crossing her arms over her chest, her wings bouncing gently on her back from the movement. She was trying to calm down, but it was still rising inside of her, the two weeks of silence, the audacity of a boy she was starting to trust, “you just fucking… disappeared… you slept with me, told me your legal name, went to make breakfast, then… what? Told me to get out and didn’t speak to me again,” a bitter laugh escaped her lips, “You sat on that roof, in your room… and fed me all that shit, just to run away because of my brother?”

Something softened in those deep irises, he broke their eye contact to look towards the carpet this time, “it’s not about Jaehyun,” he mutters.

“Then what is it about, Haechan?!” she jeers loudly, in disbelief, exasperation, “Are you going to fucking tell me or just keep being cryptic like everyone else?!”

He was silent, eyes still on the carpet, thumb running across the edge of his phone in one hand. She watched him do the thing she’d seen him do, all the way back then, on the rooftop, weigh something, price it, and return it to the shelf.

But she didn’t soften like she would’ve then.

“Figures,” she snorts, deciding that it was enough of an answer to a question she didn’t ask. Her foot steps forward, about to step passed him like she should’ve done after he tried to stop her, keep going, leave, go back downstairs to Mark and shrug it all off.

She’d only made it half a step.

His hand closed around her forearm this time, just when she was going to move passed him, barely even a grip. It was more of a question than anything, asked in the only language currently available to him. She’d stopped, which was her own decision making failing her again, she’d process that only later, because she could’ve kept walking, and he’d have let her, it was the truth no one had to say aloud.

But she turned back instead, only for him to still be there, closer than she’d anticipated. He didn’t use force for her to do it, her feet were backing up for comfort, to ease the pumping of her chest, until she felt that same wall beneath the skin of her back, cold without warning. She’d nearly stumbled before catching herself, those two drinks seeming to mess with her at the worst time.

Haechan followed her, his arm flying to lay his palm flat against the wall besides her head. The entire right side was still open, nonetheless, if she wanted to take it.

She didn’t.

Her fluttery, orange wings crumpled softly against the wall behind her, the material itchy against her skin. This close, she couldn’t erase the overwhelming scent of the vanilla she’d spent two weeks trying to forget, underneath faint smoke and the stink of someone else’s party, her body doing it’s usual traitorous accounting, eyes trying so hard not to look at the open collar, his pushed up sleeves, the crooked red horns atop his messy dark hair, the way his veins in his neck were popping enough to make her think things she shouldn’t be allowing herself to think.

“Ask me,” he rasps, “if I’m jealous.”

She told herself she was going to stand her ground, she wasn’t going to accept his shitty, lack of explanation for what he’d done. So, she exhaled, rolling her eyes, “I don’t care if you’re…”

“…Ask me,” he cut her off, firmly, almost growling with the way the words flew off his tongue. His eyes were narrowed, hand looking like it could break the wall behind her, but those irises didn’t leave hers for a mere second.

Her mouth was dry, an embarrassing fact she buried. The bass continued to move through the wall, into her spine, where a hundred people were screaming the chorus to some ridiculous pop song, as the hallway held it’s single note.

“This is nuts,” she defends, annoyed, “I’m not doing this.”

But she felt something twitch the second she looked into his eyes again. The flames were brighter now, enough that she was starting to almost feel uneasy, but also that the intrigue she was trying to erase was surfacing. Haechan looked mad, in a way she had never seen from him before, but the more shocking part was… he wasn’t trying to hide it.

“Fine,” she huffs, “are you jealous, Haechan?” She said it in a mocking tone, teasing, like she was talking down to him.

She was taking the challenge, she knew it, and she knew she was only feeding into it entirely on purpose. It was a bad habit she apparently couldn’t break, even when every single rational voice in her head was telling her to. She expected him to fume, to possibly give her an answer, some kind of reason, to admit to his wrongs, to show her that Mark was right all along.

“August,” he monotones finally, like it was a fact he was tired of carrying. The flatness of it almost made it worse, truer, no performance anywhere on him for her to deflect off.

“August,” she repeats, because the name of such a month, her first month here, sounding absolutely absurd coming from his lips.

“That’s your answer,” he nodded, a single time, “not a game, unrelated to your brother.”

Solar’s eyes were erratically wiping across every aspect of his face, trying to search for what any of this meant, because she refused to believe what was happening in her chest. “I don’t… what’s that mean, then?” she musters, voice softer now, the venom seeming to slowly start to dissipate, the true feeling underneath the shield coming out, the hurt, the ache of it all, “do you get that that doesn’t… that doesn’t tell me anything? It sucked, Haechan, it really fucking sucked.”

“I know,” he mumbles, his head hanging down, hair falling in his face, almost close enough that it could tickle the top of her forehead, “I know… I can’t… I can’t tell you the rest tonight, sweetheart…” he trails off, like he was thinking about his words, “I didn’t want to hurt you,” he whispers, “I thought it was better that way.”

“You shouldn’t of made the decision for me,” she breathes, “but I need to know, I’m tired of everyone giving me hints and pieces, I need to know what’s really going on.”

“I know,” he says again, with more assurance this time, “but you’d believe me even less than you should.”

The girl only sighs in response, a sadness lurking in her eyes, “how do you know if you don’t even try?”

He didn’t say anything in response, perhaps because he didn’t have one. Instead, his eyes moved across her face, as if checking a mix for the one frequency that was off. The silence spun between them, a chaotic tornado waiting for who would make their move first, daring them to strike.

His other hand, that had been resting at his side, rose to graze his fingertips across her jawline, his eyes fluttering. It was like she was a flower, a dandelion he was scared would blow away with too much force. “What I can tell you,” he utters, “is how much I miss the way you feel, princess.”

She should’ve said something mean, some kind of retort that would show him she wasn’t some kind of toy to mess around with whenever he felt like. After all, Solar believed she had decent comebacks, a whole inventory, as she’d been stockpiling them for two weeks by then. But yet, everyone of them dissolved somewhere between her chest and her mouth, because his forehead had dropped lower, coming down to almost touch hers. He was waiting, evidently, the boy who took whatever he wanted, holding perfectly still, an inch away from her.

“And who’s fault is that?” she sasses, raising a brow, still stubborn even when she was letting him hover over her like that, “It doesn’t fix anything, you know.”

“Never said it did.”

“I’m mad at you,” she states the obvious, even as his face was an inch away from hers, “furious, actually.”

“Mm, I know,” he murmurs, the ghost of the old crooked grin surfacing, “you’re doing so good, sweetheart.”

“You’re so fucking annoying, Haechan,” she’s grumbling, but she never got to say another insult.

His lips crashed onto hers first, nothing soft about it. There would’ve been something dishonest about soft, after everything, and neither of them had the energy. Her fist found his shirt, dragging him closer, one of his hands sliding along her jaw, tilting her the way he wanted her, the way he remembered so fondly wanting her. The sound he made against her mouth was low, wrecked, involuntarily, and it undid more of her anger than any apology could’ve. He kissed her like he was pulling a held note out of two weeks of silence, thorough and unhurried, desperate for a touch he couldn’t admit he needed. The wall was cold through the satin and he was warm everywhere else, his hand on the wall falling to her waist, the same place Mark’s hands had once been, only moments ago, gathering the orange fabric like he needed proof of her in his fist.

“You have no idea,” he whispers as his lips moved to her neck, sucking on the skin in that spot he knew made her knees shake, “how good you look tonight,” he paused to move back to her lips, kissing her again, his teeth sucking on her bottom lip like juice, “in that short fucking skirt, princess…” he trails off again, the only sound her whimpers from how good he was at this as he nibbles on her neck, “and how much it fucking killed me to watch you against him… knowing he can’t make you feel like this.”

The hallway stopped being a hallway then. It was just his mouth at the corner of hers, at her jaw, the place below her ear, her heavy breathing and the way she was at a loss for words, her only ability being to run her fingers through his hair, aching, craving. Those red horns were on the floor now, his ragged laugh against her throat when he almost stopped and she’d pulled him back by the collar. None of it was graceful, it was two people starving for a fix they could only give each other, two weeks of pretending, compressed into a corridor while a hundred, maybe three, people screamed along beneath them to whatever song was playing by now.

He finally pulls away, likely to catch his breathe from how he’d been busy sucking on her skin for a few minutes then. Solar’s chest was heaving under him, his eyes carefully raking across her face, before he observes, “you’re shaking,” his thumb ran across the line of her jaw again, comforting yet electrifying.

“It’s… cold,” she tries, though the confidence wasn’t there, and her breath was still uneven. It was her terrible attempt at playing off how much he did to her.

“Mm, it’s really not,” he ponders, sarcastically, “we have the heat on eighty.”

“Shut up, Donghyuck.”

His eyes flash back to her the second the name left her lips. A smirk spread across his, and he shook his head, in awe of her words. “Dangerous game,” he warns, his fingers on the back of her neck now, “you like that, though, don’t you?”

She just shrugged, innocently, but she didn’t get a chance to say anything before he’d leaned in to kiss her again. It was slow this time, deliberate, like an argument he was winning, but this time, she let him win it, her fingers curling back into his shirt, the last of her balance formally resigning as her legs shook, knees begging for a release, body craving the only thing that seemed to satisfy it after a night impossible to forget.

His hands wandered her body, the touch sending sparks through her veins, making her want to drop everything right there. His lips were soft, so soft, against her skin, made to do exactly what they desired to her. She’d allow it, was the truth, she’d allow every inch of what he wanted, even if it was a horrible idea, even if she would regret it later, he was a drug she couldn’t get enough of.

Somewhere against her hip, her phone buzzed, a single time, then another. The world, slowly, began to reassemble itself in pieces, the bass, the wall, sweat and fog climbing up the stairs. She broke away, far enough to catch her breath, both of them unsteady, his forehead dropping against hers while her phone buzzed for a third time, a metronome for a life she’d left downstairs.

Haechan didn’t stop looking at her, he just watched her dig in the pocket of her custom made skirt, fumbling the phone up between them, still trying to stop her breath from being so ragged.
