A lump formed in her throat, she could feel Haechan’s eyes reading the text messages upside down. Her eyes slowly looked up to watch him, seeing the way the temperature in his face altered.

“You don’t have to respond,” he mutters, his hand rising to cup her cheek, “you can put it away, princess.”

She almost did, was the thing, but the screen was still lit between them, and her friends were waiting for her downstairs. She could only assume Minji had slipped by, possibly not even noticing them, the way they were tucked into the corner. The whole impossible arithmetic of her life came flooding back into the hallway at once, Danielle, the accounts, her brother and two unprovable stories with one boy, who’d just told her, that he couldn’t explain.

Her hands drop down to her side, and she dips her head before he could connect their lips again.

“What are we doing?” she blurts, before she could second guess herself and decide she was too afraid to hear his response, “Like, what is this? You can’t… I can’t be strung along like that again.”

When she looked back up at him, for a split second, he looked like he was going to tell her, going to let everything out that popped into his brain. But the sight left as soon as it came, before the shutters came back down over whatever had been open in his face, and he retreated, behind the register he kept for everyone else, because she’d asked him for the one thing he didn’t yet have a mix for.

“Complicated,” he mumbles, hand still on her cheek, her skin warm against his palm, “you shouldn’t worry about it, sweetheart.”

The word landed like a coin flipped onto a table, not her name, just the thing he called girls, and she felt herself go cold in a way that had nothing to do with the wall at her back.

“Right,” she exhales, pushing off of the wall, gently taking his hand off of her, and straightening her skirt with two efficient tugs, “there he is, was wondering when he’d show up,” her tone was steady, which she was somewhat proud of, because nothing underneath it was, “look, I need to get back, Haechan, my friends are waiting for me.”

He took a single step back, his eyes still wandering her body. But he didn’t reach for her again, even if every bone in him was begging to. Instead, he shoved his hands in his pockets, the pills reminding him of their presence.

“Sure, princess,” he hums, “go tell little Marky who you really belong to.”

She was three steps away by the time his words entered her ears, causing her to turn right next to the steps and glare at him.

But she had no rebuttal, so she just shook her head, trying not to smile, and turned to head down the stairs. She didn’t trust what she’d say it she let herself stand there another second.

“And don’t miss anymore practices,” he calls again, just as she was nearly a third down, “that’s yours, remember that.”

53: sinister jokes and creepy costumes

Eleven minutes.

Mark Lee knew this number because he’d checked, the moment Minji pulled her away, some of the glitter from the costumes fluttering in the air behind them. It was a casual gesture, or so he tried to tell himself, his thumb brushing the screen at his hip, as if he was a man building a record. He’d checked again, subconsciously, at four, then seven, continuing to drink his watered down drink and watch his fellow frat brothers continue to make fools of themselves. And before he’d guessed it, it had been an entire eleven minutes, and there was no sign of Solar Lee.

He wasn’t trying to make it a big deal, he wasn’t trying to make it his business, or think about the fact there was more than one bathroom downstairs, the one off the kitchen everyone knew about, and the one behind the laundry room only the boys used. He tried to tell himself it was unlikely for either of them to know about it, upstairs was a natural escalation.

Pursing his lips, he tapped his foot awkwardly against the carpeted floor, trying to enjoy himself despite how antsy he felt. The party continued on around him, no one seeming to notice how out of place he was feeling right then in his own house. It wasn’t because anyone was ignoring him, people were always friendly, generally, to Mark. But he had the oddest sense of loss dwelling in his chest, twisting and curdling underneath his veins until he nearly felt them pop.

Sigma Chi had entered the part of the night it no longer felt like any old college party, or even like a house, for that matter. The keg remained in the center of the makeshift dance floor, a monument for anyone brave enough. Naturally, Jeno was on top of it for the third time that night, the same crowd of around thirty students cradled around him, screaming. Mark could only imagine how he had to be feeling right then, knowing well that he’d taken molly prior to the party starting, as he’d announced it to the entire frat with the earnestness of a man reading a weather report.

“Thank you, thank you!” he was crying out, dramatically bowing as he finished his third, and hopefully final, keg stand, “I’ll be here all night, ladies, please reserve a spot with me in advance.”

A bunch of girls squealed in response, shouting incoherences at him as he sent the crowd a wink before walking off towards the kitchen, likely to find more drugs.

Meanwhile, the fog machine continued to cough white across the floor. Fake cobwebs came down from the ceiling, catching in people’s hair, someone covering some of the framed chapter photographs in the hallway with cheap, bloody handprints, which Mark thought was quite hysterical when he saw it, because he was equipped with the humor of a child and felt no shame about it.

And at the edge of it all, near the doorway with his cape folded around himself, stood Renjun, who’d brought his lit cigarette indoors, since it was growing too cold outside in the late October weather. Though he wouldn’t typically do such a thing, he decided he no longer cared, especially with the current state of the house. So, he’d slipped inside and leaned against the entryway wall, taking a drag and staring ahead at absolutely nothing and no one in particular, because there were very few people Renjun paid attention to.

Which was why it was particularly absurd when a group of girls came over, a rather specific group of girls that looked like the stereotypical art students. After all, those were the type of girls attracted to Renjun, the same way there were certain types of girls that liked Haechan. Each fraternity boy seemed to have their own clan of people that thought they were the most beautiful being on campus, even Renjun.

The group of girls decided it would be an amazing idea to stand in front of him and monologue dramatically about their costumes, as if they were in a theatre class, simply because they knew Renjun enjoyed theatre.

“And I…” one of the girls dramatically recounts, holding up a small syringe prop, “am the very original super sexy nun,” she does a twirl, before turning back to Renjun, “so, what do you think, Jun?”

“Lackluster,” he observes without much thought, “the audience is falling asleep.”

“Asleep?” the girl gasps, “Wow, that’s harsher than my actual theatre professor.”

“That was my nicer comment,” he deadpans before taking another drag, turning his head to blow the smoke away from the girls direction.

His eyes found the rather disheveled looking Mark towards the sideline of the dance floor. The boy’s eyes were so intently focused on the staircase it was like nothing else around him existed. Jisung appeared from somewhere in the crowd of sweaty bodies, patting his shoulder a single time and leaning over to say some kind of joke to him, one Mark would typically burst into fits of laughter over, but he didn’t even react.

Twelve minutes, his brain informed, and the uninvited, abnormal panic attempted to set in again. It’s fine, it was the thing he kept reminding himself of, one he was aware of in the part of himself he tried not to consult. Perhaps, he’d told himself it was fine so many times it was starting to seem like quite the opposite. What was the worst that could happen? It had been a nice night, him and Solar were getting closer than ever. She’d let him remake her drink, called him Super-dork, danced with him in ways he’d never seen her dance before, and there’d been the slightest of moments where they’d almost gotten so close as to kiss, and he’d felt it settle in his chest with the sort of bliss he had never known to exist, a sudden blossom from a seed unbeknownst.

“Superman, just the guy I was looking for!”

Jaemin had screamed such words at him from feet away, his white hat sticking out like a sore thumb even there, moving the way he always moved, as though the floor had been installed for him personally. The line of girls was still behind him, four or five, arranged in his wake with the loose gravitational obedience of people who’d stopped asking where they were going. He arrived in front of Mark with both arms wide, hat tipping forward, nearly stumbling before he caught himself with the efficiency of someone who’d been drunk way too many times in their life to even attempt to count.

“Marky,” he drawls, the famous nickname that was beginning to irritate Mark due to the likes of his best friend, in the same terrible accent he kept trying to force, “I need you, bud.”

A look of despair takes over Mark’s expression before he could hide it. “Nah, man, not right now,” he waves a hand in dismissal, exhaling, “I’m waiting for someone.”

“It wasn’t a question, it was a summon,” Jaemin gawks in fake offense, “are you dare questioning the beloved social chair?”

“Come on, Mark!” One of the girls that had been following peeks out from behind him to say.

The boy sighed, hating the way he was caving to peer pressure, even when he was completely unaware. “Dude, okay, what do you even want?”

Pleased at the question, Jaemin claps his hands together, before placing one on Mark’s shoulder, motioning towards the front of the dance floor, “a costume contest, Mark, doesn’t it sound glorious? I need a judge who won’t be swayed by beauty.”

Mark was blinking at his friend like he was the craziest person on the planet. “And… you thought I was the person for the job?”

Jaemin shrugged, “Everyone else has gone AWOL, and Renjun is scary, man,” he shudders, “and you’re famously boring, it’s a compliment, really. You dressed like a substitute teacher at Halloween, the people trust that.”

“Bro, I’m Clark Kent.”

“Of course, that’s exactly what I said.”

That would be how Mark Lee ended up standing at the front of the living room with a plastic cup he wasn’t finishing, in front of a crowd, facing away from the staircase. He turned his head twice in the first minute, doing it before he could gain enough awareness to stop. Jaemin wasted no time to grab the microphone he’d plugged in ahead of time, as if he knew he was going to need it, beginning to go through the rules he had made up only five minutes prior. The crowd, on the other hand, that had begun to gather to listen, now that the music was turned down, began cheering and screaming nearly every time he finished a sentence.

“Now, if anyone would like to give their shot as impressing our phantasmal judges, please form a line to my left!”

Instantly, tons of students rush to line up besides the microphone, nearly knocking each other over, the living room turning into endless amounts of chatter and yelling. Someone in an inflatable dinosaur costume got attacked by a clown, deflating to a sad bunch of green plastic.

Jeno, the only other person around for Jaemin to recruit for this activity, was the one commanding them, holding both of his hands up as stop motions for them to know where to line up. Jaemin continued talking into the microphone, explaining how his imaginary rules would work. And Mark simply stood there like the dorky, nonchalant guy everyone on campus thought of him as, unless they were here freshman year.

He had a smile on his face, but his gut was telling him something entirely different, something he didn’t like.

Upstairs, Minji got the bathroom door open with her shoulder, stepping into the hallway and taking a deep breath, like she was bracing herself to dive underwater. Her mind seems to sink back into reality, and she blinks a few times to take it all in. The bass continued to bang against the floorboards, arriving as more of a pressure. The carpet ate the sound of everything so completely that she could hear the ventilation, the tick of a radiator, someone’s ringtone going off behind one of the closed doors. Bottles stood along the wall at intervals like markers on a trail.

Adjusting the strap across her chest, out of habit, she finally turns toward the front of the hall, making her way through the dimmed air. The bathroom was actually a sharp cut to the stairs after the corner, she wasn’t planning to intrude on anything going up here. Really, she wanted to get back downstairs as soon as possible, so long as Solar was okay. Besides, she figured, if something happened, Solar would probably be downstairs already.

Her peripheral caught it. As much as she tried to fight it, the urge was too strong, because there stood Solar and Haechan against the other wall.

Minji’s first thought, however, was almost to capture the shot, not out of ill intent, but because something in her chest told her to, that it was a moment worth capturing, maybe to hurt herself, or to showcase the look that was in Solar’s eyes. Her brain didn’t want to feel it, was the harsh truth. They stood at the far end, Solar against the wall, Haechan in front of her, at a proximity too close to be friendly. His arm was braced above her head, Solar’s orange satin shimmering beneath him, even in the dim light, her small wings crushed flat behind her. If she’d been shooting, she’d have killed the stairwell light and let the small lamp in the corner shine, as it was doing something to Solar’s face that a lighting designer would have spent a week attempting to create.

As soon as rationality kicked in, her brain snapped at her to leave. Go downstairs, don’t make it weird.

But her feet were glued to the ground.

It wasn’t right away that she gained control. Only after four seconds could she move them, rushing to the stairs like she was escaping a horrifying situation, despite the fact the two of them were too far, the bass too loud, to ever hear her. Though it couldn’t erase the single thing she’d saw.

The thing about Solar Lee, after two months of sitting next to her in a lab with the lights off, of walking her home, of a balcony in the cold with the party glowing behind glass, was that she was funny with her. She was easy, in the specific way of a girl who’d found one room on campus where nothing was going to be asked of her, Solar was warm, sharp. They were all real things about her, about what she looked like when she took the mask off and let herself be without concern.

But Minji had never seen Solar like this, never seen her come apart, not even in the worst week of her life, or when Danielle put her entire world into a folder, when the two of them were standing on a balcony and she’d had too many drinks. Even then, Solar was simply a girl at rest, a girl that’d taken the armor off since there was nothing in the room that required it.

Though, when her eyes landed on her for those four seconds, Solar Lee was yelling. Minji couldn’t hear a word of it, but she didn’t need to, with the way the brunette was exasperatedly throwing her hands in the air, her chin up, whole body pitched forward into it, furious and unguarded, stripped down to something with no performance anywhere left in her. And the boy in front of her was… standing there, entirely unbothered, like he was accepting every word being thrown at him without contest.

The exchange, she realized, was full of a passion she had never seen before. You didn’t do that with people who didn’t matter. Solar had spent two months being pleasant to an entire university, yet here she was, against the wall of Sigma Chi with her hands in the air, saying whatever she needed to get off her chest to the one person she couldn’t be composed about.

It was the answer, and it alone could be seen in the brown of her irises.

She kept her heels off the wood at the edges of the mahogany stairs when she went down. There was something her throat she swallowed, because it wasn’t any of her business, because she felt she didn’t have a right to feel it as heavy as she did.

The party hit her like a storm at the bottom. Someone was screaming into a microphone, she’d processed as she entered the living room again, seeing the front of the living room, the oddly nicely gathered crowd. Jaemin was at the mic, motioning for someone from the ginormous line to come to him. Mark and Jeno were next to him, Jeno looking like he was on a different planet and Mark, like he was the happy go lucky guy he wanted to be.

Standing there at the entrance, she folds her arms, chest doing something complicated, thinking about it, the way Solar said her name when she was laughing at her, dragged out and delighted. The way she’d said you look good in gold to her, feeling like she was letting go of something she wanted to hold onto more than anything. And she thought, painfully, about the fact that whatever was happening at the end of that hallway had been happening, since probably August, and Solar didn’t know it yet, but the boy very obviously did.

“Ji, oh my God, come on!” a chirpy voice suddenly delved into her ears, and the bright face of Hyein appeared in front of her like a jump scare. Before she could even open her mouth, she was being dragged away towards the endless line, “there’s a contest, we are so gonna win!”

It was when they reached the back of the line that Hanni turned to her, a soft expression of gentleness that felt that of a wave of relief compared to Hyein’s screeching excitement, “are you alright, Ji?”

Minji shoots her a small smile, waving a hand in dismissal, “nah, I’m okay,” she shakes her head, “they really…” she trails off, wondering if she should say anything, before deciding at, “real.”

Hyein had stopped screeching at this, her eyes widening at the word that told her everything she needed to know and wanted to hear. Hanni turns to her, and they exchange a glance that likely shared the feeling.

“You’re a good friend, Ji,” Hanni wraps an arm around her shoulder, “now, we’re going to win a costume contest!”

Minji let herself smile at that, reminding herself that it was what really mattered. At the end of the day, she wanted to see Solar happy.

The glittering orange, satin, brunette would patter downstairs only a few minutes after Minji, the time difference insignificant enough for Mark not to notice if the girls came down at the same time or not, since they were buried at the back of the costume line. Her eyes scan the room, before she notices what seemed to be happening, two freshmen dressed as Mario and Luigi currently standing at the mics, giving some kind of speech about how they should win the contest, attempting to sway the judges.

Jaemin, she thought with a chuckle, watching the scene take place, he’s written all over this.

Then she saw the judges.

Mark was standing there, possibly the most performative she had ever seen him. She watched him for a moment, before he noticed her with the speed he typically did, the way his eyes crinkled at the corners, the innocence on his face when a girl smiled at him, like it was a first for him. Still, it took him a few minutes to finally find her in the crowd. She had walked closer now, unsure as to where her friends were, deciding to just watch whatever chaos was happening take place. Their eyes met, and at first, he wasn’t smiling, it was like he was reading something from her she wasn’t offering. But like clockwork, the smile appeared before she could fully process what happened.

“Help me,” he mouthed to her, before Jaemin had slapped his shoulder to tell him to rate the next contestant.

Solar giggled, and he swore he could hear the blissful sound from where he was standing, over the yells, the chatter. She sends him a thumbs up in return, her eyes twinkling under the orange lights.

He grew distracted staring at her, the way she seemed to take over the room. There was something about her, the way she carried herself, she turned heads, she was so seemingly fearless of what people thought about her even if it really bothered her on the inside.

But none of those things were what was causing Mark Lee to have conflicted feelings, as the next contestant began to look to him, Jeno, and Jaemin, going on about how much blood, sweat, and juices they put into their costume. It was the fact she looked happy, blossoming in a way she hadn’t been prior to going upstairs to simply go to the bathroom with Minji. It wasn’t a tipsy happy or the bright, loose, obliging happiness she’d been running on all night, which he’d been carefully feeding and monitoring, like a fire he’d built himself. This happiness was different, in a way he couldn’t deny, her cheeks flushed high, eyes running over something behind them. She was biting the inside of her lip like someone trying to hold a door shut, and she was losing every second of it. And when her eyes met his, something flashed in those irises, briefly, a snippet of apology, shame, guilt.

The gold at the corner of her left eye was smudged, dragged a half centimeter out of the careful line Hanni had drawn. Something went through Mark’s chest, sharp, a cut across it that caused him to stir, and he let himself feel it for a split second before he’d shaken it away.

Until Hyein, Hanni, and Minji had finally spotted Solar from their spot in line. Minji stayed to keep their place, while the two girls eagerly ran over to their friend.

“Solar, Solar!” Hyein was screeching,”You’re back, you took so long!” She started, before she stopped talking, like she hadn’t yet thought of the rest of her words. “So, like, how was the…” she paused, “the bathroom?!”

Hanni glanced at her with utter disappointment. The people continued to scream around them at whatever contestant was up now. And Solar, still dressed in her orange satin and high heels, looked down at her friend with a blank expression, “it was a bathroom, Hyein, not much to see. There was just a line.”

With her completely innocent hostess smile, Hanni nodded, “mhm, there’s always a line, especially tonight.”

“Yeah, big line!” Hyein added.

Solar pursed her lips as she looked down at them. A part of her was aware how the chain of events that just happened lined up, she wasn’t a complete idiot, after all. The thought of her friends talking to Haechan, however, felt like a comedy skit. She couldn’t imagine it, and it almost made her burst into fits of laughter right there, at the way this was feeling so entirely bizarre.

“Uhuh,” she hums after a moment, deciding she didn’t want to talk about it now, “so, what is happening down here?”

“I’m SO glad you asked!” Hyein screamed, nearly as loud as some of the people around them. She grabbed Solar’s arm before she could protest, “You’re just in time, actually, and we’ll totally win with you there!”

-

The contest was a disaster, in the most Sigma way possible. Jaemin was standing on top of a chair by the end, a cup in one hand, his hat tipped back as he introduced each contestant in that painfully inaccurate accent. Mark was standing beside him, rendering verdicts in the flat, apologetic voice of a man who’d been told he was impartial and had decided to take the responsibility seriously. Jeno, next to Mark, was still mostly naked, and nearly every girl that came up walked up to him and ran their hand down his abs, citing that it was part of their bit.

When it got to the four of them, Hyein had thrown her arms in the air as if they’d already won, waltzing onto the fake stage and spinning around as she did so. Hanni followed, offering some small waves to the screaming crowd, and a small bow as she reached the microphone next to Hyein.

Then, there was Solar and Minji. Minji stepped out first, and when she noticed Solar wasn’t following, she turned and offered out a hand. Solar was physically wincing from how much she despised this, wrinkling her nose and looking at Minji, communicating everything she needed to say without saying a single word.

“Now or never,” Minji offers, “it’ll make Hyein happy.”

Solar lets out a deep exhale, knowing that she was going to give in. Minji sent her a reassuring smile, as if to show she was sharing the same conflicted feelings, before extending her hand.

“Okay,” she sighs, under her breathe, “okay, whatever.”

With that, the students crowded in the living room would burst into fits of screams at the sight of Solar and Minji dramatically walking onto stage, like two friends who had known each other forever. Their hands were in the air, and Solar did a spin while Minji was still holding her hand, her smile gleaming underneath the lights. Boys swooned over how pretty Jaehyun’s little sister was, and how lucky Mark was to have her.

And at the middle of the Sigma Chi staircase stood a boy that had just felt the soft, longing touch of her lips on his, the boy that could only move the cursor when she was in his head, the boy that was beginning to realize it was no longer simply a ploy, or a sick game he was playing to get back at his best friend. Maybe, a part of Mark was right if he’d said it a month ago, but he wasn’t anymore.

“Sol,” Mark breathes as soon as she was standing before him, while Hyein began to ecstatically talk into the microphone once Jaemin stepped out of the way, exclaiming how hard she worked on these costumes, that you couldn’t find them anywhere else, and that she would be taking commissions, so long as you paid the appropriate price. His eyes lingered on her face, before lowering, before he snapped them back to her face and his ears grew red with humiliation, on top of the fact they were standing in front of what felt like hundreds of drunk students. “Sorry…” he sputters, “I know I just saw you, you’re just… you’re something special, Sol.”

His dorky compliment still made something ping in her chest, even with her suspicions. She pursed her lips, trying not to let her mind wander, trying not to make it obvious that she had been somewhere very different up those stairs. “Thanks, Mark.

But there was the slightest swelling of her bottom lip from the way that certain boy that sucked on it like it would be his last. The gold of her glitter was still smeared, and just next to her jaw, there was the most subtle forming of a purple mark.

“And what a convincing speech!” Jaemin had been clapping loudly once Hyein had been standing there, talking for probably five minutes, “Some truly astounding competition, so, judges, please, keep your scores ready in your heads!”

The girls make their way off stage then, Hyein bouncing off the walls, insisting that they were going to win because of how loud the cheering got, especially when Solar came on stage. Solar was busy pushing her dramatic, overbearing friend off of her, when Mark was followed them a few feet, reaching out to gently graze her shoulder so she would turn around.

“Hey,” he clears his throat, the next contestant already at the microphone behind them, “let me know when you’re leaving, okay? Not because… not because it’s my business,” he spouts, nervously, “I just want to see you out.”

Her three friends watched the exchange closely, critical looks in each of their eyes. But Solar wasn’t looking at them.

“Yeah,” she nods, after a second, “course.”

The dorky boy mimics her nod, a small smile spreading over his lips. “Cool, I gotta get back now,” he exhales, “get me if you need me, guys,” he looked to all of the girls then, who each quickly fixed their expressions to be mildly pleasant.

Then he was gone, back through the crowd of people, onto the makeshift stage where Jeno was pretending to suddenly be very interested in a girl’s lifeguard costume.

“Welp,” Hyein deadpans, “I want another drink.”

“Hyein!” Hanni had called out disapprovingly, but the girl was already rushing away towards the kitchen.

Solar watched the two girls rush away, a chuckle leaving her lips at how goofy they were, before she looks back to Minji, who had momentarily pulled out her camera to take a few shots of the atmosphere, as she would say. Minji didn’t notice Solar watching her stance, her brows creasing in concentration, moving in specific positions to try to capture the perfect shot underneath the orange lights.

For a moment, she felt an overwhelming sense of peace, like maybe things were falling into place for her. As much as she didn’t want to admit it, she was happy, happier than she had been since that night.

She was still mad, she still didn’t fully trust Haechan, but she also couldn’t resist the things he did to her. It was the harsh truth, he was like a poison she couldn’t deny injecting.

“Anyone got some hot gossip?!” a sudden exclaim piped into the microphone on stage, causing both Solar and Minji’s eyes to snap back to the costume contest, confused who would be saying such a thing.

The crowd yells at the top of their lungs, spouting nonsense about different people, things that had happened recently, Solar could hear her own name being shouted various times. Something began to churn in the pit of her stomach, something unpleasant she wasn’t prepared for, hitting her in the face like whiplash. Her throat grew dry, the possibility of someone seeing what just happened upstairs feeling like the sudden cloudiness of impending doom.

And there, on the stage, was someone in an Instagram costume, or more over, a purple-ish frame, big enough for people to stand in and take fake photos. On the top of the frame, they had made a very poor attempt to tape a piece of paper on it, that read SUnews.

She was frozen, staring at it, as they continued to grovel on and make it an entire bit, like it was funny.

“Sol,” Minji calls out to her, next to her, noticing she was in a stance, but she couldn’t move.

All she could do was stare at someone making the one thing that had continued to torment her life a complete joke, like it was something from a sitcom. The exact account that stalked her during her worst times, that posted someone’s addiction like content, and that she stood in a floral room and confronted her own sorority sister about, who did not deny it, and who, in return, threatened going to her brother with what she had.

Originally, she had planned to try to talk to Jaehyun, to try to tell him what was going on, without incriminating herself, that Danielle had been running these accounts, messing with everyone, but in particular, her. She wanted to tell him, that she was insane, she was clearly stalking him and trying to ruin his sister’s life just because of how badly she wanted to be her, because of how she perceived she had too many unfair advantages in life, so she wanted to watch her suffer and fall apart.

But she couldn’t now, not now that Danielle was fired up with where she had been that Friday night, not with how much she knew about Solar and her relations with two particular fraternity boys her brother could not know she was still hanging around, nonetheless having relations with.

Danielle checkmated her, and right now, she felt entirely powerless.

Mark looked rather nervous himself, an evident lump in his throat that he forcefully swallowed down, forcing a smile on his face as the students continued to laugh and scream about the costume.

“Tell us some gossip!” someone yelled at them.

“Hmm, well, has anyone noticed how cute Solar and Mark are tonight?!” the person, who no one could actually identify due to the purple fabric that acted like a body suit covering their face, leaving only holes for their eyes, nose, and mouth, called out into the mic.

The students burst into laughter, some girls squealing, some yelling out sounds of displeasure about how they didn’t like Solar. People turned to stare at her, in all of her orange satin, standing there next to Minji, entirely paused, looking like a deer caught in headlights. It was the first time many people had ever seen her that way, because she was always, somehow, the most composed person on campus. And there on stage, Mark’s entire face fell, and he looked like he was going to be sick himself.

He’d leaned over to Jaemin, muttering something under his breath, and Jaemin had nodded, snapping back into reality, and hurriedly pushing the Instagram frame out of the way. “Thanks for that one, pal!” he cheerily hums, “Now, would our next contestant please come up?”

The night went on, just like that, and everyone moved on like it was entirely casual. The Instagram frame came off the stage, and instantly, people lunged at them, begging to take a photo, about how legendary their costume was.

“Are you okay?”

She couldn’t rip her eyes away from that stupid costume, until she started to feel something tickling, crawling on her skin.

It was Danielle, she was standing only feet away from the costume, leaning against the wall with some other girls next to her that Solar didn’t recognize, engaging in what appeared to be friendly conversation. She was holding a drink she hadn’t touched, her phone in her other hand, like it was prepared in case she needed it.

Even standing there, she looked entirely devious. And she noticed Solar staring because it felt like she was stuck there, glaring at the girl, like she wanted her to notice.

So, she did, she met Solar’s eyes, and her expression didn’t change for a moment.

Then, she smiled, and looked away like it was nothing.

“Sol, hey,” Minji’s voice finally entered her brain enough for her to snap out of it, her fingers gently grazing her forearm, “hey, you want to go home? I’ll walk you.”

As if on queue, Hanni and Hyein had pushed through a crowd of people, Hyein holding the drink she had gone looking for. Expressions of concern were wiped across their faces, and Hanni had rushed over to Solar as if she was a mother who’d found her lost child, placing both of her hands on the girl’s shoulders and meeting her eyes firmly, “Solar, I’m so sorry, that was absurd. Are you feeling alright?”

Solar, who still had not said a word, swallowed the lump in her throat and forced herself to nod.

“Yeah,” she returns, finally, with all of her courage, “it’s just some stupid costume.”

“It’s more than stupid,” Hyein grumbles, turning to angrily peer at the costume, “you know what? Why don’t I go give them a piece of my…”

The girl turns to walk right over to that frame, but Hanni hurriedly grabbed her wrist before she could. “No!” she cries, desperately, “No, let’s not give them something to post about, Hyein!”

“Fine,” she huffs, crossing her arms over her chest and instead, standing there and continuing to glare.

“I think I’m going to go home, though,” Solar finally announces, looking back to Minji, “I’ll… take you up on that offer, Ji.”

Minji was already turning to go grab their coats, “Yeah, of course, one sec.”

Hanni was rubbing Solar’s shoulder as a sign of comfort while Minji grabbed their coats. The girl returned only seconds later, handing Solar her coat with a soft, close lipped grin. Solar focused on putting the coat on over her costume, for the second time, while Minji turned back to the friends, “you guys staying?” she pends, glancing back to the stage, where the contestants were finally reaching an end, “Looks like judging starts soon.”

“Yeah, we have to,” Hyein frowns, “well, probably not have to, but… I really wanna win.”

She was clearly apologetic because she was still worried about Solar. But Solar was smiling, and her smile had not faltered despite how the girls seemed to believe she was crumbling inside. “You can’t leave,” she insists, “you’re totally gonna win.”

“I know!” the girl cries, her excitement bursting out of her before she could stop it, “I’m gonna get so many clients!”

“Hey, hey, is everything okay?” A voice interrupted Hyein’s prideful exclamations, and everyone’s eyes looked to Mark Lee, who was standing there in his Clark Kent costume, raking his eyes over everyone of them to garner the situation. When his eyes meet Solar’s, something moved in his irises, something harder that turned softer, “Hey, Sol… I’m sorry… I tried to tell Jaemin not to let them come on stage but he’s just… he’s Jaemin, and he was not listening to me because he says I don’t have any authority over him… and…”

“…Mark, it’s okay,” Solar cut him off, because he was starting to ramble and she was more than ready to just go home and try to process everything that had happened that night, “it’s fine, I’m just going to go home, it’s been a long night.”

“Oh,” his eyes widen momentarily, and he looks at her friends in confusion, “so, are you guys…”

“No, we’re staying for the contest results,” Hyein informs.

“Oh, cool,” he nods, as that had been his question, before looking back to Solar, “you want me to walk you? I could use a break from here, anyway.”

“Uh…” Solar spouts, looking to Minji, who had been secretly staring at Mark like she was going to hurt him. The girl had changed her expression the second Solar turned, however, clearly going through every emotion possible, as she tried to think of any excuse for him to not come with them that wasn’t going to break all of it open right there in the middle of Sigma Chi’s living room.

“Don’t you have some judging to do?” Minji asks blankly.

Mark briefly glanced back to the stage, where Jaemin was frantically talking with Jeno now that the final contestant had done their introduction and left the stage.

“Nah,” he responds with a shrug, “I already told him my top three.”

“Really?!” Hyein cries, “Oh, you better have picked us, Mark… I swear to God…”

“…Whoa, whoa,” he puts his hands up in defense as the girl pointed an accusing finger at him, “of course I did, you guys were always my number one.”

Hanni continued to smile her bright smile, saying something about how kind Mark was, and Hyein made a sound of contempt since that was the right answer. But there was something evident in the girl’s expressions that one could only notice if they paid close enough attention, which Solar Lee was not doing that night, not anymore.

“Alright, whatever,” Solar sighs, spinning on her heel and heading for the door before anyone else could start talking again, “let’s leave, guys, I can’t stand this anymore.”

“Be safe, Sol,” Hanni calls from behind, over the yelling of the other students, “text when you get home, please!”

And Solar headed out into the night air of Syracuse University with Mark and Minji.

54: worked in their favor this time

It was thirty five past midnight when the so called campus heartthrob walked down the stairs, only the second time of the night, with his red devil horns the girls screamed over suddenly missing, lips slightly pinker, and a smudge of gold on his left cheek. There was no telling if anyone could tell under the dim lights, if anyone was sober enough to tell. People were winding down whilst others were only getting crazier, the stench of spilt alcohol and burnt marijuana strong enough to make anyone high. Jeno was doing another keg stand, and the winners of an apparent costume contest were being announced. Still, only about half of the students in the room cared about such a thing by that point.

Not many people seemed to notice him, he didn’t move much nor attempt to call attention to himself, but he was also Haechan.

He wasn’t paying any mind to anything or anyone in particular, his eyes just casually appeared to be looking at nothing, like he was nowhere to be, no one to consider. In reality, he was searching for someone, he just knew how to hide it. He spotted Mark on stage next to Jeno and Jaemin, playing off his ridiculous facade to the entire school.

Then, he saw Hyein and Hanni, who had apparently just won first place, squealing in an egregious amount of excitement for winning a drunken costume contest at a fraternity Halloween party, jumping around and hugging each other. Hyein had accepted her poorly made award with pride, holding it in the air and leaning into the microphone to say, “My rates have gone up, but this is proof of my legacy.”

“Um, she means thank you!” Hanni nervously leaned in to pipe, and at that, people began to cheer and whistle.

Someone in the crowd yelled out about how they were missing two of their fairies, but the girls had already been rushing off the stage.

“Hanni,” Hyein was nudging the girl’s arm like a madman, clearly trying very hard to contain the noises she wanted to scream, “Hanni, did you see his horns, they’re gone!”

“Yes, Hyein,” Hanni shushes her, “Yes, I saw it!”

Haechan was moving through the room now, unhurried, continuing his slow read of the ground floor with an efficiency that was quite painful to watch, once you knew what he was doing. He checked the kitchen doorway, the corner by the breakfast table, he looked at the dance floor for a few seconds, and then at the front door that had shut only moments earlier.

The girls had been fast enough to step in front of him before he could move from where he was standing. Their actions were quick enough that the average person wouldn’t of noticed, but Haechan did, even in his slightly intoxicated state.

“She left,” Hanni offers, softly, because she felt he deserved something like that, “um, about two minutes ago.”

For a split second, something moved across the boy’s expression, almost hurt, longing, like something stuck under a rock. “Mm, right,” he clears his throat, entirely casual, as if that hadn’t been the reason he’d come back down those stairs.

“With Mark,” Hyein blurts, impulsively, partly with the purposeful intent to bother him, but also because it was information he was already gathering. Still, Hanni snapped to look at her in complete disappointment. “What?! He’s gonna find out!”

“Minji is there, too,” Hanni immediately turns to add in a calm voice, “they left together.”

Hanni noticed the way the line of his shoulders changed by perhaps, a half inch, the moment Minji’s name left her lips, the way whatever calculation he was running got a different number.

“Alright,” he monotones, and that was going to be the end of it. He was going to casually turn around, go back upstairs, they all realized it at the same time. And the girls began to feel everything, the plan, staircase, two minutes, start to slide back down the hill.

“Haechan,” Hyein practically yells like a psychopath, which no one other than him and Hanni seemed to notice, since the music was back on now, the bass slamming against the walls, vibrating the photos. The boy stopped, seeming to argue with himself before he slowly turned back around. “Look, for the record, we know Mark’s…” she suddenly cut herself off, realizing she was about to blurt out the entire thing in the middle of Sigma Chi, with Danielle herself only twenty feet away. Hanni’s elbow found her ribs so fast that she had no choice but to stop, cursing out at Hanni in annoyance, wheezing, “talking to people… like… that he shouldn’t be… Ow, Hanni!”

He didn’t move a muscle.

His eyes came up, going from Hyein to Hanni, and Hanni watched him take that half-sentence apart in his head. She understood, somehow, that he already knew, it was obvious, wasn’t it? There was really only one person it could be, the same girl Solar complained about on multiple occasions. It didn’t take a genius.

Still, he pended anyway, “who might that be?”

“We’re on the same page, Haechan,” Hanni puts a hand firmly on Hyein’s shoulder and leans in to assure him, tone soft and comforting, “we don’t want to start anything, and we don’t have anything concrete enough to tell you in confidence.”

There was not a single namable emotion on his face.

“You should go,” he deadpans, finally, and at the sight of their bewildered expressions, adds, “Jaehyun gets back soon.”

“Oh, thank you…” Hanni had started to say, but he was gone before she could finish.

The two girls stood there, feet away from the front door of Sigma Chi, the bass continuing to pump around them, students still jumping around to the beat as if they had no cares in the world. Hyein seemed to watch the carefree energy of it, for a moment, before she turned to Hanni, “was that good?”

When Hanni didn’t immediately say anything, the girl frantically continues, “I mean, that was good, clearly… he’s missing his horns, like, they clearly just made out… and you saw how happy Solar was… I mean…”

“Yeah,” Hanni cuts her off, gently, “it was good.”

And the two of them wished that they could jump with joy, celebrate like they had done a good thing and now their friend could finally be happy.

But that was in fact, the last thing they felt like doing.

“Han,” Hyein mutters, “what are we gonna do about Mark and Danielle?”

“I have no idea, Hyein.”

=

The cold outside was a physical relief to the sweaty, humid atmosphere with the heat on eighty of Sigma Chi. Solar laid a hand flat across her face as she walked the first block with her coat open, just to feel it, she claimed.

It was completely silent for the first while. The three of them made a shape, Minji on her left with her hands in the pockets of her own coat, and Mark on her right with his hands in his jacket. For two blocks, it was peaceful, just three students walking through the late fall air after a Halloween party. There was nothing crazy about it, nothing interesting to see. The music let go of them, a layer at a time, words first, then melody, before everything else but the bass, which held on the longest, thudding up through the sidewalk like the campus was refusing to give it up.

“That was insane,” Mark finally voices, something he had clearly been holding in, “if I would’ve saw them earlier, I would’ve kicked them out without a second thought, man.”

“It’s fine, Mark,” Solar repeated, “it was to be expected, honestly.”

“They could’ve at least made it a good costume,” Minji shakes her head, boots scraping against the concrete.

“Danielle made eye contact with me,” Solar announces, making it sound like she venting, trying to get something off her chest. Mark already knew she didn’t like Danielle, that she had been onto her. Solar had no idea the fact that he was closer with her than she ever thought, but she had a feeling based off of Danielle’s words, one she was simply attempting to get the tiniest bit of information about.

“Really?” Mark pended, eyes trailing away to the night sky, “Did she try to talk to you?”

“Nope,” Solar sighs, “I’m onto her though, and she knows it.”

She watched Mark’s face then, the way something flooded through him, the way he pushed it off of him and pretended his hands were still too cold in his pockets, bringing them out to rub them together. “She’s definitely suspicious,” Mark agrees.

And that was it, he dropped it and added nothing else. Minji watched the exchange happen, not knowing if she should open her mouth or let it play out. She’s already onto him, a part of her thought then, because Solar wasn’t stupid, was she? Yet, Minji still wasn’t sure if she trusted someone like Haechan, either.

Solar and Mark fell into a more light hearted conversation after that, because Solar did what she tended to do, which was push her doubt to the back of her mind and try to give him the benefit of the doubt. For she had no real confirmation that it’s who Danielle was talking about, it wasn’t like she said Mark’s name to her. She didn’t have a real reason to trust Haechan, but she couldn’t help but think back to the way he looked on that rooftop when he told her about what it felt like to get something ripped from your fingertips, to not be able to find your passion again because it’d been drained out of you. Someone who said things like that, they weren’t someone playing a game.

But what was it that had nothing to do with her brother, and how could it be anything other than Mark Lee?

“Welp, this is my stop,” Minji exhales, trying to hide the fact she was dreading it, stopping at the lamppost that cuts off towards the honors dorm. Her pink wings twinkle underneath the dim street lights, and her irises are soft as they peer into Solar’s, “you’re alright, for real, Sol?”

She was looking at her with a look in her eyes that seemed to communicate that Solar could tell her the truth. It wasn’t that she was admitting she thought something was wrong with Mark, not yet, but it was more of girl code, to check to make sure they felt safe enough. After all, it was the middle of the night, even if she had been alone with Mark various times before. Minji felt uneasy about it, thinking about all of the things he had possibly been giving to the one girl on campus that had been making Solar’s life hell.

Solar opened her mouth for a split second before anything came out, “yeah,” she nods, “go get some sleep, Ji.”

“You swear?” Minji asks again, stepping a foot closer to her and uttering out lower, so that Mark, who was a few feet away to give them space, could barely hear.

“Swear, Ji,” Solar repeats, in her brighter tone, sending the girl a reassuring smile.

She exhales a cloud of cold air into the atmosphere as she grips the strap of her camera bag, stepping back again towards her path. “Okay, but I have my phone on me,” she firmly informs her, before taking another few steps back, “night, duo.” Her eyes slowly landed on Mark, who at the notice of her beginning to leave, had turned back around to stand closer to Solar, offering a small wave in her direction. “Mark,” Minji states his name, flatter than she ever had, and sent him a single nod, as if she was telling him something.

And then she turned and walked up off the hill with her hands in her pockets, alone, and Solar watched her go for a few seconds, because something about the shape of her under the streetlights snagged at her, before the cold got into her collar and she turned back around.

She’d been so sure that she trusted Mark until she saw Haechan on the second floor.

That was the entire problem.

“You were… uh… gone… for a long time… upstairs,” Mark had sputtered out once they had walked for a couple of minutes, listening to the slush of the fall leaves piling onto the ground in the wind.

Solar’s stomach dropped about four inches. She clenched her fists in the pockets of her coat, keeping her face entirely unbothered. “There was a line,” she tells him.

She figured he would drop it then. Usually, Mark did not have the guts to push. But he seemed to be extra daring that night, like he’d seen or realized something he wished he hadn’t.

“Did you see him?”

“Who…” she tries, but the second she turned her head to look at him, she knew there wasn’t a point in trying to act like an idiot. Still, it would’ve been easy to lie, right? Even if he saw the change in her, the swelling of her bottom lip, she could muster it out anyway and leave it alone. But he was evidently asking in a way that meant he already knew, and Solar knew lying to someone who already knows is how you hand them something more to look at. “Not long,” she admits.

“Oh,” he mumbles, as if it still stung anyway, breaking their eye contact to stare ahead at the sidewalk.

“It wasn’t anything serious,” Solar offers.

“It’s chill, Sol,” he hurriedly speaks up before she could say anything more, “you don’t… you don’t owe me any kind of report.”

“You’ve got something to say,” the brunette monotones, “you might as well spit it out now, Mark.”

Just her mannerisms, the way the words flew off her tongue, was enough for him to know. But the words were stuck in the back of his throat, and he pretended to need to cough from the cold, the two of them walking another half a block. A car went by on the brick street through the campus, somebody hanging out the back window in a Scream mask, screaming out the lyrics to This is Halloween before it was gone as fast as it came.

“He’s been…” he starts but stops, the words tasting sour on his tongue, “uh, he’s been using again, Sol. It’s… it’s bad, worse than before.”

Her feet began to scrape louder against the concrete. “Mark…”

“I’m not talking about the post,” he goes on, anyway, “and don’t… the post is fucked, I don’t think it’s right, either. But it’s right, he’s relapsed worse than any of us have ever seen, and I really don’t think it’s safe to be around him right now… And I’m not saying that because of your brother.”

The post is fucked, but it’s right.

Somehow, the cold had gotten inside her coat, somewhere around the collar, taking up residence.

“I already know about the drugs,” she monotones, “like you said, the post. You know, the one glorifying his addiction to thousands of people.”

“I wish there was something I could do,” Mark breathes, “I do, I’m trying, but…”

“But what?”

“He means it, Sol.”

She stopped walking then. “Mark,” she exhales, beginning to feel like she just had some version of this conversation, “you’re gonna have to give me some context, here.”

“Okay…” the boy stops with her, taking his hands out of his pockets to run them across his face, as if the next things he was going to say would pain him, “he can’t… he can’t keep his word, you know that. He means every word, then Tuesday happens, and it’s not because he was lying on Monday, it’s because there isn’t anybody home to keep it.”

“What?” the girl snorts, “What, you think the drugs have drove him braindead?”

“No!” the boy cries, horrified, “I’m just saying, I’ve watched people build everything around something he thought he meant.”

The wind continued to rustle the leaves around them, the flickering lamppost began to come into view.

There were about nine things, nine that she could have said. She could feel everyone of them, she could feel all of the possibilities, the words hanging on the tip of her tongue. Have you ever talked to Danielle Marsh, Mark? Why would you agree with an SUnews post using your best friend’s addiction as content? And why do you and her opinions tend to coincide all of the time?

“You clearly don’t like him,” were the words she said instead, delivering them in a complete, innocent joking tone.

They started walking again, and Mark kicked a random rock that screeched against the pavement for a few feet. “Love him,” he corrects, “I’ve known him since we were twelve, that’s exactly why I’m telling you this right now.”

Maybe most of the questions she had about Mark Lee could be individually explainable, they always could. The doubt was still fresh in her mind, but she also couldn’t deny that she’d seen the bottles on the side steps, the four seconds of him under the moonlight with the laptop glowing, the empties standing at his feet. His saliva tasted like whiskey, hot on his breath, drunk likely moments before. She’d have to be an idiot to try to say it wasn’t obvious.

I’ve watched people build everything around something he thought he meant.

In reality, Mark Lee did not have the slightest clue what Haechan could have possibly said to her. He did not have any intel from Danielle, he was going off of his gut and what it was telling him to do, if he truly wanted to come out on the brighter side. So he did it, even if it felt wrong.

“You know I’m not trying to tell you what to do,” he adds after they walk for another while, “seriously, I don’t want to be like your brother.”

“I know,” she flashes him a small smile, “I get it.”

“Really, I’d just rather be the guy that said something than the guy that just watched.”

“Mark.”

“I know.”

They walked the last block without saying anything else. She was in her own world, not paying enough attention to the fact Mark was growing closer to her with each step, his hand fluttering just next to hers. Their fingers grazed a few times, his pinky stretching out to nearly grab hers, before he’d nervously decided against it.

The lamppost was flickering more than usual.

“Thanks for the walk,” she hums as soon as they stop at that corner.

“Course, thanks for the dance,” he gratefully returned, “it was still the best Halloween I’ve had, Sol.”

Something twisted in her chest for the hundredth time that night. Her lips form a straight line, and before she could fight it, she stepped forward, leaning up to leave a faint kiss on his cheek.

“Goodnight, Mark.”

It was eleven when Haechan moseyed into the kitchen, dark hair a mess atop his head, eyes squinting from the horrid sunlight peeking through the large windows. The boys had done a decent job at cleanup, though he didn’t recall much of it. He’d drank, though he hadn’t taken any pills, enough that he couldn’t think perfectly back to everything that happened after Solar left. Though, the one thing he couldn’t forget was her.

*“Dude,* seriously, Jaehyun is going to kill you,” Jeno had been shaking his head in dismay, but also with the tone of someone genuinely impressed, “Or if not him…” he cuts himself off at the sight of Haechan entering, making a whistling sound, “this guy will, won’t ya, buddy?” He calls, stepping forward to where Haechan was opening the fridge to slap his back.

“Don’t do that again,” Haechan monotones as he takes the orange juice out, twisting the cap and tilting his head back to drink it straight out of the carton.

Mark had been carefully watching his friend, though when he turned around, he ripped his eyes away like he hadn’t been. “Not that serious, man,” he finally shrugs, towards Jeno, “she’s my friend, seriously.”

Jeno snorted, “Aight, bro, that’s why you post her like that.”

At that, Mark’s ears grew red, and he broke the eye contact with Jeno to look down at the cereal he’d been munching on, suddenly extremely interested.

Haechan watched it, he’d been staring at him now. He knew he could feel the burn of his gaze, and he’d stood up straight from where he’d been leaning against the granite countertops, still holding the orange juice, and made a disappointed ts sound.

“Subtly’s never been his strong suit,” he deadpans to Jeno, before spinning on his heel and leaving, orange juice in hand, not giving Mark the slightest of chances to respond.

Jeno watched him go, waiting until he heard the boy’s footsteps going up the stairs, before he turned back to Mark with the back of his hand over his mouth, like he was in utter disbelief. “Shit,” he giggled, “I never thought I’d see the day.”

“Man, I’m really not in the mood…” Mark was sighing, feeling the bitterness rising in his veins as he recalled the reality of last night. All he could hope was that his words had done something. He took another spoonful of his cereal, praying that Jeno would drop the subject.

But Jeno never listened to him, he knew that well.

“What’s the topic today?” Jaemin piped as he entered the kitchen moments later, his eyes still rather red, skin a little pale. He was a textbook example of someone that partied far too hard, took too much, yet continued on like nothing happened. In fact, he opened the freezer to grab another bottle of alcohol, as if he’d been saving it, before he leaned against the counter to face them, “Oh, let me guess, did you guys see that girl dressed as Lola Bunny last night?”

Jeno immediately snapped his neck to stare at him, intrigued.

“She’s upstairs,” Jaemin informs, proudly, before he could even ask, “safe to say she’ll probably be out for awhile.”

“Man, fuck you,” Jeno cursed, “and to think I got stuck with that Raven girl.”

“Beggars can’t be choosers, dude, do better.”

“Oh, but, Mark and Haechan are in love,” Jeno recalls, jumping back to the old topic, much to the pain of Mark, “or, he’s doing some dumb shit again, beats me, point is… these two are fucked.”

Jaemin took a swig of his bottle as he looked to Mark, “damn, you’re fucking shameless, aren’t you?”

“Bro, I told you, it’s not like that.”

“So, you like her?”

“Nah… I…” Mark stuttered, choking on his words, seemingly unable to get the proper ones out. He took a breathe, and tried again, “Yeah, I mean, no shit.”

The two boys nodded slowly, Jeno mumbling loser before he’d sent him a fake smile. Jaemin had pursed his lips in thought for a second, like the idea of genuinely liking someone romantically was absolutely foreign. “Huh…” he hums, “so, what the fuck is up with Haechan?”

-

Some lessons have to be learned the hard way.

Solar’s lips formed a thin line of contemplation. It wasn’t Mark’s fault someone had taken the photograph, that she had kissed his cheek, nor that the second had been warm, easy, before everything else came back to complicate it. He’d been kind to her, he was always kind to her. That was the part that made the arithmetic so unbearable.

Her eyes watched the heart appear over the messages.

For several minutes after that, she laid back against the pillow of her pink. bedroom, phone resting on her stomach, staring up at the ceiling.

It was Saturday. She couldn’t miss anymore practices.

Which was why she’d thrown her legs over the side of the bed, climbing out to get ready for her day, feeling a little more energy than she’d had in recent times.

For no particular reason, though, surely.

The gaming lab had the energy of a room full of people who’d won a single tournament and in turn, had been sentenced to prepare for another. Things had already been heating up since Monday, the one she’d missed, though she hadn’t missed one since then, she just hadn’t had as much of the energy she once had, either. Even though she’d ended up performing well in the tournament, eSports had become more of an afterthought for her, even though it had been the one thing she had for herself.

That’s yours, remember that.

Olivia was already complaining by the time she entered, stretched across two chairs with her hood pulled over her head, claiming success was a scam invented to punish talented people. Haerin was beside her, a coffee in her hands, nodding along as if this was the most intelligent thing she had ever heard, or perhaps simply providing therapeutic support. And Chenle sat there, in the middle, his practice range open, appearing to be ignoring them, which meant he was listening to every word.

Throwing her bag on the floor, she pulls out the chair in between Chenle and Minji, falling into it with a thud.

Minji glanced up from her chair, in the midst of adjusting her sensitivity, dark hair tucked behind one ear. Her eyes made one quiet scan over the girl’s face, not invasively nor in a way anyone else would’ve noticed, before they’d met her irises. “She lives,” she offers finally, “the one and only Stella.”

“Don’t make me go home,” Solar warns, jokingly, though a yawn leaves her lips, “I’m frankly not in the mood.”

“You can’t!” Haerin called from the end of the row, “Olivia’s already resigning.”

“She’s a liar,” Olivia accused, next to Chenle, “all I said was achievement is labor exploitation, jeez. Ever heard of an opinion?”

“You posted it six times on your story, by the way,” Chenle mutters, “that’s not something a normal person does.”

“So what? I speak out against what I believe in,” Olivia snaps, “are you trying to silence women?”

The nerdy boy exhales, already exhausted, and turns back to face his computer screen, clicking around furiously as he monotones, “I am removing myself from this conversation.”

Solar couldn’t help the chuckle from escaping her lips as she reached down to turn on her PC, the machinery beneath the desk humming awake, colors beginning to bleed across the monitor and her fingertips. When she glanced to the side again, Minji was looking at her again, the slightest hint of a smile on her lips, as she’d been listening to their teams conversation while watching the way Solar laughed.

“Hey,” Solar urges, “stop staring, you need to focus up, captain.”

The girl stared at her for another moment, “uhuh, someone seems better.”

The words were flat enough to be casual, which was probably why they found somewhere beneath Solar’s ribs anyway. She thought about all of the things she could say, the possibilities, but then she recalled the way Minji had to know already. She was clearly in on it.

So why did a ping of guilt settle in her chest?

“Wouldn’t say that,” she finally admits, turning back to her screen, “maybe I just slept well.”

Minji clearly didn’t believe her, but she smiles anyway, not pushing any further. It provided a specific relief, the relief of being known yet not forced to explain, something she seemed to offer her so often that she’d begun taking it without realizing how rare it truly was.

Doyoung entered the lab minutes later, clipboard tucked underneath one arm, a coffee in his opposite hand, appearing far too put together for a Saturday afternoon surrounded by five college students whose sleep schedules were considered acts of violence. “How are we feeling?” he pended, raising a brow as he sets his things down on the middle table, like always. His eyes look carefully over the five, before he exhales, “We didn’t party too hard last night, did we?”

“No!” Olivia was first to cry, quick enough that it was believed by no one. The look he sent her caused her to falter a bit, “Maybe.”

“I supervised some drunk idiots,” Chenle offered.

“I watched Chucky three times,” Haerin chimes.

Solar and Minji didn’t add anything, because everyone became too interested in Haerin’s activity.

“Nonetheless,” Doyoung continues, “we must go into heavy preparation mode, regionals is sneaking up on us.”

Olivia grumbled, leaning back in her chair and pulling her hood over her eyes again.

“Every team between here and regionals has an entire bracket of footage explaining exactly how you play, how you win,” he goes on, ignoring Olivia’s antics.

“It’s almost irrelevant if we’re better, no?” Minji pipes, her cockiness seeming to overcloud her judgment.

“Wrong,” he corrects, “counters are very real, and that’s what they’re going to do. Or worse, what about when they play your comp better than you?” Some of them let out sounds of offense, but he raises a hand to silence them. “Public practice is off today, so no more comms or free footage for opponents, today is separation work, then a closed scrim. We’re not going to practice the version of yourselves they’ve already seen.”

Then, they started playing.

The first map was Rialto, and the separation part of his so called separation work turned out to be less of a concept and more of a person attack. Doyoung kept Minji on the longest available angle while Solar anchored Haerin and Chenle through the center, Olivia being given the freedom to move between the two sides, so long as she commed between. It felt wrong for the first few fights, as if someone had quietly rearranged the keys underneath her fingers, every instinct inside of her waiting for Minji to move so she could follow.

And then the fourth fight arrived.

The enemy Ana disappeared from the far opening a half second too early, their tank pretending to give space while the rest of them began to shift behind the bridge, and Solar felt the shape of it before the pressure arrived, the same way she’d seen the tournament finals change seconds before anyone else in the room could name how. “Rotate high,” she calls.

“They haven’t committed,” Olivia counters, but followed anyway.

“They will,” Solar insists.

Chenle had listened first, turning before the enemy tank pushed through main, Haerin climbing with him as Solar held her teleport instead of wasting it to arrive early. The ultimate that would’ve caught their entire backline crashed into the empty road beneath them.

“Wait, they’re ass!” Olivia was screeching into the mic, “I’m ulting.”

“Supports exposed,” Minji added.

Solar was already looking, shooting the first kunai at the Ana. The second finished her, and Minji eliminated the other support before the enemy team understood their ambush had turned into a funeral. Chenle moved forward, remaining measured rather than greedy, forcing the remaining three backward while Olivia appeared behind them, beginning to laugh like that of the Joker.

“Good read,” Doyoung commented from behind them, arms crossed over his chest.

Her shoulder relaxed, fingers continuing to move without needing to be forced. The rhythm hadn’t returned because of a boy, per se, it had never left in the first place.

By the end of the map, the last thing on her mind was some ridiculous post about her dating life. The victory screen flashed across their monitors. Chenle pushed one side of his headset away from his ear, staring at the numbers as if they’d personally confirmed a theory he’d been pondering all week.

“Your rotating instincts are back,” he mumbles, “you kinda fell off, for a while.”

Solar twisted her head at him, raising a brow, “is that your way of saying I seem better?”

“It’s my way of saying you’re rotating instincts are back,” he repeats, blankly, “try to keep them this time.”

“All I’m hearing is a yes.”

“I didn’t say…” he tries, but Minji had leaned over to cut into the conversation.

“He means yes.”

“Thanks, Le,” Solar chimes anyway.

He looked between the two girls, seeming to accept that the conversation had escaped the boundaries of logic, before sliding his headset back over his ear, “you’re welcome, I guess, man.”

The closed scrim began after that, Doyoung giving them a team from outside their conference whose names they weren’t allowed to look up until the block ended. Solar didn’t play perfectly, by any means, she’d accidentally burned one suzu too early, followed by an angle she should’ve let die, and received the specific sound of Doyoung’s pen tapping against his clipboard that had begun to haunt her in her sleep.

The difference was that she corrected it before anyone could tell her to.

She talked more than she had in weeks, tracking the enemy supports, calling the reset before Minji could, and when their formation got pulled apart on the second map, she didn’t panic or throw every resource towards the most familiar person on the screen.

They’d won the fight anyway, and before they knew it, the game resulted in another victory.

“Break,” Doyoung announced after, giving them ten minutes while he answered something on his phone and waiting for their next scrim to be prepared.

In unison, the five of them let out breathes of relief, Haerin jumping up to excuse herself to the restroom, Olivia exclaiming that she was taking an emergency nap. Solar lowered her headset, reaching for her water bottle, only to discover it’d been empty for an amount of time that would’ve earned a lecture if Doyoung noticed. Around her, chairs rolled away from desks, voices following Solar as she rose from her chair.

“Vending machine?” Minji hums, already beginning to jump up from her chair.

“Water,” Solar answers.

“I’ll come,” she chimes, “I need a snack.”

“Playing Ashe brings it out of you?”

“It’s a full time job,” the girl dramatically informs.

“I know you’re not talking,” Solar chuckles, “alright, let’s go, I need a Monster.”

Minji was shaking her head in awe, “you have a problem.”

“Right, and who’s enabling me?”

The two girls were about to head straight for the door, into the large lobby of the extracurricular building. She’d taken a single step before something moved behind the large glass windows of the eSports lab. At first, it looked like her own reflection, and she’d been too busy bickering with Minji to fully focus on it, a dark shape caught between the dead stream camera and the purple light bleeding across the lab, before the figure had shifted and the rest of them appeared further away.

Something twisted in her chest, and she took another few steps, still not leaving the lab. Minji had gotten momentarily distracted by Chenle suddenly asking her if she could get him something from the vending machine.

Haechan stood in the hallway, his hood pulled over his head, calibrated headphones resting around his neck, the strap of his laptop bag cutting across his chest, meaning he had a perfectly reasonable explanation for being there on a Saturday. The studios were upstairs, he could’ve easily been going there.

Yet, he was standing there, outside the window of the eSports lab, not looking anywhere other than at Solar Lee.

The sound of the room moved several feet away, Minji exhaling at the fact Chenle was being indecisive and starting to argue with her about what the most appropriate snack was for scrimming, the low hum of the PCs creating a white noise buzz, Doyoung’s pen busy scratching away on paper. He didn’t do anything, just stood there, not knocking or reaching for the door, body relaxed against the wall, like he’d simply happened to be there, though his eyes made the lie unnecessary.

He knew she was looking back, and he didn’t run. His chin lifted instead, the smallest greeting someone could offer, before he’d briefly raised two fingers.

Something in her stomach jumped before she could instruct it otherwise, her lips threatening to do the same thing they’d done when reading his messages.

Too many eyes, her brain yelled at her.

Haechan’s gaze moved across her face, like he’d caught it, before it’d shifted over her shoulder, at Minji and Chenle, Olivia asleep in the chair.

Then he was gone, just like that.
