56: scandalous queues with a side of denial

Alpha Phi was quiet in a way it hadn’t been in weeks.

It made sense, she supposed, given that most of the girls had returned sometime before dawn and had spent the entire day treating daylight like a personal attack. Someone left a single plastic fang on the second floor landing and no one else had cared enough, or had the energy, to pick it up. The whole house had the specific exhaustion of a place that’d gotten exactly what it wanted the night before and was now paying the invoice.

Solar had ate dinner with Hanni and Hyein at seven, about an hour after practice. The two had shockingly refrained from asking her more questions about her apparently, very interesting love life. Instead, they sat there at the small breakfast table in the far side of the kitchen, giggling away and talking about the fun conversations they had with Chenle and Renjun last night at the party, how they really underestimated them, and how weird they thought Jeno was.

“He’s not that bad,” Solar had shrugged when they asked her of her opinion of him.

Hyein had snickered to herself, and when Solar rose a brow to silently pend what was so funny, she pursed her lips for a second, debating, before she spouts, “I mean, of course you would think so.”

It was a poor joke about Haechan’s reputation and the fact they were sworn that she was in love with him. The realization of it caused her to gawk, reaching out to pinch Hyein, who had squealed and squirmed away from her reach.

“Not nice!” Hanni had exclaimed at the both of them, politely setting her fork down and swatting Solar’s insistent hand away from Hyein.

After the bizarre yet somewhat comforting chaos of her close friends, Solar told them she was feeling a bit sleepy and was going to call it an earlier night than usual. The two girls were sad, but agreed nonetheless, before telling her she was going to miss one of the best episodes of Gossip Girl as a result.

“I’ll survive,” she’d assured them softly, “I’ve seen it like three times anyway.”

“Your loss!” Hyein piped, already picking up the remote off the couch from where they’d been standing in the large living room. Solar rolled her eyes at her, spinning on her heel to head towards the stairs, and she swore under her breathe, she could hear Hyein muttering in between giggles, “Han, should I tell her to tell Haechan hi?”

“No, what’s wrong with you?!“

“Come on, she’s obviously about to go call him or something—”

“—Shush, she’s going to hear you!”

Solar indeed heard them, but she didn’t have the energy to turn and say anything, because she hated how right they managed to be, and never in her wildest dreams would she admit it.

So, she’d gone upstairs, deciding to take a warm shower at nine, and by ten, she’d already changed into the clothes she slept in, which was normal, sliding her chair out from under her desk and falling into it with a dramatic sigh.

Her eyes glance at the time that appears on the screen when she turns her computer on, 10:35.

Great, what was she supposed to do for 25 minutes?

She wasn’t waiting, was what she told herself. Yet, her fingers impatiently tapped on the desk in a hurried motion, like she was trying to speed up the clock that slowly ticked on her screen.

In reality, she had quite a lot of things to do. There was a Business reading she’d been procrastinating on since Wednesday, and the enemy team’s VOD from the closed scrim had finished processing. Doyoung had said, in that voice of his that made everything sound like a legal filing, that separation work only meant something if you kept doing it when no one was looking.

Deciding she had the time to be slightly productive, she exhales deeply before clicking open the VOD.

Her eyes narrowed in concentration, pieces of dark hair falling in her eyes that hadn’t successfully been pulled back into her ponytail.

That was, until she got bored, and decided to open her game client instead. For no reason, she thought, I just want to play my favorite game.

Sure, another voice in the back of her head laughed bitterly.

The lobby music started up, the same eight bars it had been looping since her freshman year of high school, and Solar Lee sat there with her hands in her lap, like a woman who’d wandered into a bedroom by accident. Her eyes dance to the clock on her phone, 10:47.

What a joke.

She wasn’t counting, per se, it was simply information, and she was someone who noticed information.

At 10:52, she got up and refilled her water bottle, making a smart decision to not have a Monster. And at 10:56, she returned to her chair and leaned back into the headrest, chewing on her bottom lip as her eyes repeatedly scanned the top of the screen.

She’d done this before, on a Wednesday in September at 11:45 instead of 11:00. He’d invited her without warning, and in response she’d told him she was busy yet accepted anyway because her heart refused to not. They’d played one game and talked to each other like two people conducting a hostage negotiation. But the moment she asked about Mark he’d thanked her for the game and dipped.

And she’d sat in this same chair afterward and thought, what the fuck?

At 10:59, her hand moved to the mouse before her brain filed the request, and humiliated with herself, she clicked to the hero browser instead as if she was suddenly indecisive about who she wanted to play. Her heart was doing something stupid, just to show her that she wasn’t fooling it, beating out of her chest and twisting into a knot in anticipation for something as silly as a game invite.

The invite popped up on her screen at eleven exactly.

No message before the fact, no you up or ready, no acknowledgment of the fact she had spent an entire morning informing him he couldn’t assume the answer was yes. But the invite flared across the top of her screen with his stupid username daringly peering back at her, patient as a tax bill.

What was she supposed to do?

@HA3CHAN has invited you to a group.

She stared at it for four seconds, before she clicked accept without another thought, because otherwise, she was going to run out of time. That’s what she told herself the reason was, at least.

The channel connected with a soft two-tone chime, and then there was a room on the other side of her headset. Perhaps it was the part she hadn’t prepared for. In September, it was only text chat, the safety of a text box and the option to reread a sentence before she sent it. Now there was just air, the faint hiss of his open mic, the low mechanical sigh of a computer fan, and underneath it, far and muffled through what she presumed was a closed door, was the unmistakable bass thud of the Sigma Chi house on a Saturday for one of Jaemin’s infamous recovery parties. And she swore, if she focused hard enough, she could hear Jeno’s screams.

He didn’t say a word, and she could hear him not, which was ten times worse.

“Your breathing in the mic,” she blurts to her ceiling, despite how she didn’t want to be the one who spoke first, it spilled out of her anyway.

A brief beat of silence passed, before the honey seeped into her ears like ecstasy, “I’m alive,” he’d hummed, “sorry to disappoint you, princess.” He sounded almost half asleep, considerably closer than he had any right to be, with no room between it and her ear. She’d heard him speak what felt like a hundred times, yet she’d never heard him inside of her own head.

“You didn’t ask,” she reminded him sassily instead, clicking through to the queue screen rather loudly, “just want that on the record.”

“It’s on the record,” he monotones, before softening his voice by the slightest amount, “if that’s what makes you happy.”

“I’m serious, Haechan.”

“Mm, I know,” he agrees convincingly, the exact shape of his mouth blatantly obvious when he said it, “you’re always serious, it’s one of your best features.”

“I’ll leave,” she deadpans, “don’t test me.”

“You sure?” he returns, unbothered, “You sure could— though, you’d have to close the client, because if you just sit there, I’m going to keep inviting you, and God forbid you have to explain to yourself why you keep looking at it.”

She opened her mouth to retort, not wanting to go down without a better fight than whatever this was. He was a smooth talker, and it pissed her off, didn’t it? There was no telling how many times he’d said things like this to other women.

“Queue,” she snaps.

“Queueing,” he echoes.

The wait was shockingly only eighty seconds, and she spent most of it aggressively adjusting a mouse sensitivity that’d been correct for six weeks.

The map was Ilios.

It took her exactly a single fight to recall that she had done this before but seemingly retained nothing useful from it. It was two months old by then, collected by a version of herself who’d not yet been on a rooftop, who’d never heard the bones of an unfinished track through a pair of borrowed headphones, who still believed the worst thing Haechan Lee was capable of was being an irritating man whore of a sweet talker.

But the girl sitting in the chair was paying significantly closer attention to a boy that was very far from any of those things, minus the sweet talker, and perhaps the irritation.

He took the same angles, the same identical, obnoxious, wildly overextended sight lines that had once killed her three separate times in a ranked game in September, including once in her own spawn, after which he had turned her character’s corpse and waved just to watch her tilt. Although she’d made a personal commitment to not think about that again, she’d honored it approximately never.

The difference was that they now belonged to her. Every time he vanished off the side of the objective into some position no reasonable person would occupy, something on the other team stopped existing.

The first time it happened she didn’t say anything.

By the second time, she was already moving. He’d pushed too far left onto the high ground above the well, the kind of greed that got people killed, and she felt the fight shift half a second before it did. The enemy tank turned, their support committed, and she was throwing her teleport into the wall behind him without him calling for anything at all.

“Behind,” she calls, too focused on the game that she’d forgotten who she was even playing with. Since they were the same rank, it didn’t feel any different than playing with her teammates.

Until his low voice melted into her ears, “mm.”

“Left, Haechan—”

“Heard you the first time, sweetheart.”

“Then, why aren’t you—”

She cut herself off that time, because she enemy tank came around the corner into a Widowmaker who was no longer there and a Kiriko who was. Solar cleansed the Ana nade off herself and watched him drop the support from a completely different angle somewhere on top of the opposite roof.

There was a long realm of silence that followed. One of their teammates used a nice job voice command.

“You held your teleport,” he notes suddenly.

“Obviously I held it.”

“You didn’t used to hold it.”

Her hand went still on the mouse. It was a small sentence, simple really, delivered flatly and without weight, in the tone of a man commenting on the weather in a city he didn’t live in. And it took her a moment of pondering to realize, he watched enough of her to know what she used to and currently does.

“When exactly,” she starts, having to fight every single bone in her body to hold back a smile, “would you have seen me not hold my teleport, Haechan?”

And for once, the pause was not due to her.

Down in the house below him, someone laughed at something loudly, a bellow that echoed through the entire house on top of the booming bass, followed by the sound of a door closing.

“Point,” he monotoned, as if he was deaf.

“Not an answer.”

“Sure isn’t,” he agrees, casually.

As badly as she wanted to argue, to demand at least one answer from him, the next fight started, and he was already gone onto some ledge she hadn’t even known about. And Solar realized, she was focusing harder than she had in a while on a game she was already playing at a collegiate level.

They took the well in under a minute, to which Solar said nothing in order to seem as if she didn’t notice. The rhythm had arrived somewhere in the middle of the second fight and hadn’t asked permission. It was the thing she couldn’t explain away, not to Minji, not to herself, that a person she hadn’t spoken to in what felt like weeks could occupy the other half of a map like he’d been assigned to her at birth. She swift stepped to him without checking, he grappled out before she got there, it should’ve wasted the teleport yet it never did.

This is fine, she tries to falsely assure herself, hauling herself up a wall she’d had no business climbing, this is what it looks like when two people are the same rank, you know this. You literally play on a team of people that are the same rank as you.

But the voice in the back of her head was none the wiser.

“You’re doing the thing.”

“What thing?”

“Climbing something to look occupied,” he offers, and she could almost hear the way he was trying not to snicker.

“It’s called high ground, Haechan,” she retorted, “maybe if you didn’t buy your account you’d know these kinds of things.”

“Mm, fierce one from you,” he cooed, “what, you don’t like the bottom, princess?”

There was a beat of nothing, the specific length of silence that a man allowed when he was waiting to see if she’d take the bait.

She did, every single time.

“You’re going to get venomed, idiot,” she deflected, though the annoyance was evident in her snappy tone.

“I’m not, though.”

“You literally are, they have a mine on the left—”

She’d checked, they had one on the left.

By the second point, though, she’d stopped narrating. Somewhere between the well and ruins, the two had slid into something that didn’t require sentences, and the ones that did happen were half length, clipped down to the parts that mattered, the way she and Minji had sounded by October. He called an enemy support’s cooldown before it burned, she threw a suzu at nothing at all, a full second before the nade left the Ana’s hand, because she’d seen the woman’s crosshair drift and known what it meant.

“That was early,” he’d observed.

“That,” she defends, “was correct, thank you very much.”

“Didn’t say it wasn’t.”

“You said it was early!”

“It was both,” he stated, as if it should’ve been obvious, “these things can coexist.”

There it was again, that low and unhurried voice that seeped into her skull with nowhere for her to store it. She thought, for the first time, about how many other girls had heard something like this, in rooms, in the dark, delivered with the same lazy precision because he had some innate ability to read their thoughts back with the punctuation corrected.

He does this, she told herself, jaw tightening, this is a thing he does, not a thing he’s doing.

Her Kitsune Rush went out under their feet, the point flipping again, but she didn’t seem to feel any better about it.

-

The lighthouse was where things went south.

They lost the first fight outright, which wasn’t a huge deal until they’d lost the second one on top of that. Their tank walked into a full dive with no cooldowns, causing Solar to burn her teleport chasing him, which she knew was wrong the instant she pressed it, arriving directly into the tail end of a Reaper ultimate.

“Fuck,” she hissed, watching her own body drop off the ledge into the water.

“Don’t do that again,” Haechan mumbles, almost under his breathe.

“You don’t have to tell me,” she complains bitterly, “I already know!”

“Relax, I’m not scolding you,” he chuckles, amused at her defensiveness over something so miniscule.

“You’re literally scolding me right now!”

“I’m telling you that you did it because he’s the one who called for help,” he continues, unfazed, “you go where you’re called, it’s a real problem, you should look into that.”

She sat in the spawn room, staring at her ceiling with briefly nothing to say for once. And as if that wasn’t enough, he’d hummed lowly, “Wasn’t talking about the teleport, princess.”

Oh, how much she hated him.

He’d made it sound like a rotation note, and she knew that it partly was, he was just simply an irritating human being who turned it into one of his sick double meanings. Still, it landed somewhere else entirely, somewhere down, to the left of her sternum, and she refused to think about it with sixteen seconds on the respawn timer and a boy in her ear who noticed everything but volunteered nothing.

“Third point,” was her response minutes later, “I’m not losing to a one trick.”

“No,” he confirms, “we aren’t.”

And they didn’t, even though it was ugly, their team fell apart twice but reassembled itself out of pure spite. Olivia would’ve described it as character development, and Doyoung would’ve said it was a clear learning opportunity in the voice he used when he meant a totally different thing and was trying to be nice about it. Haechan hooked into a position so aggressive it looped back around into being correct, with Solar following behind, holding the wall behind him and feeding him enough to survive.

It was when he asked her to basically go to spawn with him that she’d refused him, not once, but twice.

“No,” she insisted, “I can’t just leave our Zen.”

The boy made a hissing sound of disappointment, and almost like a whine went, “come on, pretty girl.”

Abruptly, a cough erupted from her throat.

“What’s wrong with you?!“ she cried, because his words caused her to miss what would’ve been a fight winning kunai into the Ana’s head.

“Careful,” he sternly remarks, “don’t want to ruin your aim, focus.”

The percentage climbed even though her cheeks were burning. It hit ninety nine and hung there, purely to be cruel about it, before the Victory screen flashed across her monitor. And as much as she hated it, she was shamefully grinning at a screen in her pink room at thirty past midnight like a complete loser.

“Told you,” he monotoned.

“You did not tell me anything—”

“—I told you we weren’t going to lose.”

“I said that!”

“Mm,” he hums, the sound of him settling back into his chair crinkling through the microphone, making the slightest creak, followed by the slight scrape of something being pushed across his desk, “starting to sound like me, too, aren’t you?”

Her cheeks felt like they were bound to make her sweat. Before she could think of how to respond, her phone buzzed next to her mousepad.

[minji]:

u up, i was abt to queue

gotta fix whatever happened on second point

The smile came off her face in a millisecond, the way a tablecloth would fly off a table in the wind. It was eleven forty on a Saturday, and her beloved duo was awake, doing exactly what Solar should’ve been doing, asking her to do it together. It was nothing out of the ordinary, it was their typical routine that felt natural by now, that all started from something as silly as a celebratory queue.

I’m in a game, she could type, already queued, very simple options. With a friend, her brain pinged, and suddenly everything seemed to shut down.

She ripped her eyes away from the three messages shamefully, looking at the green UI and the icon in the top right of her screen, his username flashing in the left corner to remind her he was still there.

[minji]:
gn duo

They played two more after that, winning one, losing the other, in a way that was entirely the fault of a Ball player who Solar wished the worst upon.

By the time the second one ended, it was nearly one in the morning, the bass underneath his microphone slowly beginning to thin into something patchier, the sound of a house emptying by attrition. Someone’s laugh went down a hallway and disappeared, a door shut further away than the last one.

She heard what she assumed to be his phone ding once, then twice, then a third time, before he’d hushed under his breath in annoyance and presumably silenced it. Her teeth found her bottom lip.

Neither of them queued again, but they didn’t leave, either.

The menu music started it’s eight bars over, and Solar sat in her chair with her knees pulled to her chest, headset still on, looking at a group of two in the corner of her screen. And it occurred to her, that this was the longest she had ever been truly alone, and fully awake, with Haechan in her life. It had only been maybe half an hour on the rooftop in October, whatever the hallway had been on Friday. She’d spent the night in his bedroom but that was an entirely different story she was refusing to count in the equation. But now, it had been over two hours of a boy breathing quietly into her ear across campus with nothing to talk about and no apparent interest in ending it.

It would be very easy for her to leave the group.

“Your fan’s loud,” she complained.

“It’s old.”

“Well, it sounds like it’s dying,” she muttered, leaning back into her chair with a huff and crossing her arms over his chest, even though he couldn’t see any of it.

“It’s been dying since March, sweetheart, we’ve made peace.”

How irritating was it that she had to bite her tongue to keep from laughing?

There was nothing again after that, though it was comfortable in a way that made her uncomfortable, because it was one thing to spar with him, but a complete different one to sit there while a menu loop played in both their ears and neither of them pretended to have a reason.

Ask him, the voice in her head yelled, what did Hanni and Hyein say to you? How bad is it, really? Why did you look like that on the side steps with all of those bottles? What the hell did you mean by August?!

Every single one was sitting right there, fully formed and grammatically correct. She thought about the last time she’d gotten curious in a voice channel at midnight with him, the flat gray of a lobby with one person in it. Apparently, the one thing she learned in September was that.

So, she didn’t ask.

“You’re ass at well, by the way.”

There was a pause, before her ears were filled with a sound she’d never heard before, short, low, involuntary. He’d laughed, not the flat one he did in public, the humorless escape he used like punctuation, but almost a giggle.

Her stomach dropped straight through the pink carpet.

“Mm, you really think so?” he pends, intrigued.

“Uhuh, you get hooked into the well every time off grapple cooldown, it’s actually really embarrassing—”

“And what is it when you burn teleport too early and fail to climb to high ground in time?“

“A misinput.”

“Right,” he hums, “whatever you say, pretty.”

“Stop calling me that,” she hisses, “where did you even get that from?!”

“My arsenal,” he deadpanned, as if it was funny to anyone other than himself, “saved it just for you.”

She wanted to punch him.

But he was miles away, so instead, she was sitting there smiling at nothing, alone in the dark, grinning at her ceiling like someone with no dignity left to protect. And perhaps the worst part of it all was thinking about the fact that if he could see her right now, he’d make some dry comment, and she almost wished he could.

Too many eyes, the words popped into her brain like clockwork.

Though, there weren’t any half past one in the morning, for once.

The menu music looped again. Somewhere on his end, a chair took his weight differently, and there was a small scrape from earlier, something being pushed further away from his vicinity.

“Okay,” she announces, deciding she had to put her foot down and save the smallest ounce of her pride, “I’m going to sleep.”

“Are you?”

“Yes.”

“Mm, you sure?”

“Yes, Haechan, I have things tomorrow.”

“You don’t,” he snorts.

“I might!” she counters in frustration, “How would you know?!”

“You have practice Monday, Tuesday, Thursday, and Saturday,” he recites, in the tone of a man reading a bus timetable, “what else would you be doing, sweetheart?”

She opened her mouth before closing it again, because it was much more shocking to her the information he’d just spat out like nothing.

“That’s so fucking creepy, Haechan—“

“—You’ve told me your schedule,” he corrects casually, “don’t get so ahead of yourself.”

“No I didn’t,” she cries.

“You did, you complain a lot, you know?” he returns, “Don’t be mad that I listen.”

Solar didn’t know what to say. She genuinely couldn’t remember if she had or not, since she did tend to talk, maybe she’d told him drunken that night in his room, maybe she’d muttered about it during Media and Society. She had no clue.

“You still suck.”

“Sure,” he agrees finally, letting her win, “I go up there on Sundays.”

The sentence arrived without any weight on it. He might’ve been reporting the weather in that same city he didn’t live in. He didn’t say any specific location, didn’t mention the Language Arts building, the ladder, he didn’t ask a single thing.

“Why are you telling me that?” she asked, trying to get some kind of answer out of him anyway.

“Hm, what’s the problem?” he piped innocently.

“Haechan—”

“—Goodnight, princess.”

The channel disconnected with the same soft two tone chime it opened with, and she could only sit there and stare at it. He didn’t ask, were her thoughts then, that’s the entire thing about him. He just states facts until they arrange themselves around him.

And she hated how much she was starting to like it.

57: this is what the drugs are for

Sigma Chi looked rough on a Sunday morning. Apparently, the party last night had been so outrageously wild that everyone was deeming it was Halloween pt2. The boys had all been so fucked up they hadn’t had the energy to even clean up, leaving it as a grueling task for Sunday morning, before Jaehyun returned from whatever escapade he had been of to.

Mark had been awake since eleven, spending most of the afternoon in the living room with a textbook he wasn’t reading open on one knee, listening to the sounds of Jaemin’s party dying around him. Someone left a shoe on the arm of the couch, there were four cans on the windowsill in a neat row, like someone had carefully arranged them for whatever reason. Renjun came down at one, eyes already red from whatever he had just smoked, stopping at the bottom of the stairs and raking his eyes across the nightmare of a house. And with a deep sigh, he spun on his heel and went back upstairs shaking his head in disapproval.

By four, the place had grown quiet in the way Sundays were supposed to be, the sound of a building of people sleeping off decisions. A painfully hungover, post-laid Jaemin wandered in with a large garbage bag, his pink glittery Ken vest still on as he began to chunk trash into it. Jisung came to help moments later, because he’d lost a bet to Jeno and now had the liberty of doing double cleanup duty.

Mark himself decided to help because he always did, like the guy everyone saw him as, willing to lend a hand when his friends needed it.

He’d heard Haechan come downstairs twice, once when he was returning a bottle of vodka to the freezer, and again when he returned to the living room to throw more empty bottles into the giant trash bag. He was shockingly composed as he walked through the house, padding across the carpet with his grey sweats hanging loosely off his hips, dark hair messily in his face, freshly washed and dripping beads across his forehead. The boy didn’t look at Mark a single time, he just offered a monotone greeting to the others as he slipped into the kitchen.

The temptation was building in Mark fast enough that he was having a difficult time holding it in. He knew Haechan hadn’t come down last night at all. There’d been an entire party underneath him, a boy who had recently relapsed and been seen doing all of the things he was known for doing. It was a good party, at that, the chaotic kind that used to be the entire architecture of his best friend’s personality. Yet, Haechan Lee had stayed upstairs behind a closed door with the light on until at least one thirty in the morning, suddenly looking more like Chenle than himself.

And Mark only knew because he’d checked.

Just as he decided he was done helping because he couldn’t hold it back anymore, he noticed Haechan had already finished making his coffee and went back upstairs.

So, with a deep exhale, he follows.

The door was open a few inches, which meant nothing, since it was always open a few inches, an old habit from a version of him who wanted people wandering in when they pleased. The caramel haired boy stood outside of it for a moment, rolling it over in his head, trying to figure out the best approach or way to say what he wanted to say.

He realized then, he hadn’t been in this room since September. Now, it was insane to think there had been a stretch of years where he was in it everyday, where half of his own stuff lived on the desk, and the fact he now had to decide whether to knock on it instead of waltzing in like nothing, because it used to not matter. Something in his chest ached, a melancholy sadness that he wasn’t going to acknowledge, telling himself that everything was fine, it was for the best, what he was doing.

Mark pushed the door open with two fingers.

Haechan was crouched by his desk, laptop bag open on the floor, winding a cable around his hand in loops, the calibrated headphones already slung around his neck. There was no doubt he’d heard the noise, but he didn’t care enough to look up.

Taking a couple of steps inside the room anyway, Mark shut the door halfway behind him. His eyes watch his friend for a few seconds, before he clears his throat, casually, “you’re going somewhere.”

The boy still didn’t look up. “Uhuh.”

“Where are you going on a Sunday this early?” Mark asks, nosily, before he could help himself.

“Out,” he deadpans, “not that it’s any of your business.”

“Right,” Mark retorts, “out.”

“That’s what I said,” he grumbles sarcastically, fitting his laptop in finally, then the cable, then something else Mark didn’t see fully, pulling the zip to close it, “welcome to write it down, gramps.”

His insult was purposely bad, Mark knew that, and it annoyed him anyway. It was the same maneuver from a Thursday in September, when Mark asked him the same question and he’d blatantly lied to his face with that smirk like he was winning the game. I guess I’m lying then.

Two months ago, it’d boiled his veins, and now, he looked at his best friend with something a little different behind his brown irises. His eyes scanned him until they landed on his hands.

The knuckles on the right one were still wrong, not dramatically, but there was a scab gone thin and shiny across the second and third, followed by the yellow green stain of something that’d been much worse. Mark knew the exact geometry of it, because he’d been the geometry. His own cheekbone had stopped aching somewhere around the twenty forth.

“How’s your hand,” he offered after they both stood there in silence for a couple of minutes, “does it still hurt?”

Almost caught off guard, Haechan glances down at his own hand, like he was checking if it belonged to him.

“No.”

“Dude, it looks kinda bad, though—”

“Was there something you needed, Marky?” he cut him off, clearly not intending to have any kind of genuine conversation with him.

It was Mark’s turn to be caught off, but it was only for a split second before he recovered. He slid his foot against the carpet, pursing his lips as he stared down at the pattern it made. “Look, I’m just— checking your reasoning, man,” he blustered, but the words came out unnatural, as if he was reciting a play.

Haechan didn’t move his body, but his brows knitted together before something closer to disgust took over part of his face, “what the hell are you talking about?” Of course, the boy wasn’t an idiot, he had his ideas, he knew things. But he was going to see if Mark was dumb enough, gullible enough, to take the bait he was trying to hang in front of him.

Trying not to show his nerves, Mark shoved his hands in the pockets of his shorts, “it means what it means,” he mutters.

“Mhm,” Haechan intones, throwing his bag over his shoulder, “try again, Mark.”

Something in his throat went dry. It was the first time he’d called him that, just Mark, without his insistent, taunting y at the end. He wasn’t sure if that meant anything, nor could he explain why it made him feel the slightest of unease. Instead, he goes at it a second time, “it means somebody should check on what you’ve been doing since that meeting, it’s been weeks yet everyone’s acting like it’s no big deal—”

“Do you think I’m dumb?” Haechan snorted, cutting him off so he’d stop his pretending, “You don’t talk like that.”

“What?” Mark scoffed, “Bro, what’s wrong with the way I’m talking?”

“Well, for starters,” he hums, “maybe try using your own words for once.”

Mark’s ears turned red, a horrible giveaway he had no control over. The smirk that spread over Haechan’s face seemed to show that he’d noticed.

“That’s not—”

“Whatever you say, Marky,” the obnoxious name returned with a sarcastic scowl, taking a step forward to walk past him, “I don’t have time to entertain you, unfortunately.”

“Jaemin asked what’s up with you,” Mark blurts out, keeping him from opening the door to exit, turning around to face him now. Haechan was the one closest to the door now, the tables turned, with Mark standing in the middle of a room that had only recently reeked of weed and alcohol, “yesterday, in the kitchen, after you did that shit you’ve been doing since the semester started.”

He didn’t need to explain what shit he was talking about, they both knew he was talking about avoidance. “And?”

“No one has an answer for it, obviously.”

“Sounds like something that’s not my problem.”

“You didn’t come downstairs last night, you know,” he tries again, struggling to find the pressure point, snapping louder than he meant to, “a whole party under you, Hyuck, and you didn’t come down once. If you think no one noticed, I’ve got horrible news for you.”

“You’d know, wouldn’t you?” the dark haired boy retorts, evenly, “You came up twice.” He chuckled from the bewildered look that took over Mark’s face, adding, “didn’t even have the decency to knock either time.”

He stared at him for a few seconds, the eye bags under his eyes, subtle but present. The white of them were red, like he’d smoked within the last few hours. It wasn’t like Mark had any solid proof, per se, he just had common sense and the fact everyone on campus had seen him partying again recently. But then, he stopped, as if he’d never done it in the first place.

“You’re using again,” he observes, “it’s obvious, do you think she doesn’t know that?”

She, he didn’t have to say her name. Something moved behind Haechan’s face, not guilt, something closer to fatigue, a man being asked a question he’d purposely been avoiding.

“Who are you worried about here, Marky?” he challenged, “Think you’re the big hero here to save the day?”

“Nah, man, I’m just not going to pretend I don’t know what this looks like.”

Heaving out a sigh, Haechan seemed to have enough, spinning on his heel, gripping the strap of his bag on his shoulder. He opened the door fully, not caring if Mark stuck around. “No,” he monotones over his shoulder as he steps into the hallway, “you know what you’re making it look like.”

And then he was gone, down the stairs of Sigma Chi on a Sunday evening like he had no cares in the world.

-

Solar spent most of her Sunday pretending nothing the night before happened. Surprisingly, this wasn’t too difficult, if she looked passed the suspicious glances of Hyein and Hanni, who she could tell were fighting back the urge to ask. Though, unfortunately, it was quite hard to outsmart the two people who had lit the fire just when she thought it was burned out for good.

The house, on the other hand, was operating at half capacity. Hanni had made pancakes, totally casually, at two in the afternoon, with Hyein padding down the steps in a robe with a face mask on. Solar and Hanni had been in the kitchen, talking to Yerim about the aftermath of Halloween, how she’d gotten with some guy from her chemistry class. Yerim had eventually bid her farewell after finishing her pancakes, thanking Hanni for her beloved contribution, before humming as she exited the kitchen and went back upstairs.

Hyein slid into the bar stool next to Solar, where she was minding her own business and happily eating her pancakes. She tried to act normal, but she could feel the burning holes of Hyein’s stare into the side of her head.

Until finally, she gave in, turning to meet her friend’s eyes with a look that said go ahead, get it off your chest.

“I have to ask!” Hyein exclaimed, her hands up in defense, looking to Hanni, who was shaking her head in disappointment as she placed the final finished pancake on the plate, “Come on, I have to!”

“You really don’t,” Hanni scolds, “it’s none of our business what Solar is getting up to!”

“Well, we’re the ones who got them back together!” Hyein argued, before she turned to a rather defeated looking Solar, knowing there wasn’t any world she was getting out of this one. “Can we have an update?” she pleaded, desperate, clutching her hands together at her head, “please, I just want to know if you’re okay, if you admitted you like him… or love him, or whatever it is, I just wanna know!”

She broke their eye contact to pour more syrup on her pancake, cutting a piece with her fork and sticking in her mouth. Hyein looked like she was going to jump out of her seat and start screaming from the anticipation, showcasing the fact she was indeed one of the most shameless nosy people Solar had ever had the pleasure of knowing.

“We’re fine,” she deadpans finally.

Hyein looked at her for a moment, her eyes wide with excitement, expecting Solar to say more, to go into some kind of detail. Upon realizing she was finished, the girl groans, “Dude, that’s really all you’re gonna give me?!”

“Fine is good, Sol,” Hanni softly comments from where she was across the counter, munching on her own pancake.

“Ugh, whatever,” Hyein complains, sliding off of the bar stool to pick up a pancake with her bare hand, chomping down on it completely dry before she headed towards the doorway, “I’m going to finish this season of Gossip Girl.”

The two girls left in the kitchen finished their pancakes, before following their friend into the living room and taking seats with her. Naturally, Hyein cried at the part she always cried at, because there was something particularly painfully emotional about Blair thinking Chuck was sabotaging her prom queen votes, just for him to be the one who caused her to win.

“It’s just so cute!” she was whining, wiping another tear from the corner of her eye and leaning over to lay her head on Hanni’s shoulder. The angelic girl nodded in understanding as she wrapped an arm around her to pull her into a comforting hug. “God, what do I have to do to be loved like that?!”

Solar sat on the arm of the couch and watched the rest of the episode, her legs tucked under her, enjoying it the way she had the other three times she’d watched the entire show through. Something about it hit home for her in a way none of the other commonly watched TV dramas did. And for awhile, it was an enjoyable Sunday with her two close friends.

I go up there on Sundays.

The six words entered her brain like poison, dropped into a voice channel at one in the morning by a boy who then hung up on her. And since then, she had been trying her hardest to shove them into her back pocket and pretend she didn’t badly want to run out the door right then and there.

He hadn’t asked, he never did, that was the annoying part. He didn’t tell her he wanted her there, that she should come, he’d given no time or mentioned anything about the language arts building, meaning that if she went, she was making it up entirely herself. And if she didn’t go, she’d be sitting there thinking about it the rest of the day with regret puddling in her chest.

He’s a coward, she informed the ceiling bitterly. But the voice in the back of her head laughed at her, you’re gonna go anyway.

At twenty past seven, Solar had stood up from the couch, much to the dismay of her friends who had all been bundled under the same large blanket, announcing, “I’m going to the lab.”

Hyein, who had been falling asleep on Hanni’s lap, nearly fell off the couch from how fast she sat up. “Really?!”

“In the dark?” Hanni blinked, leaning to the side to grab the remote off the arm of the couch, pausing the television to focus on the conversation.

“Yeah,” Solar shrugs, “not a big deal, guys, I go practice there late sometimes.”

“Uhuh,” Hyein snickered, and Hanni gently shoved her to tell her to stop.

“Text us when you get there,” Hanni sends her a reassuring smile, one she was more than grateful for.

“Course,” she nods, before she’d spun on her heel, slipping on her shoes that were next to the door, making sure she had her phone in her pocket. And then, she slipped out into the night of Syracuse University without a trace of doubt in her mind.

Though, she wouldn’t text when she got there, because she wasn’t going to the lab. But from her friend’s reaction, it seemed they already had some kind of idea about that.

Outside, November had arrived properly at some point during the weekend, and only then was she noticing it as her sneakers scraped against the concrete of the sidewalk, shoving her hands into the pockets of her comfy shorts that she hadn’t thought to change before she walked out. It was the first genuinely cold night of the year, the kind where the air had teeth in it. By the time she’d cut behind the Language Arts building, into the back alley, her ears had gone numb and she was starting to regret every layer she failed to put on.

The ladder was still there, as if it was even possible for it to not be. Her eyes lingered on it for a split second, standing there at the bottom, thinking with clarity that this was insane.

But she’d still gripped the sides of the cold metal and heaved all of her weight to put her foot on the first bar. Her hands burned from the cold as she climbed, a slight breeze only making it worse, goosebumps forming across her arms. Such a bad idea, she was telling herself, why the hell did I not grab something warmer?

Finally, she reached the top, hurling herself over the lip of the roof onto the top. Heaving out an exhausted breath, she dusts her bare legs off, as if something as simple as climbing a ladder took it out of her.

Looking up, her eyes scan across the dim of the rooftop, the sun above beginning to disappear and be replaced by the gaze of the moon. Haechan was already there, and the sight of him caused something ethereal to buzz through out her body, like a breath of fresh air you didn’t know you’d been holding. His legs were over the side, laptop bag beside him, hood up against the cold.

He didn’t turn around when her sneakers scuffed against the gravel lingering on the roof, meaning he’d heard her from the second rung and simply elected not to make it so simple.

“You’re late,” he mumbles, eyes focused on the lowering skyline.

“Not like you gave me a time,” she defended, “or an invite, for that matter.”

“Invites that important to you, hm?”

“I wasn’t going to come,” she ignored his question, “I was going to the lab.”

He looked at her then, twisting his neck only slightly. His eyes lingered on her face, like he was studying every feature, memorizing the curve of her nose, the way her lips plumped. And he pended, teasingly, “Sure, so how’s the lab, princess?”

She crossed the roof then, sitting down on the ledge with about two feet between them, which was closer than in October.

“Be quiet,” she muttered under her breath.

Shockingly, he obliged.

Below, campus was doing it’s Sunday night thing. Someone’s bike sped past the library, the lamps down the walk had that yellow sodium color that made everything look like it was straight out of Twilight. Laughs echoed upwards through the air, and she watched crowds of students funnel by, screaming and boasting about their weekends, the parties they’d gone to, presumably Sigma Chi and how great it was.

Out of nowhere, he’d held out something to her without looking. She’d jumped from the sudden movement, turning to see a Monster there in his hand, Pink Punch at that, meaning he’d bought it before he left the house, which meant he’d bought it not knowing if she’d show up at all.

Pursing her lips, she internally debated if this was smart of her, before she’d taken it out of his hand. Did she really have the right to ask herself if anything was smart anymore?

“I’m going to ask you something,” she announces, staring out ahead, “and I already know you’re going to do the thing where you make it a joke, but I’m telling you, I will just ask again.”

“Really efficient method there,” he monotoned beside her.

She stared at his side profile for a minute, thinking to herself that he was too distracted to know, when in reality, he knew.

“How bad is it?” she blurted.

A wave of silence washed across the rooftop, the sound of leaves rustling beneath them shuddered through the air. The moon was beginning to show itself now, the white crescent blossoming from over the hills. Wind brushed on by, taking it’s time with nowhere else important to be.

And then, he’d turned to her, much to her surprise. His eyes raked across her again, before he’d exhaled, like a disapproving parent, “you’re cold.”

Solar narrowed her eyes at him, knowing he was trying to avoid the subject, “Haechan—“

He ignored her, instead shifting to slip off his black jacket. The lump in her throat shut her up then as the fabric wrapped around her, immediately shielding her with not only warmth, but the overwhelming bluster of vanilla.

Then, like he’d done nothing at all, he reached into the pocket of his hoodie, taking out a lighter and a blunt, the exact choreography of October like a broken record. Something in her went hot and furious in a way, the way he could do such nice things before completely ignoring her like she didn’t exist.

“Don’t,” she warns, not unkindly, but in a pleading manner, trying to prove to him that she wanted to know not because of ill intent, because she cared.

His hand stopped from where it’d almost lit the blunt, thumb on the wheel of the lighter.

“Just— wait a minute,” she sighs, “you can do whatever you want as soon as you answer my question.”

He chuckled, or something similar, a huff of air leaving his lips as he diverted his eyes to the ground again. He had a hundred available replies, he could’ve said something about her being no fun, about how pushy she was and how bad it made him want her, how she was similar to Jaehyun. There were half a dozen, if not more, things he could think of.

For once, he didn’t say any of them, he just nodded a single time and put it back in the pocket of his jeans where he’d retrieved it from.

“It’s not that bad.”

“That’s got to be a joke,” she muttered, unimpressed.

“Not a joke,” he corrects firmly, “that’s my answer, sweetheart.”

“It’s the answer you’d give Chenle,” she counters anyway, stubbornly, much to his dismay, “Or Jaemin, it’s the one that makes people shrug it off and go, yeah, good enough for me.”

“Yet it works, doesn’t it?”

“Not with me,” she deadpans.

He opened his mouth to say something before closing it, like he was hesitating on the words he was choosing. It was perhaps, and very likely, the first time Haechan Lee had ever done that in his life. She watched him exhale, watched it leave him and go white in the cold, before disappearing over the edge of a four story drop.

“I didn’t take anything,” he finally offers into the cold.

Another wave of wind brushed through, and she subconsciously pulled the jacket tighter around her shoulders, carefully confirming, “On Halloween?” The look on his face seemed to answer the question well enough. “I’m not talking about Halloween.”

He turned his head again, his face doing the thing it always did, which was often a whole lot of nothing. Still, he was looking at her like a number had come in wrong and he was checking the work. “Wow,” he teases, almost mockingly, “you’re not going to let this go.”

“No,” she exasperates in frustration, “and it’s not funny!”

“I’m not laughing,” he affirms blankly, shifting his weight a bit on the ledge. She hoped then, he was finally going to say something honest, until he deadpans, “Mark told you to ask.”

And there it was.

“Do not start right now.”

“Mm, I’m simply saying—”

“You are doing what you do, Donghyuck,” she snaps, and his eyes whipped to her like a crash from the word that flew from her lips, unexpected, a rarity that caused conflicting feelings he did not know how to process. The girl sat up straighter, feeling the aggravation seeping into her bones, “you’re going to make this all about Mark, because if it’s about Mark then it’s a fight, and we all know you’re extremely good at fights,” her voice had grown louder than she meant for it to. “I saw you on the side steps, you know, you didn’t look up for four seconds and I stood there, like a fucking idiot, and walked the other way.”

She was breathing harder than she typically would from that speech, causing her to look away in embarrassment, swatting a bug away from her face. “So don’t tell me who put the question in my mouth,” she mumbles, quieter.

He didn’t say anything.

So much time had passed of him not saying a word, she began to think he wasn’t going to, that he was going to get up and leave like he always did when something started to become too real.

Then, without any ceremony whatsoever, the way a man might mention the time, he mutters, “bad.”

It was a start, is what she told herself, because there was something about a boy who’d shut everyone out finally telling an ounce of truth. Perhaps there was something about the moonlit sky, or the Language Arts rooftop that made him feel like he could just say what he needed to say, or at least some of it.

She cleared her throat as quietly as she could manage, trying not to seem like it was as big of a gut punch as it was, “okay,” she breathes, “it’s… it’s okay.”

“It’s not what it was,” he offered, barely above a whisper, not looking at her because it would only make him want to shut down. He cut himself off, before starting again, “this is more like…” he trailed off again, making a gesture with two fingers, opening and closing, “a thing I keep… putting down and still finding in my hand again.”

She nodded in understanding, considering his words, wondering if she was the first and only person he’d ever told this to. A part of her thought back to his friendship with Mark, the way they probably were before she’d come into their lives. She wondered, for a moment, if it was technically all her fault they didn’t have each other anymore like they once did.

“When did it start again?” she hesitantly asks, softly.

A bitter snort left his lips, “you know when.”

Sour piled in her mouth that she pushed down without a trace. She did know, she’d been in the house that morning, in his bed that morning, and she’d left down the staircase with her shoes in her hand while a meeting happened in the living room without her entirely about her.

“It’s not your fault,” he maintained, flatly, “so don’t do that thing with your face.”

Heat flew to her cheeks in crimson pink, her hands covering them as she turned her face away. Flustered, she shook her head defensively, “I am not—“

“You’re doing it right now, pretty.”

That stupid fucking name, she grumbled internally, glaring out at the campus and cracking open the Monster finally. But she didn’t tell him not to call her that, not because she liked it, but because she wasn’t going to stray away from the important topic at hand.

“So, why?”

“Why what, sweetheart?”

“Why does it work,” she asked, “what does it do?” She gestured vaguely with her hands, a useless one at that, “I’ve watched you take things that make you slower, dumber, and you’re not either of those, so I don’t — I don’t understand what you’re buying.” She wasn’t trying to sound critical, though maybe it came off that way. It was true, she failed to grasp the concept. She knew that he struggled with money, that he mixed beats to afford his schooling, so why would he throw any of it at something that was only damaging him, especially in the long run?

A leaf falls onto the ledge next to him, and he reaches over, crumpling it in between his fingertips. The sound almost echoes through the quiet of the campus, the pieces flying out into the wind in swirls of freedom.

“You know,” he starts slowly, “when I told you, I hear rooms,” he puts his elbows on his knees, hands loose between them, “it’s not a party trick, princess. I walk into a place and know who’s pissed off before they do, who’s lying, when someone’s about to say something they’ll regret, by the second,” he pauses, seemingly growing embarrassed by how much he was saying, because these things had never entered the air before. Solar grimaces, concern washing over her in a daze, and she thoughtlessly extended her hand to grab his, covering it with her own, trying to pretend there weren’t shoots of sparks up her arm in petrifying tingles. Haechan tensed up at first, shocked at the abrupt, foreign touch, before he’d relaxed, gradually turning his hand so he could intertwine their fingers.

“That’s what it does,” he finishes, “it makes it quiet, I got good at it because I had to be, and I don’t know how to not be that way anymore.”

The breeze blew his dark hair out of his eyes for a split second, and she could see the twinkle in the brown before it’d fallen in his face again.

“So, it’s loud,” she offers softly, “and it turns it off.”

“Yeah,” he mutters, “yeah, for awhile.”

“That’s the most honest thing you’ve ever said to me,” she blurted in disbelief, “and for what it’s worth, there’s always another way, Donghyuck.”

His thumb was rubbing circles on her knuckle, voice barely above a whisper, like he was afraid of the next words he’d say, “mm, you might be right, sweetheart.”

58: when it feels right

There was no telling how long she’d stood there, focusing on what it felt like to sit there in the silence of the night, holding the hand of the only boy who’d ever caused her to feel such a conflicting whirlwind of emotions. His thumb never stopped moving despite the minutes that passed, the only sound the continuous rustling of the leaves as they fluttered through the air. Haechan wasn’t looking at her, he was still watching the night sky, the blinking lights of planes coasting by through the clouds, the moon peering down at them in a glow.

It was such a small thing, the back and forth of it across her knuckle, the callous of a musician that caused her to wonder how his music had been going since all of this happened. She decided, somewhere around the third pass, that she was going to let herself have it, alone on the rooftop, with no one else aware of the moment they were currently having. And she knew not to say anything, because he would only become too aware and stop.

So, the two sat on the ledge in the cold, the campus going about it’s business four floors down, and she finally ripped her eyes away from his dazzling side profile to peer up at the sky herself.

In the dawn of the night was when she finally noticed. Her own thumb had moved, too, absently, the way a hand does when it isn’t being supervised, back and forth across the top of his, when it’d passed over something that wasn’t the smooth of skin. She swallowed something bitter down her throat, thinking back to two nights ago, the glint in Mark’s eyes that was uneasy, like he was holding something back from her. She runs her thumb over it again, something ridged, slightly raised, a texture that her fingers had been reporting for probably two fully minutes while the rest of her was busy pretending she wasn’t internally beginning to lose her mind.

His attention fell on her too late, because she’d lifted his knuckle to her face, eyes squinting underneath the moonlight. “Hold on…” she muttered as the realization spread across her expression.

It wasn’t a dramatic injury, there was a scab gone thin and shiny across the second and third, flattended out into something that had clearly once been larger. Around it, the yellow green wash of a bruise was in it’s last stage of healing, the color of an old apple.

“This is weeks old,” she notes, mumbling.

His gaze was studying her carefully, his hand twitched under her touch, but he didn’t pull it away. Haechan knew well enough that once she found out, there wasn’t any point in trying to hide it. “Mhm.”

Ripping her eyes off the bruise, she snaps her eyes onto his with a disapproving glare, “Haechan—“

“It’s a hand,” he monotones, trying to ease his way out of the conversation with wit, like he always did.

Her eyes only narrowed, but the irises softened, “Donghyuck…” she trails off as the name leaves her lips, still feeling rather foreign, delicate enough that she was afraid to allow it into the harsh wind. She swore, you could almost see something lighting on fire inside of him, like a switch that’d been flipped. “How old?” she whispers.

He exhaled, “couple weeks.”

“How many is a couple?”

The boys eyes stared into hers in utter bewilderment, before the blank expression returned. He shook his head in disbelief, “two, it’s two, princess — that’s what a couple means.”

Another gush of wind passed, and she turned her head to stare out at the buildings, allowing herself to ponder when two weeks ago was. Mid-October, she thought, that Saturday, the morning he made her breakfast, gave her his name, the morning she was, for a split second, entirely convinced in the revelation of Haechan Lee being the complete opposite of everything they labeled him as. It was also the Saturday everything turned upside down, when she’d let herself outside into a beam of sunlight that was far too bright for the ache in her chest.

She thought, about the voices she heard when she’d been sitting there, on the edge of his bed, trying to arrange her own head. It’d clearly been two of the boys, going up in volume before it’d abruptly stop, she’d shrugged it off, it wasn’t her business. She was sure it was nothing serious.

Now, she was gravely rethinking that presumption.

“Who?” she demands, the word echoing through the atmosphere. He didn’t answer, didn’t look at her, and she sat there, on the ledge of a rooftop, gripping his bruised knuckle as if she was afraid to let go, embarrassingly, desperately, and angrily, all at once, “Who was it, Haechan?”

“Mark.”

Although she was expecting it, the grimace took over her face anyway. Her grip must’ve changed, because he’d glanced down at their hands before he’d seem to decide it was a bad idea, looking back out at the black shape of the hill past the library.

“He was in the kitchen,” he deadpans, almost bored of talking about it, “asked me stupid questions, wanting to know about breakfast.”

Her brows furrowed, and she nervously bit down on her bottom lip in anticipation. “About breakfast,” she slowly repeated.

“About who it was for,” he corrected plainly.

Who it was for, her mind screamed, her mouth suddenly growing dry, the cold sending another trembling shiver down her spine. The vanilla aura from the jacket around her shoulders coated her in a seeping warmth, somehow, as his words sank through her body. “And…”

“He swung first,” he offers, “for your information, from me, because he’s going to want to spin it the other way — right here,” he lifted two fingers gradually to tap his own cheekbone, “I hit him back, obviously, then he hit me again… he was going for another one, but Mark’s never really compared to my strength,” he cockily retorts, mockingly, his ego getting the best of him momentarily, “Jeno and Jaemin came in, it should’ve ended there,” he cleared his throat, “and well, of course, your brother walked in the door.”

Her wind wandered back to the last time her brother called her, told her something about how he’d handled it. She began to feel very far away from her body, drifting off to some kind of unknown place her mind conjured for safety. “Jaehyun saw—”

“—a skillet on the floor and two guys bleeding in a kitchen, yeah,” he sarcastically intones, “he’s very far from dumb, sweetheart.”

Her hand, still covering his hand, fell onto her thigh, his fingers automatically gripping the flesh. She pursed her lips into a straight line, deciding to ignore his snappy comment, to stay focused on the important matter at hand, “sure, and he said what?”

He reaches a hand up to run it through his dark fringe, shaking his head slightly, “a lot of things,” he deduces, turning his other hand to intertwine their fingers, so she wouldn’t keep staring down at it, “he told me he wasn’t going to insult me by pretending my record gave me a lot of standing… and, something about how he wasn’t going to have the conversation a third time.”

She almost felt bile come up her throat. A third time, her head echoed, unhelpfully. The first was all the way at her first real event at Syracuse, the tailgate she’d been forced to mask at, like she’d done her entire life, displaying herself as the preppy rich kid the entire school already saw her as. She recalled the scent of grass in the air as she’d leaned against the back pole of the bleachers, and the nonchalance of a boy who wanted the world to believe he had no cares in the world, other than conversing with a girl he barely knew. Now this, this was the second, and thinking about her brother saying such a thing to him, made something painfully raw flip in her heart.

“God…” she muttered, bitterly, “I’m going to kill him — you know, he called me later that day, told me he handled it, that it was for the best…” she trailed off as she thought back, her voice growing lower,”he told me he’d get our father involved.”

The wind blew across the roof for the hundredth time, blatantly on purpose by this point. She pulled his jacket tighter with her free hand, trying not to show how much the memory hurt. He noticed anyway, due to his oddly accurate ability, squeezing her hand with his bruised knuckle tighter.

“He’s not gonna find out,” he quietly assures, “not about this.”

Not about this… but what exactly is this?

She had to hold back the bitter laugh that nearly escaped. She wanted to ask, to ask about Mark in that meeting, what her brother said to him, why he was so determined anyway and didn’t seem to worry about her brother in the slightest. A part of her admired it, but another wondered how long it would be until Danielle spread the news in Jaehyun’s direction and everything went south. The last thing she would ever need was her father learning about the kind of things she’d been getting up to in Syracuse. If he ever learned she even so much as thought about attending a frat party, he’d likely remove her from school immediately, and she’d be punished to go to a preppy Ivy League for good.

The imaginary scene caused her to shudder.

I don’t know for sure that he’ll find out, she tried to tell herself, I don’t know for sure that Danielle has ever talked to Mark. Mark is nice, he wouldn’t do that. He just hates Haechan.

But why?

Still, she wasn’t going to ask what her brother said to Mark, she wasn’t going to pester him about what this meant, about what they were really doing with each other, what he really knew about Danielle, if he’d ever seen the two interact. There was so many questions she wanted to ask, even just to see the shift of his jaw. But more than that, she wanted to keep sitting there, basking in the bliss of vanilla and feeling the spark shoot up her arm at the itch of his calluses against her fingertips.

There was one thing she couldn’t help but think back to.

“What else did he say to you… before the fight?”

Haechan winced, as if that was the last question he’d wanted to hear. His eyes didn’t look at her, nor the sky, they fell to his lap, to the sight of their feet dangling off the edge hundreds of feet in the air. The tension in the air could’ve been cut with a knife, followed by a pause long enough to count three separate cars going down the far road.

“Solar—“

He cut himself off, her first name coming off her lips wrong, almost aching. Confusion sprinkled across her face as she stared at the side of him, brows knitting together, it has to be serious if he’s using her first name. He rarely used her first name, if ever, hence why it sounded so weird coming from his lips.

“What did he say?” she pends, softly at first.

But he was silent, continuing to stare down at his lap.

“Haechan, what did he say?” she urged again, sterner that time. Did he admit to something, did he mention Danielle?

“He asked me if I’m in love with you,” he finally monotones.

The entire world seemed to still.

She was scared to ask, was the horrible truth. But she was going to anyway, because Solar Lee could never say no to impulses.

“And you said?”

“Nothing.”

He didn’t add anything, didn’t mutter it wasn’t true nor it was, didn’t look at her or take his hand back, and slowly, with the awful, unhurried logic of something arriving from a long ways away, she understood that was his genuine answer. That he’d stood in a kitchen with a bruised cheekbone, his best friend’s fist still ringing in his face, and had been asked the only question that mattered, said not a single word, and let Mark walk away believing whatever he desired to believe.

“Alright,” she nods, but her voice almost cracked at the end.

“Hey,” he calls out, automatically noticing from how he paid attention to the smallest of details, or as he would say, from how he read the room mindlessly. When she doesn’t react, feeling ashamed of her reaction and frankly humiliated, he reached out to put two fingers on her jaw, turning her face to his again, cooing out in the quietest whisper, “hey, pretty girl.”

Her cheeks burned, and the teasing tone only irritated her more. Shamefully, her hand makes a poor attempt at pushing his cupped hand off her cheek, “stop it—”

The corner of his mouth twitched upward, his thumb ran across the soft of her bottom lip, smearing the bit of lip gloss she’d put on earlier that day. “Say you want me to stop,” he dares, “say it, and I’ll stop.”

His head tilted ever so slightly, his neck slowly inching closer to her. He was going as slow as he possibly could, clearly on purpose. Solar’s eyes couldn’t help but linger on him, raking across the plumpness of his lips, the mole on his cheek, the way his delicate black hair fell into his eyes. Up close, he was almost like a harmless doe, she swore if she looked deep enough into the small of his irises she could see it, a harmless boy that had never known anything other than what he’d been shown.

She thought about the new information she’d learned that night, about the fact that he was using again, how it didn’t make her think any less of him, because she was beginning to believe he was maybe the most real person on the entire campus.

And that thought was enough to cause her to put her hand on the back of his neck, pushing him forward so she could connect their lips in the most euphoric explosion of tension, the universe rumbling beneath them from the touch. Haechan, being far from an amateur, immediately took control, his teeth finding the bottom of her lip and sucking angrily. Their lips moved in a symphony of disgusting noises no one else could hear, his tongue slipping into her mouth, their saliva combining in ecstacy.

He gently pulled away, her lip gloss smeared across the side of his mouth. Her breathing was ragged, feeling like she’d ran a marathon, as if the wind had been knocked out of her.

Of course, he wasn’t giving her anytime to relax, as he tilted her chin upwards to lean forward, his nose grazing her neck before his lips connected to it, teeth biting down and sucking. A whimper escaped her lips, as hard as she was trying to stop it, her other hand finding it’s way to his hair, running through it and gently tugging at his scalp.

“Don’t worry,” he whispers on her neck, lips tickling her earlobe, “your little head, pretty girl,” he sucked on that spot on her neck again, causing her entire body to twitch,”this — is all that matters.”

“Fuck…” she helplessly curses from the tingle, feeling her thighs shiver. She could feel the smirk spreading across his lips on her neck, before he slowly pulled away to climb off the ledge.

Before she could think, he’d reached out to take both of her hands to pull her off the ledge. She squeaked out in surprise, but he’d caught her waist before her feet even hit the ground, his biceps popping through the fabric of his long sleeve shirt. Her hands instinctively went to his shoulders, eyes wide with shock as she met his again. He was already inches away from her, hands protectively at her waist, fingers digging into her skin underneath his jacket.

His hands roamed her body without another word, going underneath the hem of her shirt and up her stomach. Leaning forward again, he attacked her neck in another spot now, causing the heat between her legs to blister at this point. She whined out in desperation, and in response, he put his leg in between hers, letting her grind against his thigh.

It couldn’t be wrong when it felt so right.

She was convinced of such a fact.

59: schedules and shapes

She knew before she opened her eyes.

Not the specifics, to be clear, just the general sense of her own body reporting something it’d been reporting for several hours without supervision. Her body still tingled from the hands that once roamed them less than twelve hours prior, a tenderness low on her throat, on the left side, the kind of ache that had a shape to it.

Solar laid there in the grey of a Monday morning with her arm over her face and groaned into the safety of her pink bedroom in complete and utter agony.

“God dammit,“ she cursed to herself, though she knew it was entirely her own fault.

Throwing her legs over the side of her bed, she pushed herself to her feet and headed to her vanity, leaning over the table to peer into the mirror.

It was worse than she expected, which she supposed was fair, given that she’d spent a rather significant portion of Sunday night with a rather experienced boy’s lips on her neck, four stories above the campus, and had said not a word whatsoever to stop it. There were two, she noted mentally, one under her jaw that she could likely pass off as anything, and another right where a collar wouldn’t fully reach, turning a specific plum color that no reasonable person would mistake for a simple bruise.

You did this to yourself, her brain monotones as she meets her eyes in the mirror.

With a huff, she accepted this as fact and plopped into the chair, opening the drawer.

Still, she couldn’t help but think it was fairly ridiculous, the whole operation, twenty minutes of color correcting, setting powder, and three separate passes with a brush, done with a precision she had never once applied to an actual assignment.

“You’re blending too harshly, dear,” her mother’s words echoed in the back of her head, “you can’t make a good impression if you walk out there like a clown.”

Her mother had taught her most of the things she knew about makeup, beauty in general, sitting behind her in the penthouse of the Upper East Side, for completely different reasons. That version of her was a faint little girl, a child who did not know anything other than ensuring that everything about her appearance was desirable, appealing, all so she could make her parents appear to have the stunning, breathtaking family they aspired. She learned to cover a sleepless night before a foundation lunch, a sponsored event, before her mother’s assistant could stick her head in her room and go, “your mother wants to know if you’re ready, miss Solar, she says it should not take you this long.”

The words faded away into the pink walls of her dorm, because this version of Solar Lee was covering Haechan.

She stared at herself when she was done, her neck looking a lot more normal. Though, the face above it was doing something she didn’t authorize, a sort of low involuntary brightness sitting under everything, and no product on earth was going to change such a thing.

Which was just great.

Jumping to her feet, she turns and heads to her closet. Her hands reach out for a turtleneck, which she knew was cheating as she slipped it over her head. She was wearing it anyway.

She’d thrown one of her coats on over it, a brown one her mother had bought her from her friend, who owned a million dollar brand. Once she was dressed, she went back to her vanity to check herself one last time.

Good enough, she thought, surely they won’t notice.

She turns to head out of her bedroom, before her eyes caught on something laying over the back of her chair.

His jacket.

She’d taken it last night, not because she wanted to, although she did, but because he’d looked down at her at the bottom of the ladder and deadpanned, “I’m not going to be the reason you freeze to death,” before he’d ran a thumb along her jaw, “see you tomorrow, pretty,” before turning around and disappearing around the corner, pulling the blunt out of his pocket and lighting it as he walked.

The brunette angrily bit down on her bottom lip, shaking her head before she’d headed out into the hallway.

She’d braced herself at the kitchen doorway.

That was habit now, apparently. A week ago, she’d walked into that room on a Monday morning wanting nothing more than her beloved sparkling water, and instead, had received Danielle Marsh pouring coffee and observing that she looked rough. Now, it was like a muscle memory she didn’t know how to erase, her shoulders tightening before she’d even cleared the doorframe.

Her eyes quickly scan the tiled room, Danielle wasn’t there.

That was a good thing, her mind reminded her, though something still felt off in a way she couldn’t explain.

“—no, cause he texted her, then at Halloween, he acted like he didn’t know her,” Hyein was in the middle of telling a story, something that happened to a girl she knew in her English class, that she had just gotten back from since it was earlier in the morning, leaning over the kitchen island with her phone above her face, “Like, come on, that’s psychological warfare, no? A war crime, arguably.”

“Very cruel,” Hanni nodded in agreement, in the middle of cutting a banana into a bowl at the counter behind Hyein with the deliberateness of someone who’d never rushed a thing in their life, “she can do better than that, though.”

“Mhm, that’s what I said,” Hyein mused, “screw guys like that, seriously, there’s nothing worse than stringing a girl along like that.”

Yerim wandered through in a Syracuse crewneck, taking a parfait out of the fridge she had apparently been saving, sliding the drawer open and grabbing a spoon. She turned back to the two girls for a split second, observing the scene, “was the guy one of the frat boys?” She’d apparently overheard part of the conversation.

Hyein was in the middle of eating cereal, and she’d chewed her current bite before shaking her head, “nope, not even, I don’t even think they would do that.”

Curiously, Yerim leaned against the counter, beginning to eat her parfait as she pends, “how would you know?”

Hanni nervously glanced behind her, where Hyein was blankly meeting Yerim’s eyes, like she was flabbergasted to be asked such a question. “Uh, cause I know them?” she deadpans, as if it should’ve been obvious.

“Girl, since when?” Yerim cries, surprised, “Swear to God you guys were just talking about how much they suck,” she pauses for a second, her thoughts growing deeper, brows furrowing in confusion, “wait… why would you be hanging around them in the first place? Every time I see any of them they basically ignore me.”

Hyein chewed another bite of cereal, unbothered about the conversation, whilst Hanni looked like she was going to faint from how nervous it was making her. She didn’t know why it felt scary that the other girls were catching on that they knew the frat boys decently well compared to the rest of Alpha Phi. Really, she was a bit worried that Danielle would get word of it and somehow, it would blow up in their faces.

“I don’t know,” Hyein shrugs, “we’re friends, they’re not all so bad, most of the time.”

Yerim blinked at her, almost gawking, “really, do you think you could get me Haechan’s number?”

Hyein choked on her cereal, Hanni nearly dropped the knife she was using to cut her banana. “Uh,” she starts once she regained her composure, “I don’t… I don’t have it, otherwise I would, sorry, girl.”

The girl had pouted slightly, shrugging, “it’s cool, you think you guys could like… introduce me next time or something?”

Oh jeez, the two girls thought in unison.

“You probably don’t want to do that, Yerim,” Hanni waved a hand in dismissal, “he’s… quite difficult.”

“She’s trying to say he’s an asshole,” Hyein chimes.

Solar entered the kitchen then, unaware of the conversation that had just been happening. She’d gone to the fridge, like any other day, opening it and grabbing one of her sparkling waters. Twisting the cap, she took a long sip before she’d turned to face the three girls who were hanging around, raising a brow from the way they were all looking at her like an insane person, “good morning?”

God, they noticed my hickeys, I’m so screwed.

“Morning!” Hyein practically screamed.

“Did you sleep well?” Hanni had immediately asked, “Want some bananas?”

Solar’s eyes carefully studied her two friends for a moment, stepping forward to take a seat in one of the bar stools across from where Hyein was leaning over the island. Yerim casually slipped into the one next to her, still eating her parfait, being the only one who had offered her a normal greeting.

“Alright,” Solar clears her throat, turning to face the girl, “Yerim, why are these two being weirdos?”

She’d glanced at Hyein and Hanni, who were pretending to be too engrossed in what they were doing. “I don’t know, we were just talking about Haechan,” she shrugs.

Her throat grew dry.

Haechan?

“Oh,” she mutters, clearing her throat because her voice faltered more than she’d wanted it to, “what about him?”

“I was asking if they could introduce me,” she informs her, “since they’re friends with Sigma — oh, aren’t you, too?”

Introduce her…

“Yeah,” Solar nodded, swallowing the saliva that was building in her mouth, “something like that.”

“Could you introduce me?!” she pipes up in excitement, “Do your sorority sister a favor?”

“Uh—“

*“Sorry,* wait, do you guys like — have a thing still?” the girl cries, slapping a hand over her mouth at the realization, “I’m so sorry, I totally forgot, cause like… everyone is saying you’re with Mark.”

Solar bit the inside of her cheek to keep herself from saying something that would give away way too much. She knew Yerim was friendly with Danielle, though she had nothing against her as a person. She could not take that risk.

“No,” she smiles with a shake of her head, “I’m not with either, but Mark and I are good friends.”

“Oh, that’s good,” Yerim hums, “I felt so bad for a second there,” she exhales in relief, before clapping her hands together, “so, what do you say?!”

“You know what, I just remembered something so important I need to talk to Solar about!” Hyein had exclaimed out of nowhere, standing up straight abruptly and bolting around the island to grab Solar’s wrist, “sorry, we’ll be right back!”

Hanni had taken the hint as to what she was doing, and turned to ask Yerim an irrelevant question to distract her.
