Hyein dragged her into the living room, far enough that their conversation couldn’t be heard from the kitchen. The girl looked horrified, like she was about to witness a murder right in front of her. Solar took in her expression, “why do you look like that?”

“Girl, cause I almost witnessed you kill someone in real time!”

“What — I was not going to do anything,” Solar snapped, “why the heck would I care that Yerim has a crush?!”

Her friend was looking at her in complete bewilderment and irritation that she would even bother trying to say such words. “For starters,” she sasses, reaching up a finger to poke under her jaw, “I know you didn’t give that to yourself.”

Solar swatted her hand away with a grimace, “shut up, I don’t wanna hear it from you!”

“Just saying, I rest my case,” Hyein puts her hands up in defense, “God, I can’t believe you told us you were going to the lab just to go makeout with Haechan,” she started giggling furiously, the high pitched sound ringing through their ears, “that’s so cute, so scandalous, you guys really are the modern day Chuck and Blair, I mean, come on—”

The brunette cut her off by gripping her arm and dragging her back to the kitchen, knowing she was going to have to update Hanni now that Hyein already figured it out.

She never stood a chance against them, clearly.

Afterwards, the three girls sat at the small breakfast table, eating their breakfast in a comfortable silence. She’d answered the girls nosy questions about Haechan, before she’d grown too flustered and told them she was done updating them on her love life.

They didn’t push her, the two were happy she trusted them enough to tell her everything she had.

Instead, Hyein had started telling another story, something about a girl that had DM’d her on Instagram asking her about her prices because of how good their costumes were on Halloween.

In the middle of her story, Solar’s phone buzzed on the table next to her bowl of cereal. Her brows furrowed as she picked it up, noticing the icon was an email one, which she didn’t get very often anymore.

It came from an address she didn’t recognize, on behalf of a name she did. The subject line read, LEE — NOVEMBER SCHEDULE (REVISED). Copied on the email was her brother, and she tapped it, only for it to open not with her name, but a table.

Something deeply unpleasant pooled at the bottom of her stomach. Her eyes carefully scan, Thanksgiving week, arrival windows, a foundation function on Monday, a line about press attending in limited capacity, a note that a car would be arranged, and a request to confirm her travel by the fourteenth so the arrangement could be fully finalized.

She took a bitter bite of cereal to try to swallow away the frustration, sitting there in a pink kitchen in Syracuse, feeling four hundred miles of the Upper East Side arrive through a screen the size of her hand, in an eleven point font, from a person she had never met. She wondered, then, if she had jinxed it that morning, for anytime she thought about home it would always appear or find it’s way back into her life.

Two weeks, with the sorority camping trip before it. At the very least, she had plenty of time, right?

Although it would be smart to tell her friends, to get it off her chest, she pushed her chair away from the table, causing the two girls to halt their conversation and look at her. Picking up her bowl, she padded across the tile to place it in the sink, shoving her phone in her back pocket before she informed them, “I’m going.”

“Aw, you didn’t want to hear the end of my story?!” Hyein whined.

“Catch me up later,” Solar tells her, already exiting the doorway with a wave, “I need coffee!” she’d called behind her, a half truthful explanation for leaving earlier before her class started, even though the girls hadn’t asked in the first place.

The coffee, she would decide, was a mistake.

Well, not the coffee itself, but the decision, as it meant she’d arrived eleven minutes early instead of two minutes late, which was long enough to sit in a lecture hall watching the door and thinking hard about the perfect words to say.

Some lessons have to be learned the hard way.

The caption only pissed her off the more she thought about, some stupid, ridiculous photo of her with Mark during the Halloween party she was supposed to have no boy drama at. It was an absolute sick joke, and she remembered locking eyes with Danielle and feeling that twist in her stomach, yet she was too intoxicated to consider the consequences.

Truly, what did she expect? She was the one who danced with him like she had no cares in the world.

Still, the caption hadn’t read like a taunt, taunts were disposable, made up on the spot and thrown away. That caption had edges to it, it read like something that’d been said before, out loud, to somebody. It was not the first time she had thought about it since that photo dropped, and it wouldn’t be the last.

She was going to ask, she affirmed to herself, that’s the plan. She’d built it on the walk over, refining it down to something casual enough to be deniable, knowing well that if she came in swinging, Danielle would just smile and hand her absolutely nothing to work with.

Be flat, be bored, act like it doesn’t matter. It was exactly what Haechan would do. In fact, it was precisely what he did, every single day, to every single person. She’d watched him do it Sunday evening from two feet away reluctantly impressed how he could do it so easily. How hard could it really be? She wore a mask everyday of her life.

Danielle came in at three minutes past with a folder under one arm, sitting down a couple of seats over today. No one was going to sit in the seat between them, they never did when the two were this close, perhaps they could sniff the tension and decided it was not worth the trouble.”Good morning, Solar,” she’d offered in that bright, pleasant register that had never once meant anything at all.

“Morning, Danielle,” she returned.

The girl had met her eyes with a small, close lipped smile, before opening her laptop and focusing on the professor at the front of the room.

And that was the thing no one warned you about.

Solar had walked in, braced for a needle, and received seventy five minutes of a girl taking notes. Danielle wrote things down, highlighted something. At one point, the professor made a joke about compound interest, causing her to laugh, briefly, along with the other students. And Solar sat there, with her coffee growing cold underneath her palm, her prepared, practiced question rotting in her mouth.

She’s doing it on purpose, she thought, bitterly.

By minute forty, she’d stopped hearing the lecture entirely. She wrote the date at the top of the page, then wrote nothing else for half an hour, thinking about the concealer under her collar, whether it’d held, about the email sitting in her phone with the words confirm your travel plastered across it, and a boy on a rooftop whispering bad like the time of day.

Her jaw ached from how tightly she was clenching it. Closing her eyes for a split second, she regained her composure and unclenched it.

The professor released them four minutes early, meaning the room emptied fast than ever in eagerness, the shuffle and scrape of two hundred people bolting away in joy. Solar, on the other hand, packed slowly on purpose.

So did Danielle.

“You look better than ever,” she hummed, sliding her laptop into her bag.

“A good sleep schedule does that,” Solar offers bluntly.

“Totally, it sure shows,” she nods, but of course, she would never leave it at that, “the picture was cute, I thought.”

Solar kept her hands moving, notebook, pen, coffee cup still unfinished. She was trying her hardest not to crack, but the seams were starting to show.

“Cute or a total invasion of privacy?” she retorts.

“Oh, relax,” she rolls her eyes, “you looked happy, Solar.”

“Well no shit, I was drunk.”

“Those aren’t mutually exclusive, now are they?”

The brunette narrowed her eyes. She wanted to hold it in, she really did. But the words spit out of her mouth before she could stop them, “any idea who took it?” It wasn’t flat, nor bored, it was a half step too fast, a half tone too sharp, and she watched it enter her ears and realized she’d completely failed the task.

Danielle’s face was the same one she always wore, pleasant and unhurried, the expression of a woman being asked directions to a building she was standing in front of. There was something behind it that Solar had only ever seen twice from her, in a kitchen the Monday before last, and now, a kind of appetite, subtle and quiet.

And then she’d zipped her bag, the smile returning to her lips as she shook her head in contemplation, “how would I know, Solar?” she chuckled, “there were about a hundred and fifty people at that party, everyone has a phone.”

She’d stood then, hunching the bag over her shoulder. Solar followed, pursing her lips in a straight line. She’d gotten her there, it was a fact no one could deny.

“The caption,” she begins instead, “some lessons have to be learned the hard way,” she said it lightly, casually, “where’d you get that one?”

The next sound from her lips wasn’t a chuckle, it was a laugh, not the flat, orchestrated one, either, or the one she used on Chungha. It was a real laugh, small, quick, closed mouthed, there and gone within a second, doing something to the back of Solar’s neck that had nothing to do with it being early November.

“I can’t tell you,” she giggles lowly, “because I didn’t write it — though, it really is true, hm?”

“Danielle, we both know—”

“—You know,” she cuts her off, “you’ve only been here three months, Solar, some of us have been here longer,” the smile left her face by now, replaced with the look of something sinister underneath a blank expression, “why don’t you ask around to people who might have a better idea? I can sure think of a few to start, so I bet you can, too.”

Then she was gone, up the aisle and out the door into the noise of the hallway, before Solar could get a single syllable of the eleven she had ready in her throat. She stood there, in a nearly empty lecture hall, nearly crumpling her cardboard cup of coffee in her hand.

People who might have a better idea, she thought, God, I wonder who she’s talking about.

She did not appreciate her inner selves sarcasm.

Solar dropped the coffee in the bin by the door and headed out, into the cold with her ears ringing. It was fine.

Everything was totally fine.

-

Mark was already in Stats when she got there, bag on the seat beside him. He took it off the second he noticed her, which was very quick, an act he’d been doing for as long as she could remember now.

That dorky smile was on his face as he nodded his head in her direction, “yo.”

“Mark,” she offers his name as a greeting, sliding down into her seat and setting her notebook on the table in front of them.

“You look—” he stops himself, recalibrating mid-sentence, “awake… that’s a compliment, by the way.”

“Mm,” she hummed, chuckling, a phrase that only made her think of one person, “thanks, that’s probably the best compliment to get on a Monday.”

He’d giggled at that anyway, shaking his head before he’d went back to lining up his pens on the desk.

She didn’t usually pay enough attention to Mark Lee to notice minuscule things. But today, her eyes went down to his hands. She’d sat in this exact seat two weeks ago, a question in her mouth but no nerve to deliver it. Now, she was sitting there with an arguably worse one in the back of her throat rising like bile, and her eyes couldn’t seem to rip away from his knuckles.

They looked fine, three fingers on a pen, the other hand flat on the desk. There was maybe a shine across the third that could easily be explained as knocking it on a doorframe.

He swung first, Haechan’s words popped into her brain, unhelpfully.

Eventually, she had to look away, because the lecture was starting. Yet, her eyes found their way to him again, as hard as she was trying not to. Girls kept glancing at the two, whispering to their friends, likely talking about that ridiculous post from Halloween, how the two of them were so obvious, the new campuses couple, something about deja vu that was too cryptic to pinpoint.

She watched Mark highlight a formula in yellow while her brain thought about a kitchen she’d been directly above, the skillet on the floor, a version of that morning where she went down the stairs instead of out the front door.

The professor briefly paused to allow students to catch up on their notes. The boy next to her had noticed her daze, turning and raising a brow, “ay, you good, Sol?”

“Hm?” she nearly jumped, eyes widening, “Oh, yeah, I’m kind of tired.”

“Huh, I’d never guess.”

“Yep, it’s the concealer,” she almost choked on her words from the realization she was perhaps giving away too much. She did not need him focusing on how much makeup she’d put on this morning.

The professor picked back up, and went on to talk about regression for forty minutes.

Once the lecture ended, Solar and Mark were left alone enough, thanks to the students mostly pouring out of the room, for him to look up at her, bending over his chair to pack up his things. “Hey, uh, not to overstep — but, did you happen to run into Haechan yesterday?”

Her hands didn’t stop what they were doing, she continued to pack up her things completely casual. It was probably the most impressive thing she’d done all day, putting a notebook into a bag while every other part of her dropped four stories onto the pavement.

“Yesterday?”

“Yeah, like, Sunday evening,” he explains, noticing the confused look on her face, adding, “he just left in a hurry, I guess, wouldn’t tell me where he was going… I mean, I know we’re not that close anymore but, it was weird.”

Solar pursed her lips, throwing her bag over her shoulder and finally standing up straight. “Well, I don’t have any info for you,” she hums, “why would I have seen Haechan on a Sunday?”

A dumb question it was, and they both knew it, but neither of them was going to say a thing.

“I know, sorry, it came out wrong — not like, purposely, but just around, is what I meant,” he stutters, trying to regain his footing.

“Nope, I was at the lab.” It was a sentence she’d now said too many times to count, shamefully, false every single time.

The caramel boy just nods, a small smile spreading over his lips. She really couldn’t tell then if he believed her or not. Still, he didn’t push, which was somehow worse, because Mark Lee not pushing meant he’d gotten what he came for, or had simply decided the cost of asking twice was far too high.

“He just never used to do that,” he mumbles, eyes lowering to the desk they were standing by, “he used to be, like, so annoying about it, bragging about whatever girl he was going to see, where they were going to hook up at,” he pinched the bridge of his nose, recalling the memory with a dry chuckle, “now, it’s like living with a rumor.”

The words were on the tip of her tongue, he was on a rooftop with me, telling me how bad it really is, giving me his jacket that’s hanging on the back of my chair as we speak. The recollection caused her to nearly twitch right in front of Mark, hurriedly shaking her hands at her sides and shrugging, “he’s an adult, Mark, you shouldn’t worry about it so much.”

“I know,” he nods, “I’m just worried he’s going around the wrong people again, given, you know.”

He didn’t need to explain what he meant.

Friday night, he’d walked her home under the streetlights, telling her Haechan meant things he couldn’t keep. And two days later, she’d sat on a ledge and heard the truth right out of his own mouth like the time of day, felt his lips on her neck in a complete bliss.

So, Mark was right, she supposed, which was the unbearable part. He was standing right here being right, and he’d been right on Friday, too. But the thing was, every time he was right, he told her as if it was some kind of gift she’d been dumb to refuse.

A lot of things rushed through her mind. As badly as she wanted to ask about the fight, about the scholarship, it would only give away that she had indeed saw his best friend last night.

“Did you take the picture?” she blurted instead.

He looked up from the spot he was staring at on the table. “The picture…” he trails off in a whisper, thinking about what she could be on about, before a wave washes over his face, eyes widening, “no.”

“Did you send it in?” she asks next, voice softer.

“I — no, of course not, Sol.”

A deep exhale she didn’t know she was holding leaves her lips. He didn’t ask why she was asking, which she was thankful for, because she had no idea how to explain.

“Okay, thanks,” she breathes, “I wasn’t trying to accuse you, it just — I just want to make sense of it, in my head, to get to the bottom of all of this.”

“Yeah,” he nods in agreement, “yeah, me too.”

He pulled his bag further up his shoulder, not angry, but tired, which she had not budgeted for. His eyes linger on hers for a second, breaking away and falling to his feet, where he nervously shifts his weight.

“He’s still my best friend,” he admits hesitantly, “I keep thinking I can go in there, say the right thing, that he’ll — I don’t know, put it all down, stop hurting himself.”

All of the things she wondered about Mark didn’t consider the fact he was still a boy’s friend at the end of all this, that he did genuinely care, that he wanted him to get better, even if he was partly the reason for it.

“I used to enable it,” he continues, “I used to do it, too. I mean, I still do every now and then, don’t get me wrong, but not like this,” he clears his throat, almost looking like he could cry, “you know, I just worry that I’m making it all worse.”

Making it worse, her brain collected, but you didn’t take the photo.

“You’re not making it worse, Mark,” she consoles.

“You don’t know that, though,” he frowns.

“Hey,” she steps forward, a part of her feeling guilty, reaching out a hand to place on his forearm. The boy jumps from her unexpected touch, eyes searching her face for any sign of hidden meaning. “I don’t know, you’re right, but it’s clear you care,” she sends him a small smile, “so, don’t beat yourself up.”

Although, she wasn’t sure if she entirely believed it. Right there, in daylight, was still a boy who’d punched his best friend in a kitchen and never told her, on the same day he decided he had no choice but to pick up the substances again.

And throughout it all, even if it was right in front of her, she couldn’t decipher if it was a technique or a person.

“Thanks, Sol,” he finally grins, her hand falling back down to her side, which he almost looked sad to see, “sad stuff aside, you still down to hangout, maybe Saturday?”

At the look on her face, he hurriedly adds, “no pressure, I know you’ve still got regionals prep, so seriously don’t feel like I’m holding you to it, there’s plenty of time—”

“—Mark,” she cuts him off, but the boy was still in a fit of rambles.

“—for us to hangout after all that’s over, so, you can tell me if it’s a bad week—”

“—Mark,” she cuts him off again, sterner this time, and the boom caused him to shut his mouth finally. She replaced her firm look with that of a smile, “sure, we can hangout on Saturday.”

His whole face seemed to reorganize itself, immediate and unguarded, landing in her chest like a thrown stone. There was nothing smug about it, that was the part she couldn’t get around.

“Chill,” he beams, “super chill, actually, I’ll text you, yeah?”

“Sounds like a plan.”

He was smiling like a schoolchild, beginning to jog down the steps in pure excitement he was not afraid to show, nearly taking out a girl who had stayed late to catch up on work, “Sorry — sorry — okay, sick, see you, Sol!”

She watched him leave before making her way out herself.

Outside, the cold got into her collar, but she didn’t notice. The girl was too preoccupied rolling over the conversation, the fact he had said no twice, without decoration, and she had believed him, looking for the crack and failing to find one. In return, it had left her with a boy who threw the first punch, never mentioned it, who had been right about Haechan twice in three days, who thought he might be making it worse, who seemed to want his best friend to be sober more than anything.

None of it fit together, her brain stated the obvious.

Or, it fits perfectly, yet you don’t like the shape.

She had forty minutes before Media and Society, which she spent thirty eight of pretending she wasn’t thinking about a rooftop in the night.

60: marks under the collar

Solar stopped pretending two minutes before, focusing on walking to the anticipated class. By the time she reached the building, her brain had gotten all the way through some lessons have to be learned the hard way and he’s using again, Sol, arriving unhelpfully at see you tomorrow, pretty, which had been said to her at the bottom of a ladder by a boy who then lit a blunt and walked around the corner like nothing had happened.

And here she was, today was tomorrow, after all.

She blew air into her cheeks before dramatically huffing it out as she pushed open the door to the lecture hall. No one was really present yet, giving her a clear path to the seat she’d taken every Monday and Thursday since August, four rows up the aisle. Setting her notebook down, she slumps into her chair with her hands flat on the desk like a woman waiting for test results.

Expectantly, the room began to fill the way it always did. Media and Society was a core class for her degree, meaning it was a core class for about a hundred and some other people who didn’t want to be there. Those people arrived to said class in the specific slouching wave of a two o’clock lecture, their coats still on and coffees full. Somebody two rows down was quietly, yet confidently, talking about the Halloween party, followed by Halloween pt2 that apparently happened on Saturday, recounting mostly the insane acts of Jeno.

However, the brunette couldn’t focus much on the conversation because her eyes kept wandering towards the door.

Ridiculous, her brain supplied at her in shame, causing her to shake her head and aggravatedly look down to her notebook, flipping to a clean page before writing the date at the top. She tried to tell herself it was definitely not a mechanism meant to distract her, doodling some stars around the margins of the page.

Five minutes before class began, the boy at the top of her mind walked in, always five minutes early. His eyes scanned the room, casually, landing on hers and lingering there for a few extra seconds. Her throat welled, and she ripped her glance away, continuing to pretend to be intently focused on her notebook.

He’d made it four steps up before a girl had reached out to touch his arm. Solar hadn’t noticed because of her poor performance, doodling more stars until the page looked like it was going to rip.

The sound, however, was distinct enough to be more like a weather pattern, a rise in pitch, two voices, then three, a laugh that went up at the end like a question. She kept her eyes on the empty page, tuning into the conversation at the last minute, the temptation taking over her, listening to Haechan Lee be painfully famous.

“—seriously, though, you’ll be there on Friday, right?” one of the girls had been pouting, “We missed you Saturday.”

He didn’t spare her a glance, he just halted, one leg on the next step, and hummed, “I’m sure you did,” entirely ignoring the question she’d asked.

“Is that a yes?” the girl had called, but he was already walking up the steps without another word.

Solar bit the inside of her cheek as the scrape of the chair next to her echoed through the noise of the hall. In September, she’d spent a solid three weeks constructing an elaborate internal case about why he had chosen to sit next to her, analyzing the proximity from the door, the angle of the projector, or perhaps just the fact that he was a menace who enjoyed bothering her in his free time. Through all that, she had never thought about him possibly just wanting to sit next to her.

He dropped into the chair, hood down, black fringe in his eyes, letting his bag slump against the leg of the desk. A girl from the far row down was turned in her chair dreamily staring at him as if he was a statue, and hurriedly looked away when Solar caught her gaze.

Neither of them said anything.

How absurd was it to think that thirty six hours ago, his lips were on her neck. Recalling the memory caused her to nearly snort aloud in class, and she pondered it with the composure of someone reading a shopping list.

“Nice sweater,” the honey tone observed from the seat next to her.

Her pen stopped from where’d she’d been drawing another intricate star. Slowly, her head turned, only to find him staring ahead at the front of the room, invested in the projector all of a sudden despite the fact it was off. His face remained blank, though the corner of his mouth was doing something structural that she had to fight not reaching over to stop.

“Well, it’s November,” she deadpans.

“Wow, very observant of you.”

“People wear sweaters in November, Haechan,” she grumbles, annoyed already with his mocking tone of voice.

“That they do,” he nods, twirling a pen around his fingers, before he’d finally looked at her, tilting his head to the side only slightly to monotone, brown eyes lingering on the collar for the slightest of seconds, then back to her eyes, “warm in here, though. We don’t want you to get hot for the wrong reasons, pretty.”

She could embarrassingly feel her cheeks growing red, and the smirk that spread across his lips told her he’d already noticed.

The girl faced forward anyway, not giving him the satisfaction of an answer. The real reason was the fact she didn’t have one that wasn’t going to come out of her mouth sounding like a confession. God, I hope no one else is looking right now, she thought with humiliation, though she could only feel the burn of the boy next to her in her skull.

It’s fine, she assures herself, you’re going to be normal for the next seventy five minutes, and go home like nothing. That’s what you’ll do, right?

She was, of course, gravely incorrect, but for all of the reasons she wouldn’t have expected.

The professor entered on time and began to turn all of the proper equipment on, standing at the podium and beginning to organize his things. In the meantime, students continued to chatter, the sound filling up the room with a mediocre noisiness that was almost comfortable by now.

What wasn’t comfortable was the boy that suddenly appeared next to the desk, stopping at the end of her row.

“Solar, right?” he offered, causing her head to whip up in surprise that someone else was talking to her in this class, “you went through the wall.”

She observed this boy she had never met, a nerdy boy that likely went unnoticed. He was standing there with a laptop bag pinned under one arm, beaming down at her as if he was meeting some kind of celebrity.

“Sorry?” she blinked, still too stuck in her thoughts to realize what he was talking about.

“On Rialto, second point,” he stated, like they were already halfway into the conversation, “everyone thinks you teleported to the Ana, but you didn’t — you held it for like, what, four seconds? Then you put it through the wall behind the Widow,” he was nearly clapping his hands from how excited retelling it made him, “I mean, flawless play, their tank was absolutely flabbergasted!”

Her eyes widened in surprise but her own form of happiness, at the same time. She’d been recognized on this campus a great deal since August, and every single instance had nearly been because of her name, being Jaehyun’s sister, something about her status or love life. And here was someone in front of her who opened with something about her cooldown.

“Five,” she corrects finally with a kind smile, “it was five seconds.”

“Five,” he nods in confirmation, satisfied, as though a small argument had been settled, pushing his glasses up his nose, “my friend said it was luck.”

“It wasn’t luck.”

“I know!” he cries, offended on her behalf, “that exactly what I said.”

Beside her, Haechan hadn’t moved a muscle, entirely still in the way of a cat deciding whether something on the other side of a room was worth standing up for. His pen continued to twirl around his fingers after a moment, face entirely drained of any emotion.

The boy had shifted his bag to the other arm, running out of the part of the conversation he planned. He nervously shoved his other hand into his pocket, shifting his weight from one foot to the other, before stuttering out, “so, how about a duo?” He was oddly confident despite his mishap, and she could only presume it was something he’d practiced in the mirror before.

Solar watched a wave of horror cross the boy’s face before she could answer, approximately the speed of sound. It’d taken her longer than she planned to register what had been said until then. “What rank are you?” Haechan’s flat tone pended, finally turning his head to boredly meet the eyes of the nerdy boy.

Her head whipped to him, face doing all of the talking as she mouthed what are you doing only to be completely ignored. In return, the boy blinked, looking past her for the first time, utterly confused at the question, “Oh — uh, I’m Diamond 3.”

Haechan rose a brow, snorting, “little low for someone of her skill level, don’t you think?”

“Well, I can—”

“—You can try someone in your own bracket first,” he’d monotoned, cutting him off due to disinterest, “the ladder exists for a reason.”

Solar’s eyes bulged with how petty he was being, bewildered at the sight she was witnessing. In disbelief, she kicked his shin under the table, but he didn’t even make a face or spare her a single glance. “Haechan—”

“Aim lower, maybe, everyone knows you can’t start at the top,” he hummed, with an expression of such profound and courteous emptiness that she could feel it in her teeth. Finally, he looked over to her as if he hadn’t done a thing, “Relax, I’m offering friendly advice, sweetheart.”

The thing about it, he wasn’t loud, and she would realize that much when she rolled it over in her head moments later. It was said in the same register he would use to order food, to answer a question in class, but had still flown through the lecture hall like a knife. Three rows of people were suddenly extremely interested in their laptops. Two girls near the aisle had turned all the way around with their eyes bulging. And Solar, Solar understood a second and a half too late to do anything with, that not one of them was going to remember the rank joke.

No, they would remember that Haechan had called her sweetheart in a room with a hundred people in it, entirely bored and uninterested.

A bitter huff of disbelief left her lips at the fact it’d only been two days since he’d told her she wouldn’t want everyone to see the way she smiled at him.

She turned to the boy in the puffer jacket, who had gone a light and unfair shade of pink, smiling at him apologetically, “ignore him,” she exhales, “it’s solsystem, my Battletag, one word, no caps.”

The entire room likely felt the way Haechan’s jaw shifted beside her.

But the boy had fumbled his phone out of his pocket, delighted, typing with his thumb and bag sliding off his shoulder. “Awesome — so cool, thank you, seriously,” he piped to her in revelation, before he’d awkwardly turned and continued walking to his seat, whispering to himself, “my friends are not going to believe this, holy shit.”

Of course, she didn’t have any intention of queueing with this random Diamond player. She’d done it solely in front of him on purpose, a statement they both knew, and it was still the most satisfying thing that had happened to her since Friday. Though, the boy beside her did not say a single thing.

In fact, he wouldn’t say anything for the rest of the lecture, seventy five minutes, which she learned was a thing he would do at a volume, the same way he controlled music.

The professor talked about audience construction and who a message is built for. And Haechan sat there next to her, neatly writing in his notebook with bullet points, a thing she had never paid much attention to. She found there was something obscene about watching a person be furious and take clean notes at the same time. The sight didn’t scare her in the slightest, it actually made her smile deviously to herself.

At minute forty, her phone buzzed on the desk between them.

Her eyes scanned over the messages in about three seconds. It was nothing, a boy confirming a plan, offering a place he wanted to take her, two friends, she tried to tell herself, just Mark. She had said yes, and she would end up saying yes to this, because a part of her genuinely wanted to believe in the good of Mark, because she had seen it, in the twinkle of his irises, she wanted to believe it so bad. And there was no version of this that was any of Haechan’s business, he’d never once made anything his business because it would require him saying something he didn’t want to.

Something formed in her throat anyway, causing her to flip the phone face down. Her eyes dared her to look up, only to see he wasn’t looking at the screen. He hadn’t even glanced at the screen, his deep eyes were focused on her face, where they’d been for however long it’d taken her to read those messages, to witness what her expression was doing in the meantime. Nothing was in his expression, not a single thing she could note to herself.

I walk into a place and know who’s pissed off before they do — who’s lying, when someone’s about to say something they’ll regret.

The words echoed at the back of her mind. He’d told her that what felt like only hours ago, sitting on a ledge in the dark with her hand over his, like a confession. She’d held it, calling it the most honest thing she’d ever heard from him.

Never did she consider he could easily use such a mechanism on her, and probably had multiple times by now. She was only noticing it now that he’d told her.

He turned back to the front of the room. The professor said something, causing a few students to laugh, and Solar sat there in the fourth row with a face down phone under her palm with thirty five minutes left on the clock, thinking with the sinking, unhurried clarity of a person watching a car arrive at an intersection they were already in, he’s going to say something, he won’t be able to help himself.

As if to confirm that belief, she felt a hand graze her thigh underneath the table.

Thirty five minutes.

That was how long Media and Society had left on the clock when Haechan decided that his hand belonged on her leg, and thirty five minutes, was an extremely long time.

It started as nothing, a graze, the backs of his knuckles against the denim of her jeans, the kind of contact a person could do accidentally. She didn’t move, didn’t react, just kept her eyes forward, pen on the page, waiting to see if he had the audacity to continue.

Naturally, he did, he always would.

His palm flattened over the outside of her thigh, assigned there without argument. The worst part, the unforgivable part, was that he did all of it with his right hand while his left kept writing, neat little bullet points marching down the page in that irritating handwriting of his. And in the meantime, his fingers slowly etched to her inner thigh, applying a ticklish amount of pressure, the perfect amount to send a tingle through her body.

He’s sitting there taking notes, she observed bitterly, he thinks he’s so smug right now taking his stupid fucking notes.

With a deep sigh, she wrote the word audience at the top of her page, underlining it four times with the concentration of a surgeon, telling herself nothing else was happening. At the front of the room, the professor continued the lecture, raking his eyes across the students to ensure they were all listening.

His thumb began to move in circles, the final straw that got under her skin, because it was only seconds before he reached an area she did not need his hands near right now.

“Stop it,” she hushes at him in annoyance.

He only partly glanced at her, harmlessly, “hm, what’s wrong?” His brown eyes fell back to his notes, where he continued to write something down while looking up at the projector.

“You know what,” she hissed under her breath.

“I’m listening to the lecture, princess,” he murmured, but his thumb moved again, slowly riding up near her heat, against the middle seam of her jeans, and she had to physically close her mouth before she squirmed or yelled in irritation.

Two girls in the row ahead were on their phones now. The professor was three slides deep into whether a message can be said to have a sincere audience. Someone behind them coughed, and Solar sat there in the fourth row of a hundred person lecture hall, pressing her thighs together, trying to pretend like her ears weren’t on fire, and a boys hand in between her thighs, who was apparently deeply invested in media theory.

She let it go on for three minutes, not because it was doing something to her, she swore, but because she did not want to give him the satisfaction of successfully winning the I don’t care battle.

Until she couldn’t take it anymore, and frustratedly reached down without looking away from the screen, taking his wrist between her thumb and two fingers and lifting it off her thigh to set it back on his own desk with a thump.

He didn’t react at first, until he’d started chuckling to himself, only loud enough for her to hear.

-

The class ended four minutes late, resulting in a scrape and a rush of a hundred people deciding at once they’d had enough media studies for one day. She watched them pile out in groups, the last few always lingering, some talking to the professor. Rising to her feet, she began to pack her own things slowly, a talent she’d developed only recently.

Haechan didn’t pack nor move. He sat there with his pen twirling around his fingers, notebook still open, watching the room drain, a group of girls arguing about a party, the professor bidding the student he was speaking to farewell and turning to unplug things at the podium.

He was waiting, of course he was waiting.

The last two people were a boy in a Syracuse crewneck and, unsurprisingly, the professor, who paused at the door with his bag over his shoulder, noticing the two students, before giving them a vaguely benevolent look and deciding, presumably, that he didn’t care. The door swung heavy and slow on its hinge behind him.

It didn’t lock, lecture halls didn’t. Anyone in that building could put a hand on that door in the next ten minutes and open it, they both knew that, it wasn’t exactly a campus secret.

And finally, he turned in his chair to face her, looking at her with his elbow hooked over the back of the seat, messy dark hair atop his forehead, the specific patience of a man who had been sitting through a lecture for seventy five minutes with a plan. His eyes studied her in careful admiration, memorizing the details, the way her eyes shone under the fluorescent lighting.

Then, it left him, the flatness, “that was cute, sweetheart.”

“Cute?” she blurted, accidentally letting the bewilderment show on her face.

“Mm,” he hummed, “watching you be proud of yourself like that, priceless.”

“You’re not — I know that bothered you,” she deflected with a huff.

“Didn’t say it didn’t,” he monotones, nonchalantly.

She exhales, pinching the bridge of her nose to recollect herself. She looks then at the boy peering up at her, not feeling the need to continue the endless game of banter. They were past that, weren’t they? How many times had they done it before? What she really wanted to ask was how he was doing, if he’d done anything since last night. She wanted to ask if he was okay, but she knew she couldn’t say any of those things.

So, she chose something else she’d been carrying since she walked into a bedroom and confronted a girl who knew the right thing to say at every given moment.

“Remember Danielle?”

Something almost washed over his expression from the unexpected change of topic, nonetheless at what it was. Whatever he had turned around expecting had not been that, and for a quarter of a second, the patience slipped off his face and something else took over it, unattended.

“The creepy sorority girl,” he returns, “how could I forget?”

Creepy sorority girl almost got a laugh out of her. Crazy to think, in September this boy had leaned into her space at a party, telling her not to tell that supposed sorority girl anything she didn’t want turned into a weapon, but feigned ignorance that it was anything he’d learned from experience. Now, here he was, sitting here monotoning, in that bored yet faintly amused register he used for people he didn’t offer a single thought to, and as a result, she felt the floor of the conversation drop by a foot before she had even decided her next words.

He’s sniffing it out, deciding how much I’m going to say, how serious it’s going to get.

Do I trust him, she asked herself.

“She runs the accounts,” she blurts, which was answer enough to her own internal question.

“Runs what?”

“The — the accounts, Haechan,” she sasses, knowing he was bullshitting and acting clueless on purpose, gripping the strap of her bag tighter with anxiety, “she’s the one making those stupid fucking posts, about me… about you…” she trails off, swallowing an ache in her throat at the remembrance.

He was watching her, every twitch of her fingers on the strap, every way her eyes kept looking instead of at his, his face blank as he studied her. His pen was still in his hand leaning over the back of the chair, twirling it, “you think it’s her,” he hums, knowing the answer but interesting more in what her expression would do when he asked.

And she knew that, which he could gather from the unimpressed look she gave him. “No, I know it,” she corrects sternly, “she literally quoted the caption to me before it was even up… so, I confronted her.”

“Wow, and here I thought you’d be used to the attention by now.”

“Well, it wasn’t over…” she stopped talking, because she wondered if she wanted to tell him that. His brow raised in question, she wasn’t going to get out of it. “It was about the relapse post,” she admits, biting on her bottom lip gently, “I was mad… and she didn’t deny anything, it was like she was enjoying it.”

For once, he had to look away from the emotion that spread over his face, embarrassed. He twisted his head to look down at the desk, tapping the pen against it a few times.

“Alright,” he exhales, “you shouldn’t of worried about the post, princess.”

“It’s not — of course I worried about the post,” she cried in exasperation, “it’s horrible to do that to someone, nonetheless you,” her voice cracked when she said it. She regretted it almost instantly, feeling like she gave away too much, too much she hadn’t even admitted to herself. His eyes jerked back to her, surprise hidden underneath the deep brown. She knew he wasn’t going to say anything to that, how could he? It wasn’t in his nature. So, instead, she nervously sputters, “anyway, the point is… it’s her, it’s all her.”

“Alright,” he repeats again, unbothered.

She looked down at him in the chair in absolute bafflement. “Alright?!”

He tilts his head up at her, “you want me to be surprised?”

“I mean, yeah, anything would be nice!” she snapped louder than she’d meant, accidentally, from the way he seemed to bother he even when he didn’t mean to. Closing her eyes for a split second, she opens them again to sigh, “Plus, she knew about the meeting — in the living room, the one my brother called me after, when he told you the third time thing.”

Abruptly, the pen stopped tapping. He grew quiet, not in the sitting very quietly while a boy in a puffer jacket embarrasses himself quiet, either. This quiet was a different kind, complete and immediate, the stillness of a machine that had been left running then suddenly switched off. He was staring somewhere away from her, about two feet to the left of her head, almost in a daze, in utter contemplation.

He’s counting, she realized, without knowing what that exactly entailed.

His brain was moving, rolling over the entire thing, the way he remembered it, even though he’d been in a hungover, mess of a state. Jaehyun, Jeno, Jaemin, Mark, myself…

“—Haechan,” she called out, cutting off his thoughts.

“Hm?“

“Hi, ready to come back to Earth now?” she snapped her fingers in his face, half sassily and half playfully, “You literally just despawned.”

The corner of his mouth twitched in amusement, “I’m right here, sweetheart.” He’d come back into his own face like someone stepping through a door, so smooth she almost let it go. “Just recalling the specifics.”

She stared down at him in confusion, “okay, and, what’s the verdict?”

He met her eyes again, but she could not find the answer in the twinkle, because every time she laid eyes on it she felt herself disappearing with no memory of what mattered before. Still, something was in her gut, something dark and visceral, she didn’t have the slightest idea where to put such a feeling, either.

“Come here,” he deadpans, completely ignoring her question.

“That’s not an answer,” she complains, but the boy reached out to grab her wrist, gently tugging her forward, “Haechan — I’m not letting this go, you can’t just—”

“—Mm, can’t what, pretty?” he whispered, pulling her onto his lap, which she shamefully let happen. His thumb ran across the line of her jaw, tilting his head and inching closer one millimeter at a time, “That’s enough talk, don’t you think?”

She reached up to slap his hand, huffing, “No, I think we need to put our heads together because you live in that house—”

He shut her up that time by kissing her.

It was not like last night, that much was evident. Sunday had been a rooftop with chilling air, his hand coming up slow enough that she’d had time to decide about it. This was not gentle, it was a hand at the back of her neck with an immense amount of force she would only ever allow him to produce, his mouth against hers before she’d finished the sentence she was in the middle of.

And the entire structure of her afternoon, everything important she was trying to talk to him about, flew out the window.

Mid kiss, he slid her bag off her shoulder and chunked it on the floor somewhere next to them, hands gripping her thighs to pull her closer to him, if even possible.

“Someone could literally—”

He’d stood up with his hands on her thighs, setting her on the desk that had been in front of them, one hand at her jaw and the other at the small of her back to hold her up, like choreography.

In between kisses, she managed, “—those doors don’t even—”

“—I know,” he said into her mouth, but didn’t make the slightest effort to stop anything he was doing. Whatever careful, bored, unbothered thing he had been running since he entered that room had come apart somewhere between she knew about the meeting and him saying he was recalling the specifics. She could feel where it’d gone, because it was in front of her, into her jaw, her waist, the way he pushed the collar of her turtleneck down with his thumb to find the mark he’d left on her Sunday before nuzzling into her neck to suck his teeth onto the spot, checking his work, whispering against the skin, “didn’t want to show everyone your prize, hm?”

She couldn’t properly retort due to the sounds leaving her lips, a slight catch of her breath and a humiliating whimper she wouldn’t admit to making. “Haechan.”

He ignored her that time, continuing to suck angrily on her neck. If he’d told her he was a vampire, she’d believe it without question. Her body cried, ached, longed for something more, and he knew it, with the way his hands rubbed her upper thighs, daring her to say something else. They rode up until they were at the button her jeans, and it took every single bone in her body to speak again.

“Donghyuck—”

*“—pretty, you know* that only makes me want to do more.”

“I have to—” she tries again, ignoring his annoying insistence, but he’d kissed her again, his hands riding from the button of her jeans under her shirt, under her bra, until he was cupping her breasts with a force that was strong enough to cause her to choke on her spit.

Her phone buzzed in her pocket, a single time, shooting her back into reality, into her body all at once, with a boys hands under her bra and thirty seconds of somewhere to be.

“I have to go,” she finally finishes, her hands on his wrists to pull them out from under her shirt.

He let her, hands falling back down to rest on her thighs, but he didn’t step back. Haechan stayed exactly where he was, close enough that she could feel him breathing, looking at her for a long moment with his hair a mess, lips swollen pink, and something moving quickly behind those irises.

“You’re going to see him,” he monotones, not as a question, not as a guess. He hadn’t looked at her phone or read her texts, he read it off her face, and had been sitting on it since.

It wasn’t like it was something he could tell her not to do.

But it made her feel weird saying it anyway.

“I — yeah,” she stutters.

Say something, her mind screamed in desperation, somewhere between a dare and a plea, say one thing, that you don’t want me to, what this is, anything with a word in it that actually means something.

Until, he’d casually yawned and took a step back, “alright.”

He bent and picked her bag from the floor, holding it out to her. Her eyes watched him for a moment before she let herself fall back onto her feet, taking the bag. The boy turned then to pick up his notebook, sliding the pen into the spiral.

The temperature in the room dropped about fifteen degrees, yet there was not a single thing to push against.

He could not say it didn’t bother him, he couldn’t tell her all of the things he knew. He wasn’t an idiot, he knew he didn’t have any standing, that they had never once said a word about what this was because he didn’t want to say it. There was not a single sentence either of them could point to, and if she’d have said don’t be like this, he would’ve looked at her with that empty courteous face and asked like what, princess in which she’d have been speechless.

He’d found one place to stand where she couldn’t reach him, and it’d taken him only about four seconds.

She tried anyway. “Haechan.”

“You’re gonna be late,” he hums, but didn’t make an effort to move.

If it’s about Mark, then it’s a fight, and we all know you’re extremely good at fights.

And here he was, doing that exact thing right in front of her.

She couldn’t fully grasp why they both insisted she could not trust the other yet refused to give her clear answers as to why. Even if she felt uneasy about Mark, she did not have a concrete reason she could point to that showed he wasn’t the sweet, dorky guy she knew him as. And if she had learned anything from Media and Society, it was that she shouldn’t judge someone based off of rumor alone. Haechan taught her that, too, but still, sometimes she seemed to process that there were parts of those rumors that were true.

Like the fact he couldn’t seem to let himself feel anything.

“Okay,” she breathes, spinning on her heel and walking down the stairs without another word. She wasn’t going to play this game with him. She’d decided she was better than that.

The signs would stay anyway. There was a smear of lip gloss on the back of her hand from where she’d wiped her mouth, her hair doing something she could feel without a mirror, and the collar of the turtleneck she had put on specifically to hide the actions of Sunday night had been dragged down and left where it fell. She hurriedly fixed it, smoothing down the craziness of her dark hair, before pushing open the door with a deep exhale.

Mark was against the wall opposite the door, hands in his letterman jacket pockets, bag between his feet. He’d clearly been there awhile, to the point he almost looked half asleep.

At the sound of the door flipping open, he’d stood up too fast, fast enough he nearly stumbled onto the tiled floor. “Hey!” he practically yelled, before lowering his voice from the weird looks people passing were sending him, “Hey — you didn’t text back so I thought I’d, like, wait… you know, like a guy who stands in hallways like a weirdo.”

Solar chuckled, standing in front of him and meeting his soft eyes. They were soft in a way Haechan’s never were, delicate, the fluttering petals of a flower blossoming from the dirt. “You’re not a weirdo,” she chuckles, “sorry, I was packing up.”

More like, on a desk.

“No, it’s chill, you don’t even need to tell me that,” he insists hurriedly. It was three fifteen and the corridor around them continued to empty itself, hundreds of people trying to be somewhere else at once, and Mark Lee was standing there smiling at her as if she’d done him a favor by existing in the same building.

That morning, she’d spent twenty minutes on her neck so no one would notice the aftermath of a rooftop, and now, there was nothing under her collar but the sweater. The thought dried out her throat.

“Ramen,” she offers, raising a brow.

“Oh, yeah, you totally don’t — wait, is that a yes?”

“Saturday, ramen,” she stated again, unable to stop the giggle that left her lips from how thrilled he looked, “yes, I’m saying yes, Mark.”

He grinned from ear to ear, a bubble about to burst, “great, that’s… I’m really excited, I’ll work out the details, okay?”

She nodded in agreement, and the two began to walk towards the exit doors.

He was good at it, talking the whole way down the corridor and out into the grey, something about a group project quietly falling apart without him, a girl in his Wednesday English lecture who ate an entire sandwich during a quiz. It was so easy, unbearably so, and Solar walked beside him with their shoulders touching, ears still burning, with the most prominent mark on her neck yet that was only ninety seconds old, laughing at the sandwich thing because the dorky, bewildered way he was saying it.

She hadn’t looked back a single time. There was no reason to, she knew what was behind her, sitting in an empty lecture hall with his notebook in hand.

Little did she know, Mark had, and the caramel boy locked eyes with him. They’d maybe made it thirty feet down the hall when the door of the lecture room swung out and his supposed best friend came out, his hood over his eyes, bag over one shoulder. He made eye contact with Mark for a few seconds, face blank, before turning the other way towards the far stairwell. A group of girls came around the corner and practically jumped with joy at the sight of him, running up to him and trying to engage in conversation, likely about the party that was always happening on Friday. And like that, he was suddenly preoccupied, unbothered and bored.

Solar didn’t notice, she was in the middle of telling her own story. “Yeojin said she was cooking dinner the other night, I think it was Saturday, after I got home — and then she ate the entire serving of pasta herself,” she was humming, “Hyein was very angry, and you can imagine what that looks like.”

Mark got the whole interaction with his friend to himself, which was, he’d think later, kind of the story of his life. He didn’t know why he didn’t think of it sooner, he knew they had that class together. They’d had it together since August, and he’d spent three weeks being super normal about it while being considerably less normal internally. It was safe to say there were a lot of questions that popped into his head regarding two people leaving the same lecture hall ninety seconds apart.

Except, Solar had come out of that room with her hair pushed off her face on one side and her collar sitting funny, with a flush on her that she’d had to walk off for a minute. She’d said packing up, and Mark let it go like he always would, cause letting it go was the entire architecture of being the person she called her friend.

“Wow,” he’d noted as he faced the front again before she could look at him, “she should get, like, a strike for that.”

“I know right,” she boasted, and they kept walking.

Ask her, his mind yelled at him. He wasn’t going to. Mark wasn’t a dumb ass, there were only two ways such a thing could go. Either it was nothing, and he looked like a jerk who accused her of something in a parking lot on a Monday, losing every inch of ground he’d spent six weeks earning. Or, it wasn’t nothing, and she’d lie to him and know it.

He didn’t want either of those. In reality, he wanted the third thing, which didn’t exist, which was for it to be nothing and for him to be sure of that fact.

You could tell Danielle, his brain offered. The thought stood up, causing him to frustratedly bury it back down, hard, the way one would step on a bug. That trade only ran one direction, he gave her the house, her brother, and the shape of an afternoon, and in return, she’d give him proximity. And if he handed her this, Danielle wouldn’t just hold it. She’d plaster it somewhere public, and Solar would go through the world wondering who’d done it, and God forbid it somehow came back to him. Not to mention, he liked the current public narrative.

So, he’d done nothing about it, instead he laughed down at her as they walked out the front doors into the November chills, telling himself, it’s patience.

He walked her to Alpha Phi, a routine neither of them thought very hard about anymore. Solar appreciated it, the way she appreciated Minji walking her, and had turned on the first step with a genuine smile on her face.

“Thanks,” she tells him, “I’ll see you around, Mark.”

“Yeah,” he nods, trying not to study her as closely as he was, “yeah, always a pleasure with you, Sol.”

She pursed her lips in a thin line, before offering him a nod. Then, she was gone, into the door of Alpha Phi to get ready to go to practice that evening.

Mark stood there for another minute, debating with himself internally, before pulling his phone from the pocket of his letterman.

61: he knows it

The dining hall on a Tuesday was the closest thing Syracuse had to a public square, which meant that Hanni Pham had spent the last eleven minutes eating a bowl of soup that was definitely a little undercooked in a room where roughly two hundred people could watch her. It wasn’t an abnormal experience, her and Hyein liked to come there every now and then, when they didn’t feel like cooking in Alpha or when Yeojin ate all the leftovers again. Today happened to be one of those days, in the chill dim light of November, with everyone wearing coats and gloves and pretending their teeth weren’t painfully chittering.

“She just left, like, I want to know more!” Hyein was in the middle of complaining, elbows on the table, entirely unbothered about the full hall of students, “I mean, come on, no details, nothing. Four minutes of my life I gave her and she gives me a sweater!”

“She told us a lot, actually,” Hyein offers quietly.

“Five things is not a lot!” the girl whines, desperate to know every minuscule detail about Solar’s love life.

“That is a lot for Solar,” Hanni objects.

With a sigh, Hyein pointed her fork at her in response, meaning she was conceding without saying so, and went back to her pasta. Across the hall, someone dropped their tray, causing the room to erupt in mocking applause, a commonality around SU.

Though she wasn’t going to say it, Hanni had been thinking about it, too. How Solar and Haechan were whatever they were, what happened Sunday night, that Solar lied about the lab, which Hanni had already worked out on her own based off everything she’d told them yesterday. There was something evident from the way she beamed when she talked about him, clear as day to the two girls who remembered what it looked like the week they did not speak.

Unlike Hyein, Hanni had spent most of the conversation thinking to herself, how many people will I have to lie to about this? Because while she was happy to see her friend happy, she was also concerned about the dangers, and the fact she hated lying. It came with too many strings attached, and filled her chest with the most uncomfortable anxiety.

Even though she was suspicious of Mark, she still hated the idea of lying to his face.

is sol doing okay?

The messages were still sitting in her phone from last night. She’d answered in about forty seconds, warm and easy, before putting her phone down on her comforter and laying there feeling like she’d done something.

Of course, she hadn’t done anything. That was the point of it, she was telling the truth, just omitting some details. Solar did tend to tell them pretty much everything.

“Hello, earth to Hanni?!” Hyein piped, snapping a finger in front of her face and waving her hand in a circle dramatically.

“Eat your pasta!” Hanni lectured, gently pushing her hand back down to her food.

“Fine,” the girl huffed, pouty, “keep your thoughts from me, I thought we had a mutual agreement.”

“Hyein, I am not keeping anything—”

“—Hey guys!”

Hanni jumped from surprise, dropping her spoon up to the handle into her tomato soup. Hyein’s eyes widened in surprise, though she hadn’t jumped. The two’s conversation was cut short as their heads whipped to see Mark Lee standing there at the end of their table in his letterman, a dining hall grocery bag hooked over two fingers, looking like a boy who’d spotted people he liked from across a room and didn’t think twice about it.

His eyes raked across them, before he nervously sputtered, “sorry, are you guys — like, is this a thing? I wasn’t trying to intrude or anything.”

“Nah,” Hyein waved a hand in the air, moving her bag off the chair without a flicker, “sit.”

Hanni sent him a warm smile before picking her spoon out of her soup. Mark nodded, beaming at the two as he sets the grocery bag down and falls into the seat, fidgeting with the handle of the plastic with one finger. “Don’t worry, I’m not staying, I have a thing at two… I just noticed you guys and wanted to say what’s up,” he explains, “so — hi, what’s up, people?”

He was so painfully awkward, in an endearing way, were Hanni’s next thoughts. Hyein, on the other hand, was less impressed, as she gawked, “wow, Mark, we’re just people?”

“That came out — you know what I mean!” he cries in defense.

“I don’t know if I do, actually,” Hyein shakes her head stubbornly, chomping down on an abnormally large bite of pasta.

“My bad,” he laughed, “my friends, is that better?”

“Yes, she’s just being hard on you,” Hanni assured him.

The grin on his face clearly stated that he was pleased, pleased about being made fun of, so much so that Hanni felt something turn over unpleasantly in her ribcage. This was the problem with Mark, it had been from the beginning, from the first week when he’d asked her what is her drink order and she’d told him with delight, thinking she was helping someone love her friend correctly. Mark Lee was nice, in a way that had never once had a seam in it, and every single time Hanni sat across from him she thought, should I have told him anything at all, did I give him too much, is any of this my fault, how close must he be with Danielle?

The thoughts always made her head hurt.

“Anyway,” Mark hummed, “I actually — this is gonna sound dumb, please don’t laugh at me — I’m really stressing about Saturday.”

“Saturday,” Hyein repeats, confused and interested in what he was talking about.

Of course, he was happy to be asked. “We’re getting ramen, downtown — she said yes, it’s kind of a thing, but also, don’t make it a thing.”

The two exchanged a glance. “We’re not making it a thing,” Hanni disputed softly.

“Sounds like you’re making it a thing,” Hyein accuses sternly, “you’re totally into her.”

Mark opened his mouth then closed it again, caught off guard by the bluntness of Solar’s friend. Hanni’s neck snapped to Hyein hard enough to break. Nervously, the dorky boy scratches the back of his neck, “I mean, there’s no lying to you guys,” he chuckles, “I just don’t want it to be — like, I keep thinking she had the worst couple weeks, with you know, everything,” he gestures vaguely to the atmosphere, “so, I want it to be good, and I literally have no idea what she’d actually want to do, cause she never says, she just agrees.”

Hyein nodded along in agreement, “yep, that’s what she does.”

“Exactly, she always says sure!” Mark laughed, joyous that someone else could share his experiences.

Hanni, on the other side of the table, set down her spoon, wiping her mouth with her napkin. She was going to have to say something, otherwise Hyein would say something else in her blunt, honest way, and she was growing worried she would say something she shouldn’t.

“She likes stuff that’s calm,” Hanni leans forward to inform, “relaxed, things that aren’t noisy.” The statement was, in fact, truthful, which made her feel weird telling him.

And Mark looked at her like she’d handed him something beautiful. “Yeah, that totally makes sense,” he blustered, “I should’ve known that!” He tapped his chin with a finger in thought, “You think she’s outdoorsy, like camping or hiking, that kinda thing?”

Hyein burst into giggles, “Solar, in what world?!”

“Okay,” Mark titters, “so, no.”

“Dude, more like never.”

“She’s not un-outdoorsy!” Hanni objects, on instinct, due to the fact she was constitutionally incapable of letting anyone be described badly at a table she was sitting at, “she… she goes running.”

“On a treadmill, Hanni.”

“That’s still—“

“Well, we’re about to find out anyway,” Hyein shrugs, “with that whole thing coming up.”

They had guessed Solar had already told Mark about the Alpha Phi trip, because the boy nodded along like he’d already known and had thought of the same thing himself. “Nah, she’ll be fine,” he decides, “it’s only a few days.”

“True,” Hyein agrees.

His caramel hair fell into his eyes as he’d checked his phone, making a face at the same time. With an exhale, Mark rises to his feet, grabbing the bag, “okay, I gotta go, but thanks for the help, guys — it was helpful, for real.”

“Course, Mark,” Hanni grins politely.

“See you guys around, I’m sure,” he beams, holding two fingers to his head in a salute. Then, he’d spun on his heel and walked in the other direction, adjusting the cap on his head as he did so.

Hyein slowly went back to eating her pasta. In between bites, she mustered, “he is so—”

“Yeah,” Hanni cuts her off in agreeance, because they were likely thinking the same thing.

Hanni looked at the doors he’d gone out at for a second longer than she needed to, though she couldn’t fully explain why, before she’d come back to her sense and picked her spoon back up.

Her soup has gone cold ten minutes ago.

-

Solar had been sitting on her bed after her painfully long lecture on Tuesday morning. She should feel happy about it, but her mind was in the gutter. If she was smart, she would’ve been spending her time practicing for regionals.

She was not smart.

Oddly enough, she hadn’t seen Mark waiting outside her building. It wasn’t that she wanted him to be, though she did enjoy getting free Dutch Bros. She supposed, she was getting so used to him always being there that it was suddenly weird for him not to be. It almost felt like second nature to see him standing outside of a building for her.

She wasn’t sure how to depict the feeling it gave her.

But, instead of doing the smart thing, she was contemplating the exchange she’d had yesterday with Haechan. She’d tried to take it off her mind, but even in practice yesterday evening, she couldn’t stop ruminating. Was he upset with her? He clearly hadn’t wanted her to go, yet he was clearly not going to say it. A part of her was almost touched, almost liked it, but the other part sort of wanted to hear him object.

She hated how much it bothered her, causing her to let out an agonized groan as she fell onto the mattress, stretching her legs out until her bones popped. There was way too much going on, the Mark and Haechan situation, Danielle, her family trip, and this ridiculous camping trip she had to go on.

Way too much.

Eventually, in the midst of her mind, she realized she was going to have to do something about at least one of these things.

Then her phone started frantically buzzing next to her before she could pick it up to do what she planned to.

An Instagram call.

“What the hell…” she muttered, but slid her thumb across the screen anyway, “hello?”

There was some rustling on the other line, shifting against a surface. “There’s a full moon tonight,” he finally deadpans.

“What?” she puzzles, “Haechan, why are you calling me to tell me there’s a full moon tonight?”

“I like to go to the valley,” he hums, low toned with a side of honey, “when there’s a full moon.”

Oh, her brain processed, oh, this is an invite. He wasn’t going to actually say that, though. And perhaps, that was part of the entire problem.

“Okay,” she slowly ponders, “what time might that be?”

“Two AM.”

“I — did you just say two in the fucking morning?”

“Mhm.”

“You’ve lost your mind,” she guffaws, “I am not staying up till two in the morning.”

“Sweetheart, how many parties have you been to in the last month?”

“Irrelevant question.”

“Whatever makes you happy, pretty,” he monotones, “two AM.”

And then, he’d hung up, leaving her sitting there in disbelief, before she could open her mouth to say she was not going to stay up that late, nonetheless go meet him in the valley. This boy is insane, she decided, absolutely insane.

She stared down at her home screen for a few minutes after the line went dead. A part of her almost felt petty enough to call him back, until she decided that would be too much.

Plus, she had other plans, anyway.
